The best film of 2012 (so far, and in my opinion, of course), ARGO is a timely and completely absorbing political thriller that firmly and unequivocally establishes Ben Affleck as one of the best directors working today.  Tonally, the film strikes a perfect balance between enormous tension and some wonderful moments of levity (primarily in the movie's first half), and neither of these "moods" interferes with the effectiveness of the other.  As the lead, Affleck brings a nicely subdued quality to his performance that anchors the movie in a solid way, and he's backed-up by an estimable (and deep) roster of supporting talent, with the likes of Goodman, Arkin, and Cranston leading the way.  Affleck the director does an incredible job of creating a frighteningly credible sense of time and place, and the third act is a masterclass in film editing; indeed, even though a moderately-informed viewer will know the story's outcome, the movie is very suspenseful, and the editing is one of the chief reasons that's the case.  With GONE BABY GONE and THE TOWN, Affleck showed he had good directorial chops, but AGRO is much more than just the next step in his maturation as a director.  It's an exciting and nearly masterful work that intellectually engages and entertains the audience with equal measure.  No small accomplishment.

Argo has an awesome beginning and an awesome ending, but the middle turns out to be only mildly entertaining. It opens with an extremely angry mob of Iranians trying to get into a U.S. embassy. You can really feel the crowd's energy and the rush of the people inside flailing to get rid of classified documents as the crowd gets closer and closer. Six Americans find refuge in the Canadian Ambassador's house and hide there. Months later, Tony Mendez (played by the fantastic director Ben Affleck) comes up with an idea to get the six people back home: disguise them as a film crew for a movie called Argo. I was amazed at the detail of everything; from hairstyles to television sets, everything about Argo is a dead-on match with its time period (1979-80). I really liked the cast as well; Ben Affleck, Bryan Cranston, and John Goodman are all great in their roles. The ending was an incredibly tense, edge-of-your-seat affair, despite being a bit predictable. It's a great film, but I can't deny that Affleck's previous two directing credits (Gone Baby Gone and The Town) are both better. Argo is still a really great movie that I can see being better with repeated viewings. Original score: 8/10.
UPDATE: Now that I've seen it twice, I can happily report that I liked it more the second time. Revised score: 9/10.

A professionally crafted piece, Argo is a classy and reserved film that pays off in a tense final act.  The story is an interesting one that captures the Iran hostage crisis from one, relatively sanitized angle, a markedly less perfunctory exercise than The Town.  Various entertaining preparation activities occur in the US on the fake film-side of things, which later progresses to the more sober Iranian action and tense escape.  The 1970s Iranian setting of the story makes it more interesting than either of Affleck's previous Boston films.  Ben Affleck gives a quiet, quality acting performance, definitely feeling more comfortable in his skin with each film he makes.  John Goodman and Alan Arkin are perfect as the Hollywood members of the operation and Cranston is fine as Affleck's CIA supervisor.  Victor Garber is also good as the Canadian Ambassador.  In terms of visceral impact, it felt pretty PG-13 and didn't really need the R rating besides for language.  Istanbul stands in somewhat acceptably as Tehran, though easily different compared to the actual Tehran of A Separation.  Easily spotted CGI is used to Tehranify Istanbul, adding mountains or monuments.  Great attention to detail is evident, as I didn't notice any obvious anachronisms in its portrayal of 1970s Hollywood and Tehran.  The production design was downplayed compared to the sparkly 70s of Dark Shadows, but felt more real as a result.  Despite having the same cinematographer as Brokeback Mountain, and the Inarritu films, the look was sober, bordering on drab.  Though this film and its somewhat interesting 1970s story represent course correction from the massively overrated Town, the overall experience is still a little too reserved or stylistically conservative to be any more than an effective, but fleeting human story.  Though I do believe he will get there, Affleck is perhaps still perhaps two echelons away from making his first great film. (19 October 2012)

There is a scene in the The Town where Ben Affleck's Doug MacRay is attempting to cover a certain clue on Jeremy Renner's James Coughlin that could give away both of their identities to an unsuspecting Claire Keesey (Rebecca Hall). In this single scene Ben Affleck, the director, is able to put his audience in the most vulnerable of states as we feel as exposed to the possibility of this guys entire world shattering around him as he does. We are set in this moment and the tension is palpable. Affleck clearly has a gift for creating these types of moments on film that all have to do with pacing as he creates moment after moment of such suspense in his third directorial effort Argo. After exploring the cinematic landscape of his hometown of Boston in his first two films Affleck now seems to have the confidence to venture outside of this comfort zone and take on a story that deals with issues in the bigger scope of the world. What Affleck has now gone on to accomplish is to create what feels like a very authentic period piece that pulses with intrigue and keeps its audience first informed, second engaged, and third on the edge of their seat. It was clear from the vintage opening credits to the storyboard history lesson we receive in the first moments of the film that set the stage for the relationship between the United States and Iran at the time that everything here was meticulously planned out in order to elicit and implement the specific kinds of reactions and thoughts it wanted. This, for me, only exemplifies the kind of director Affleck is and shows us the care in which he takes on each project even if his craft does receive more attention because of his name. The point is the craft deserves the attention.

Based on true events, this is the riveting story of a joint covert operation between the CIA and the Canadian government to rescue 6 American diplomats trapped in Tehran during the Iran Hostage Crisis of the late 70s/early 80s. The six managed to escape the U.S. Embassy and find shelter with the Canadian Consul. But just because they were they doesn't mean they were out of harms way.

Besides directing and producing, Affleck stars as CIA exfiltration expert Tony Mendez. The plan he comes up with as a cover for the rescue operation is a great one: he gets Hollywood makeup artist/occasional CIA consultant John Chambers to help him (along with film producer Lester Siegel) create a fake science fantasy adventure film called Argo that is to be shot in the Middle East, with Tony and the six diplomats posing as the film crew.

The film has a top notch cast, with John Goodman as Chambers, Oscar nominated Alan Arkin as SIegel, and various other roles filled by Bryan Cranston Victor Garber, Taylor Schilling, and RIchard Kind, Kyle Chandler, and a crap load of others. Of the six people playing the diplomats, the most notable (for me at least) were Clea DuVall and Rory Cochrane (Slater from Dazed and Confused. All of these people, no matter how brief their appearance, are all rock solid. The film is somewhat unbalanced as far as extreme depth and development go, but we get just enough to keep people from being totally one dimensional. 

The story is fascinating, and really holds your attention, rarely letting up. Yeah, some fabrications are done to heighten the tension, drama, and make the story more cinematically exciting, but those are minor quibbles. I just honestly can't believe that the central ruse that was used is actually true. I have a love/hate thing with the CIA, but this idea was cool, but maybe that's just because I'm a sucker for movie making and films about it. Maybe the biggest gripe I have is the interpretative change that the movie does by downplaying the role of the Canadian government and putting the emphasis on the CIA. They could have found a way to make it more balanced, but it may have resulted in a longer, more expensive film, so I guess I can let it go.

The film is well shot, tightly edited, Affleck gives some solid direction, and the look of this film is great. The costumes, hairstyles, and touches done to bring the time period alive are impeccable. Like many, I'm bummed that Affleck was snubbed a directing nod, but at least that was made up for by the film winning best picture (nabbing him a statue since he also produced it). The music ain't too shabby, either.

One could argue that the release of the film isn't exactly timely, and the portrayal of Iranians is a little insensitive, but given the subject matter, it is rather fitting and true to the era. All in all, this is a sterling piece of work, and one I have no trouble recommending.

To act decisively, making the right call at the right time, is an art form which can mean the difference between life and death. Much in the same way that authenticity in the performances can separate mediocrity from a dynamite movie. Argo, on all levels, is an impressive epitome of the latter. With meticulous attention to detail, it re-recreates the tumultuous period that is revolutionary Iran in the late 70's. An agitated mob, infuriated by recent events involving their former and USA-friendly Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, has breached the American embassy in Teheran and taken the personnel hostage. Six of them manage to escape, but fall into unimaginable peril. Argo is the true story of the CIA-Canadian joint operation whose objective was to get them home to safety. A mission so secret, that it wasn't declassified to the public until 1997, by President Bill Clinton. Odds are grim and alternatives few. Tony Mendez, an exfiltration expert, hatches an idea so daring that it might actually work: to venture to Iran under the cloak of a phony film project (ostensibly entitled Argo) and via false documents smuggle out the Americans as part of the production crew. It's intrepid, adrenaline-ridden and not seldom with your heart in your throat. A situation so charged, that the nerves are strained to their breaking point and the air seem all but squeezed from your lungs. Surely, it's been spiced up a bit in the highly intense suspense segments. It is, despite everything, not a straight-out documentary. Even so, it thoroughly comes off as a legitimate depiction of this in many ways interesting coup de maître. Ben Affleck, now warm in his director's chair, scores his third straight bullseye. That he has furthermore assembled some of Hollywood's crème-de-la-crème (encompassing within the comically supreme John Goodman and Breaking Bad's Bryan Cranston) creates more than enough Argo-ments to see and relish this extraordinary political thriller. http://www.facebook.com/pages/Mikes-Movie-Reviews/281824101875153?ref=hl

When the movie opened, I was awe-struck by the superb directing. The classic and virtuoso craft of combining real life footage of the Iran raid on the U.S. embassy in 1979 mixed with filming of a reenactment was genius. That is Academy Award Winner Ben Affleck for you (Good Will Hunting, The Town, Shakespeare In Love). Not only does Affleck bring such power to this leading role, but he gives his heart and soul in a performance that is without a doubt the best acting performance I have seen him give since Good Will Hunting. Thank you, Mr. Affleck for crafting one of the best films I have seen this year, and prepare yourself for the Academy Awards with Mr. Arkin, Mr. Cranston, and Mr. Goodman, because you have a major hit on your hands.

Argo is a dynamite thriller that takes a story based on true events and makes it work as a high stakes suspense feature.  Regardless of whatever facts may have been embellished or altered for the sake of the film, Argo works very well because it has a grounded sense of reality and a terrific cast, chock-full of character actors, all providing understated performances that do not attempt to overthrow the strength of the overall story.  It also benefits from having a 70s-style handle on the type of thriller it is, positioning it well amongst other well-plotted old school films.  Argo is about one thing, and it achieves that by working as a rock solid caper/rescue mission film, with some great direction from star Ben Affleck.

Performance wise in my opinion Alan Arkin seems to steal the show as a big time Hollywood mogul and Bryan Cranston fleshes out his supporting role nicely. The movie opens with an old-school Warner Bros. logo, and we're suddenly transported to 1979 and 1980. And the film hasn't even started. Argo has received widespread acclaim and plenty of public announcements and discourse from director/actor Ben Affleck. On almost every news channel both national and local this film and director were mentioned. It had me thinking of Kevin Smith's outlandish appraisals for Ben Affleck. At the time I heard Smith explode about how great Affeck is, I just rolled my eyes. For years, Ben Affleck seemed to be an afterthought only to be dismissed each time audiences saw the latest promo for an upcoming flick. He's had an acting career consisting of ridicule despite some being hits, something that had even me doubting he ever co-wrote Good Will Hunting which earned him and buddy Matt Damon an Oscar. Affleck always had this goofy, boyish heartthrob presence especially when he sobbed manly tears of bad acting. He was just a pretty boy and no matter how hard he tried to show-off his acting chops and film roles, he was often given the shaft. For a good half of the last decade, he just seemed to be in a rut at least until he made his directorial debut in Gone Baby Gone, which I have to say again, is one of the best dramas and gut-wrenching films of the last five years. And people realized that he's better behind the camera. Then The Town was released, which was equally just as good. And here we are with Argo.

For a thriller, it's very fast-paced. The fastest two hours I've sat through in a while. Guess it shows how invigorating the story is. By all means it's a great story, and a unique one at that. Text, narration, and archived news reporting let viewers know right away what is up. During the Iran Revolution and hostage crisis that took place in the late '70s to the early '80s, the US Embassy was stormed by the locals taking 50+ hostages, but six Americans fled and hid at the Canadian embassy unbeknownst to local Iranians. The CIA needs to act quick before the revolutionaries discover that six Americans are unaccounted for. They come up with some rather terrible plans like sending in fake bike instructors (so the hostages can bide-ride 300 miles to safety); the only person with common sense is CIA extraction specialist Tony Mendez (Ben Affleck) who points out the flaws in these proposed plans but doesn't have a plan of his own until a viewing of Battle for the Planet of the Apes gives him inspiration: create a fake Canadian movie project scouting exotic film locations for a cheap sci-fi movie called "Argo." Sounds almost like bad filmmaking but as we know, truth certainly is stranger than fiction.

There are three different tones of the film. One is the CIA, which is as bureaucratic as they come (like exposition stops, but also leads into character development), the second is the Hollywood scenes with John Goodman and Alan Arkin which are light-hearted and funny (like a breather from all the real-world conflicts at the time), and the third are the scenes in Iran where it's tense and dangerous. None feel out of place, they're evenly sequenced and create atmosphere. Some of you may know how the story resolves but Argo still manages to create thrills without the use of violence or usual Hollywood chicanery (outside of creative liberties). I like how sometimes simplicity is grandeur than overly elaborate ruses.

If there's one complaint or two, it's the thin character development. They seemed rushed which in turn makes the story itself seemed rushed. I felt like stuff were cut for time, and though this is a nearly two-hour film, it zips by fast. Again, it's invigorating but I felt like something was missed. They just listed facts and got the setting and time period down to a T, and that's good, but whoever wrote the story didn't have a knack for character development. Everyone in turn also came off as stock characters so there's no emotional attachment like there was in Gone Baby Gone and The Town. Because of this thin characterization, sometimes the dialogue didn't fit. Still, there are memorable likes like, "Argo fuck yourself." Now that's a tagline, fitting especially for a late 1970s/early 1980s movie (has a sleazy ring to it). And this movie is funny, did I mention that? Rapid-fire banter and wits but not too hip that it sticks out like a sore thumb. Alan Arkin and Bryan Cranston have some of the best lines. Another part of the film's charm is the replication of the time period. Historical inaccuracies notwithstanding, this looks like it was made in the 1970s/1980s. The clothing that looks itchy, the vintage accessories, the cool-looking vehicles, the grainy film quality, the horrendous hairstyles, the dilapidated Hollywood sign... all top-notch.

Want a good slice of American history, check out Argo. Despite my own nitpicking (and I'm sure historians will rage and have a field day with this flick), it stands as another achievement for Ben Affleck. This may be his most widely accessible film yet. Some critics hail it as his best film which it very well may be. My favorite is still The Town. Nevertheless, Argo is one of the year's best films.

Argo is the drama that I had been looking forward to the most in 2012. After being disappointed by the numerous summer blockbusters this year, I was hoping to watch a great drama. I got a funny, intense, crowd-pleasing drama that unfortunately lacked memorable characters and therefore wasn't as engaging as it could have been.

Argo is a movie based on the true story of the rescue of six Americans in the Iran hostage crisis. The movie starts out with an enthralling, intense scene where the US embassy in Tehran is stormed by militants. Six of the Americans are able to escape, and they are hidden in the home of the Canadian ambassador. After that, Ben Affleck's character is introduced, and he makes the plan to rescue the Americans by pretending to be a Canadian film crew filming a Star Wars ripoff in an exotic location. While setting this up, Affleck's character comes into contact with John Goodman's character; a make-up artist, and Alan Arkin's character; a film producer. Most of the comedy takes place in the scenes with these aforementioned characters, and it usually produced a few chuckles. The laughs die down when Affleck's character enters Iran, and the movie becomes quite intense again. We spend more time with the escapees, but unfortunately, they are all quite one-note. There are too many characters and not enough time to properly develop all of them. I can't remember any of their names, or even their physical appearances. Audiences probably let out a sigh of relief when the Americans safely made it back to the US. The ending is pretty satisfying, but it would have been a considerably better if the film had been more engaging.

Though I am giving this film an 8/10, I can't help but feel disappointed. The cinematography is good, the production design is great, the cast is talented, the editing is good, but the film ultimately failed to connect with me in any sort of significant way.

Argo is the Academy Award Winner for Best Picture of 2012, and while it was an amazing film, the actual story was far less interesting. In 1980, the tensions between Iran and The United States began, and the U.S. embassy in Tehran was overrun. Hundreds were held hostage for over a year, but six did manage to escape and went into hiding. Knowing that their lives were even more in danger than those of the hostages, the C.I.A. developed a unique plan to get them out of Iran. They sent in one of their top agents, with credentials claiming that he was part of a Canadian film crew. Armed with fake documents, he would smuggled the six out of the country. The film was intense and featured one close call after another, but in reality, getting them out was almost too easy. They were never stopped or questioned, and slipped out under the cover of early morning, without a hitch, but what kind of a movie would that be? Once these classified files were released by the U.S. Government, Hollywood saw the chance to tell this story in an extreme manor, and did so much to the delight of audiences and much to the chagrin of the other countries involved. Ben Affleck both stars and directs this film, and while everyone raves about his performance, I thought it was typically cold and flat. Ben Affleck wasn't interesting, the character he played was. Affleck wasn't any more likeable or skillful here than he was in any other role and that's why he didn't win best actor. I've said it before and I'll say it again, the man is a fantastic Director, but a very mediocre actor. That being said, the extreme locations and huge cast, were his biggest challenge to date as a Director, and I was very impressed by the way he managed to pull it off. Argo is based on a true story, it's fast paced, and even though we all know what happened before seeing the film, it's still an edge of your seat thriller that really shouldn't be missed.

Argo is about the astonishing true story of a CIA specialist, who concocts the "best bad idea" to free 6 Americans who are hiding in the home of the Canadian Ambassador during the Iranian hostage crisis. The story begins with Islamist militants mobbing and crashing their way into the U.S. Embassy in Iran. 50 some Americans are taken hostage and held for 444 days. However, 6 Americans snuck out of the Embassy and find refuge without the Iranian rebels noticing. The CIA, lead by agent Tony Mendez, greatly played by the director, Ben Affleck, hatches a plan to rescue the house-entrapped Americans by posing as a producer of a fictional sci-fi movie. Mendez' plan was to arrive in Iran and convince the 6 Americans to assume identities as directors, producers, screenwriters, and camera crew of the movie. Then they would all fly out of the country together claiming they were in Iran to scout locations for the fake movie. In order for the mission to look legit, Mendez recruits a Hollywood producer (Alan Arkin) and Special Effects guy (John Goodman) to approve the script and give the fake movie credibility. No part of the plan is made up for dramatic sequences, Affleck sticks to the facts of the true events and gives a nail-biter type thriller that is guaranteed to be the top contender for Best Picture. In the last 20 minutes of the film you will be on the edge of your seat even if you're aware of the outcome. I saw Argo about 2 months after it was released in theaters with a small audience... as the rescue attempt hits its ending, audience members applauded. Feedback like that goes to show you how Affleck's direction grabs you by the heartstrings and how much we care about the fates of the characters.

As the director of the extraordinary fact-based story Argo, Ben Affleck is firing on all cylinders. Argo is bristling with pulse-pounding pace, humor and suspense, and it's easily one of 2012's best. Argo is also a departure for the Oscar-winning screenwriters, taking Affleck out of his native Boston where his first two films were set (Gone Baby Gone and The Town) in favor of the global stage, specifically Tehran, Iran circa 1979, when Iranians stormed the U.S. embassy and held 52 Americans hostage for 444 days. Affleck details the attack marvelously, showing how it was attacked by Islamic student militants and how six U.S. embassy staffers escaped but desperately needed help leaving the country. It all adds up to a terrifically exciting thriller, one based on fact, but also one that doesn't fudge facts so much you want to throttle it.

Although Argo isn't Hollywood-ized to the point of inanity, it was Hollywood that had a hand in rescuing the six embassy employees. Top CIA extractor Tony Mendez (Affleck, wonderful, and underplaying his role nicely) recruits a dream team to help him rescue the escapees, currently hiding out at the home of Canadian ambassador Ken Taylor (Victor Garber). Mendez not only poses as a Canadian film producer looking to scout locations in Iran for a sci-fi epic called Argo, but he must also school the six escapees to convincingly play members of a film crew. The scenes of Mendez putting together a sham film is ripe with satire, and a welcome respite from the tension. There's casting calls, production meetings, even posters made. Mendez gets help from real-life Oscar-winning make-up artist John Chambers (John Goodman, way excellent) and Lester Siegel (Alan Arkin), a composite of just about every film producer you could think of. Arkin is comic gold, nailing every cynical line.

And believe me, you'll love the shenanigans Arkin and Goodman bring, even as the tension rises, especially in one great scene of the gang walking through the Grand Bazaar.

The whole film climaxes in its final third, and it's in this set piece that officially cements Affleck as a first-class filmmaker. Kudos too to Chris Terrio for his amazing script that deftly puts all the major elements in motion, namely Mendez and his more than nervous crew as they attempt to flee the country via the airport. As CIA boss Jack O'Donnell (Bryan Cranston) says, the whole operation was the 'best bad idea' the agency could ever come up with. Chamber and Siegel man the fake film in L.A., while the Canadians get much of the credit.

The Argo operation remained top secret until it was declassified in 1997 by President Clinton, but it's no less timely or timeless today given current events. Shot by the extraordinary Rodrigo Prieto, with Istanbul playing Tehran, Argo is filled to the brim with pulse-pounding energy. It's so good you won't even mind the spiced up climax, with its chase down the tarmac. No worries. One of the year's best.

Ben Affleck is a really interesting figure in modern cinema. He's one of America's most popular stars, yet it's not easy to name why other than his association with Matt Damon. He's been criticized for being the exact same character in every role, and took the criticism. Then he made a complete 180. Suddenly, Ben Affleck, the quintessential handsome white American movie star, is proven to be a very talented crime director. I liked Gone Baby Gone, I thought The Town was pretty good, but I usually would never expect Ben Affleck to create the tension and pacing that he does. So we come to Argo: Affleck's first spy thriller, one of the best in recent years.

It's 1979, the eve of Iran's cultural revolution. The Ayatollah Khomeini has returned, and the United States has angered the revolutionaries by offering the ousted Shah asylum. Protestors take over the American embassy and hold over fifty employees hostage. But six intelligence workers escape and hide out in the Canadian ambassador's house. It's only a matter of time before they're discovered, and the CIA is stumped. But exfil expert Tony Mendez (Ben Affleck) comes up with an idea: have the workers pose as his Canadian film crew, pretend to be scouting for a crappy sci-fi movie called Argo, and have them fly out together. It's a huge gamble, but when the camera rolls, they gotta roll with it.

One piece of advice: don't look up the actual operation Argo is based on; it makes the film much more effective. Not knowing the ending allowed me to notice a lot more in the film, and as a result I enjoyed it a great deal. Argo is a movie based in detail; there is a huge effort put into making everything look like it did then, from how cities and people look and talk to the way scenes are constructed based on photos and stock footage. Ben Affleck makes a real and successful push to make sure his audience feels the intense atmosphere of the situation. As a result the script works much better with the direction, and it's much easier to get invested in the story and characters.

And Argo's characters are what makes it worth watching. The direction, the script, and the cinematography are all great, but the characters shine as the driving force behind the film. The great Bryan Cranston is great as Affleck's boss, John Goodman is as fun as always as a famous makeup artist, and Alan Arkin steals the show as Argo's foul-mouthed producer. Even the minor characters have done a lot of research into their roles and try to bring their all. They portray the seriousness and tension of the story, the most important part of the film, very well and very convincingly. As such Argo manages to stay realistic and dark but also funny and exciting.

Like last year's Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy, Argo is a great step forward for spy movies. Keep in mind that "spy movie" is basically just a synonym for "James Bond" in popular culture. But as a big fan of John Le Carre and classic thrillers of the forties and fifties, I like stories that are meticulous and dense, with realistic characters, actions, and tons of tension. James Bond is a character whose adventures have no stakes and no real consequences, whereas in Tinker Taylor and Argo, the stakes are very high and the consequences dire. Knowing this film is a true story only impresses this. Argo is genuine; the story and screenplay are good, the acting is great, and the direction is very well done. GO undercover and see Argo.

After knowing and understanding, this movie has such a high ceiling and I could not wait to be able to watch it. 
	Based on true events, Argo is a story about a covert operation to rescue six Americans involved in the Iran hostage crisis. On November 4, 1979, Iranian militants blow open the U.S. embassy in Tehran and take forty plus Americans hostage. But in the middle of all that chaos, six Americans manage to escape out a back door and are taken in by the Canadian Ambassador. As America knows it's only a matter of time before the six are found to be alive and likely killed, a CIA "exfil" specialist Tony Mendez (Ben Affleck) comes up with an incredibly risky plan to get them out safely and back home.
	Every movie Affleck either directs (Gone Baby, Gone and The Town) or stars in (Good Will Hunting and Pearl Harbor), they all seem to be instant hits. He has starred in and directed some pretty incredible movies through his day, but I think his best one yet is Argo. From the screenplay to the script to the acting, it all seems to be exact and on perfect point. The writing of this movie was just mind-blowing, every scene was critical and there was never a dull moment. To be able to go from early November of 1979 to late January of 1980 in a span of two hours, put every important part that's needed, and it be loved across the country is pretty special. But that's what Affleck does. 
	Not only was this film deep in thrilling and fact-based scenes, but it had a star studded killer cast. With Ben Affleck in the main role, he is surrounded by Alan Arkin, Bryan Cranston, John Goodman, Kyle Chandler, Rory Cochrane, Victor Garber, Richard Kind, and Michael Parks. Without the cast this movie had, it wouldn't be what it was. Every role was so important and delicate to portray, everyone involved from Mendez (Affleck) to the hostages to everyone else. Every role had a significant cameo and was decisive for this movie to succeed. And every single person did an extremely good job playing their parts, especially those who played the hostages, who were so critical to this movie. 
	Trying to recreate a past event can be very difficult to do in a movie. Trying to recreate a past event that is so important to our history in a movie, that is more difficult then all. But Affleck and his team have been able to do that and much more with Argo. The entire movie is spot on from beginning to end about such an extremely important part of our history, the film is a total triumph. Argo is an well written and directed film with a spell-binding story, thrilling and intense drama, and ferociously exciting to watch. Affleck and his crew did not only research this event incredibly well, but they used every fact to their advantage. With every scene as real as the day it happened, Argo is a smart film with incredibly good acting, a suspenseful middle, and a hell of an ending that you truly won't want to miss.

Ben Affleck has finally found that happy medium between caring about characters and caring about plot. While watching Gone Baby Gone I felt like I didn't much care about the discovery of the little girl after a while, I was more interested with the main character's relationship with everyone he met. That didn't ruin the movie, but it made it less than what it could have been. However, with Argo Ben Affleck knew how to include many characters into a scene, draw an emotional connection to each one, then focus on the plot. We don't need to keep going deeper into the John Chambers character or each of the characters stuck in the Canadian embassy. We understand they're terrified and want out. Perhaps they have more family at home they miss, or maybe they want to speak to someone that haven't spoken to in years. But that doesn't matter. What matters here is Tony Mendez trying to get the six people out of the embassy without any kind of big attack. If the American troops fight their way in then it will cause an all-out war. These six will probably die. And he already feels guilty for letting 44 people in Tehran to get captured. He feels so guilty that we can feel it on him every single second he's on screen. The undercurrent of his motivation is always around, which really makes me believe that Ben Affleck deserves a best actor nomination. The movie opens with the American embassy in Tehran getting overthrown and six people escaping out of a secret exit. It's tense and really well done. The story picks back up almost three months later and the CIA is called in to bring these six people out. That's why they ask Mendez to get involved. He's the best of the best and knows how to do stuff like this. The only problem is that almost all of the Canadians are gone and there aren't many people left in Tehran. The best option for their escape is to give them bikes and have them cross the border of Iran. Mendez can't help but laugh at this idea. 300 miles in the middle of the winter. There's no way. Instead he suggests after speaking to his son that they make a fake science fiction movie that could possibly shoot in Tehran and bring in a location scout. The six will pose as people in charge of making the movie and they will leave by pretending to be Canadian citizens. It's a crazy idea. The ridiculousness of everything makes it more fun when he starts to weave in comedy with the heavy drama. The final scene of the film works really well even though it never happened. It's tense to see these people try to get on the plane with the Iranian soldiers all around. I don't think I've had as much fun with a close-call scenario in such a long time. Affleck says he was inspired by All the President's Men for most of the dialogue scenes with the CIA, and it comes off very well. Argo is easily one of the best films of the year and it deserves every bit of praise it received.

One of the Best Movies of 2012, Ben Affleck is proving himself to be quite the director.  Argo is based on unbelievable-but-true events that led to the release of Iranian-held American hostages (52 of them) after the fall of the western-friendly Shah of Iran in 1979 after six of them secretly fled the American embassy to take refuge with the Canadian ambassador in Tehran.  As the Iranian Revolution raged on, a CIA operative (Ben Affleck) comes up with a fantastical plan of resucing the six hostages before they are discovered missing by posing as a part of a Canadian film crew scouting locations for the next Star Wars-esque motion picture.  To set up a cover and make the production appear legit, a Hollywood producer and director (John Goodman, Alan Arkin) are brought on board to lend credence to the entire orchestration.  The film is tense and taut and quickly paced.  Affleck wisely cuts much of the drama with the hilarity of Hollywood lavish-ness which makes the film a crowd-pleaser as it isn't all nail-biting suspense.  That we know how the hostage crisis ends doesn't matter ... the film is pure escapist reality Hollywood-ized into a docu-drama of a time of the past --- a time when politics didn't matter like they do today.  Americans were in trouble and neither party played a crisis against the other ... today that would be complete fiction; but in Argo it was the way it was.  I applaud Mr. Affleck for reminding us of who we should be.

The real difference in this film compared with Afflecks other noteworthy directorial pursuits (The Town, Gone Baby Gone) is the polished feel and a clearly developed sense of style. While "Argo" has a very distinct Soderberg like feel to it, it also has a gritty quality that is a recurring substance in Affleck's movies. The movie plays out much as you would suspect, seeing as the story is based on historical events, but, the humor, the emotion, the pacing, these are where "Argo" truly shines. Easily one of this years best films and, in my opinion, the early leader for "Best Picture", "Argo" delivers on every front and is an absolute must see.

Argo is educational but it suffers from being too specific. The Iranian hostage crisis is an event that could be covered with fascinating detail but the majority of the film deals with six hostages in the Canadian ambassador's house. This declassified information is interesting (and the C.I.A. mission is undoubtedly heroic) but I feel like it isn't enough to fill up a 2 hour film. The beginning scene is frantic and filled with quick dialogue but everything follows is laboriously paced. Even the climatic scene where the six American hostages escape from the airport is way too long. It is sickening in its suspense but it is too mundane to be emotional. 

None of the characters are fully developed. Ben Affleck's character is devoid of any personality. And no character is made out to be complex. Even Bryan Cranston, who is excellent without having to try, is given the part of a man who yells a lot at the end of the film. Even the American hostages are one note characterizations.

The science fiction aspect of the film is insubstantial. There is a scene in the middle of the film that cuts between hostages in Iran being mentally tortured juxtaposed with actors doing a reading for the fake film "Argo". The scenes being intercut with each other felt like they were supposed to have some emotional resonance when the fake movie aspect of the film has no meaning. It is an amusing note in an otherwise more interesting story. Alan Arkin and John Goodman get in some good quips about Hollywood but it all feels out of place in this movie and irrelevant.

The large majority of the film has important government people having conversations that all basically say the same thing: "This mission is unlikely to work." Over and over again that is thrown in the audience's face. Instead of genuine suspense being built from multilayered scenarios, we get boring scenes between one dimensional characters restating how difficult smuggling the hostages out of Iran will be.

I appreciate that the film never glorifies American values too much. Even Ben Affleck's character is told that his role is essentially thankless. And there are hints throughout the film that America helped contribute to the horribly intense conflicts in Iran. But I have to wonder why Ben Affleck made this film at all. I agree this mission is to be celebrated but I think two hours is much too long to talk about a singular event in an otherwise bigger movement.

Argo is a well-crafted riveting thriller with an unrelenting sense of purpose and tension as it tells the (mostly true) story of six American diplomats who were exfiltrated from Iran in the wake of the Iranian Revolution in 1979. Director and star Ben Affleck has proven himself as an emerging leader in this type of film making with his previous films, and Argo establishes him in that company. Affleck smartly balances the tension of the events with darkly comic moments, mainly provided by the Hollywood office of Seigel (Arkin) and Chambers (Goodman), but he never allows those moments to steal from the story. There are a lot of layers to Argo - Hollywood, the CIA, Iran, Canada, the hostages, the White House, the setting of 1980 - and Affleck keeps them all balanced well. His performance is surprisingly deep, in the vein of what might have been expected of a young Al Pacino or contemporaries like George Clooney (who, perhaps unsurprisingly, served as one of the producers of this film).  One of the downfalls of the film is some of the liberty it takes in creating that tension by inventing events or tweaking the interpretation of the roles of the people involved, even as it seems to pride itself on its historical accuracy (particularly in recreating a number of the iconic photos from the crisis). This is not present in the film itself, but a cursory examination into the real history of the events takes away somewhat from what Affleck accomplishes here. I wish that Affleck had had the wherewithal to avoid the overt American patriotism and to stick to the story a little more closely, and also to be more sympathetic in his portrayal of the Iranian people, but perhaps part of the irony of the film is that it is a product of the system, even as it satirizes the way in which Hollywood operates and pushes itself as a system. The film itself is a fantastic thriller, an entertaining examination of entertainment and government in a past era, and one of the best films of the year.

Basada en hechos reales, ARGO relata la situacion de vida o muerte que tuvieron que enfrentar los operativos que llevaron a cabo un rescate de 6 diplomaticos americanos, que develaron los secretos de una crisis de rehenes en Iran, cosa que fue oculta al publico durante decadas. Cuando la revolucion Irani llega a su punto intenso, militares asaltan a la embajada de los Estados Unidos en Teheran, llevandose a 52 amricanos como rehenes, pero solo 6 se las arreglaron para huir y esconderse de ellos, encontrando refugio en la casa de un embajador Canadiense. Solo es cuestion de tiempo para que los 6 sean encontrados y asesinados. La CIA al enterarse de esta situacion, solicitan la ayuda de Tony Mendez (Ben Affleck) para ejecutar un plan demasiado peligroso para sacar a los 6 de Iran, El plan consiste en hacerlos pasar por estrellas de cine que estan filmando una "pelicula" de ciencia ficcion llamada ARGO, haciendo que el plan sea demasiado peligroso, tanto que solo se veria en las peliculas.
Dirigida, producida y protagonizada por Ben Affleck, ARGO es simplemente su obra maestra, es algo que cono toda tranquilidad puede llamar suyo. Vale destacar que este filme marca la tercera vez en la que Affleck hace un buen uso se sus habilidades para dirigir, esta vez tomando una historia basada en un evento clasificado como uno de los mas volatiles en 50 anos. ARGO cuenta con una gran elenco de estrellas aparte de Affleck. Bryan Cranston se mete en la piel del asistente general de la CIA Jack O' Donnell, una de sus mejores lineas es cuando le dice a uno de sus superiores que "Esta es la mejor mala idea que hemos tenido hasta ahora." Tambien esta John Goodman como un pionero en el arte del maquillaje en escena, John Chambers y Alan Arkin como Lester Siegel, un productor que ayuda a que la pelicula falsa se sienta tan real como nunca. Los 4 actores hacen de ARGO una solida entrega de suspenso y drama que incorpora varios elementos de los anos 70 y tambien tiene sus momentos divertidos. Aparte del elenco estelar tambien estan los 6 americanos que antes del caos estaban procesando visas haciendo ventas y luego intentando escapar de furiosos Iranis, todas estas emociones se ven bien transmitidas hacia el publico. Ben Affleck: Director, productor y protagonista de su propia pelicula, se las arreglo para hacer una gran pelicula en base a un material clasificado. ARGO simplemente es la mejor pelicula del 2012 y es seguro que estara nominada a varios premios Oscar.

A movie that'll make you sweat bullets right until the end, "Argo" cements Ben Affleck's status as one of the best actor-turned-directors.  Heck, if Affleck had decided to simply act, his career would be over.  Thank God he took the chance.  "Argo" is the kind of movie he directs best-- dark, suspenseful, and tense.  Based on a true story, "Argo" takes place in 1979-1980: there's been a riotous Iranian revolution in Iraq, and because of the situation, six Americans escape-- but become trapped in the house of the home of the Canadian ambassador in the process.  After a few weeks, the CIA decides to intervene, and Tony Mendez (Ben Affleck) is put to the job.  Following much thought, Mendez makes up a complex plot-- pretend to make a movie in order to get them out of Iraq.  It's outlandish, but with the help of a big-time producer (Alan Arkin) and a make-up artist (John Goodman), the decision begins to look a bit more realistic.  But when he arrives in Iraq, Mendez has all sorts of problems-- and getting the six hostages out of Iraq may be a bit harder than he believed.  From the minute "Argo" starts, we become aware of the situation, and almost immediately we're glued to the screen: we know something bad's going to happen.  Affleck grabs our attention, and slowly but surely the plot unfolds, with wry, dark comedy that makes every situation believable.  The '70's lure is an added bonus to the fun, but the fact that this really happened makes the slow wait even more absorbing.  The wait is eventually worth it-- once we get into Iraq, the film commands out attention, and shakes us.  It's so intense and suspenseful, that every minute you wish there was a fast-forwading option.  "Argo" is so well-written, so smart, and so well-directed, that it will for sure be one of the leading Oscar movies of 2012.  Recommended.

Superb. An extremely tense true-life spy drama which, like all the best true spy stories, is so incredible as to be almost unbelievable. It's 1980 and the Iranian Revolution has begun. The US Embassy in Tehran is overrun and everyone inside is taken hostage...except for 6 staff who escape via a back door, and are given shelter in the Canadian Amabassador's home. Cue a frantic race against time as the CIA plans to extract them from Iran before they are uncovered. The idea? Build a cover story that the six are all Canadian members of a Hollywood movie production company, location-scouting for a Star Wars ripoff film in pre-production called "Argo", and bring them out on their false identities. It sounds far-fetched and alsmost farcical - indeed there are plenty of moments that raise a laugh - but the genius of the film, and the true story, is the lengths that are gone to in order to make the fake film production seem genuine. Ben Affleck has become an excellent and bankable director with this as his follow-up to the great crime drama "The Town". The story flows superbly here, accelerating to a real edge-of-seat nailbiting third act as the plan is in motion on the streets of Tehran. The period authenticity and attention to detail are all on show, from the clothes and hairstyles to the background props, and the recreation of real scenes copied from old media. The six at the centre of the story are all cast by unknowns - but that is the point, to make them anonymous - however they are complemented by a supporting cast of the highest calibre. This is a classic and highly rewarding film, one of the best spy thrillers in years.

The Short: Argo is smart, politically potent, sharply written, incredibly well directed and chock full of important ideas and messages - all while being entertaining and enjoyable by even the most pedestrian of movie-goers.  Argo is a tough film to review.  Not because it is a tough film to swallow - quite the opposite.  Argo is the "Inception" of historical political thrillers.  Sure, on the surface Argo is a historical political thriller.  But digging deeper Argo is so much more.  Argo is a meta homage to science fiction film, an unexpectedly exciting look at an event that changed history, an often times funny and laugh out loud comedy, an intense and exciting thriller, all while being a smart and incredibly potent political statement along with taking a sharp and incredibly smart stab at Hollywood.  Yeah, that's a lot to digest, I know.  But the brilliant thing about it?  Argo presents all of these major ideas and messages so incredibly well.  It doesn't become muddled, cloudy, or boring.  Rather, Argo is a slow-burner that keeps you invested by continually introducing elements that have never been effectively used in a historical thriller, which it does it rather well.  Argo doesn't fall prey to the long and droning office banter that most historically "accurate" thrillers offer, but rather changes the sets, characters, and scenery frequently.  From Iran to Hollywood to Washington and back, Argo progressively feels something like a Bourne or James Bond "secret agent" style flick, and while it never features intense shootouts or the quick elimination of a room of bad guys in a stylish fashion, it still maintains a sense of intense thrills and a finale where all suspense simply just boils over.  Argo is no doubt exciting, but it accomplishes this in its own, very unique way.And what the about the cast?  Well, you've got the stoic Affleck donning both lead role and director's cap, the great John Goodman playing the anti-Hollywood big shot, and the hilarious Alan Arkin (recently played chief in Get Smart) in the main roles.  The supporting cast is strong as well, both funny and incredibly dynamic.  There are a couple of film cliches that permeate this otherwise fantastically original film.  Other than that, there are seriously no other flaws that I could find watching Argo.  Nor did I care, because Argo was awesome.In the end, Argo is something seemingly normal that feels fresh, and at the helm is someone who knows how to get those ideas across tremendously well.  Argo is something special, and it's timing couldn't be any better especially with the rising tensions with Iran some 30 years later in 2012.  Argo is not only good, it's so crazy you won't believe it's actually a true story.  Bravo, Mr. Affleck.  Bravo.Second Opinions: I'ms standing by my 4.5.  Saw it again, and it just wowed me how incredibly well it maintains all of the tension even a second time around, yet it remains at the "so close" to re-watchable perfection.

The Story which is based on true events, is set in the late 1970's where during political unrests between the U.S.A and Iran was happening, the US Embassy is robbed by Iranian terrorists and 6 of the workers there manage to escape to the Canadian Embassy of Iran, and they must be saved by the CIA agents and must be brought back to the U.S. So A CIA Agent Tony Mendez(Ben Affleck) is brought upon to make a plan on how to save the 6, and he comes up with a plan of making a movie where they were kept as hostages and then make those 6 Americans as film's crew and somehow bring them back to their country.

Well, Ben Affleck always makes sensible and smart movie which are very logical and very pleasing to watch and can be enjoyed by all movie lovers and critics, and he did the same in making Argo, which a unique movie in its own, Argo is a very smartly made thriller and Affleck keeps you glued to the edge of your seat from the very beginning to the finish and keeps you wondering how Mendez will get those 6 out of Iran. Affleck both directed AND Acted in this movie and thats a very difficult thing to do, and he both the jobs so brilliantly that he really deserves most of the credit for the movie. 

The Story(which is based on true events which had occurred on the dates shown in the movie) is a smart topic to make a unique suspense-thriller out of, but Affleck did just that in making this one, and he never overdid any part of it, and just showed what had actually occurred brilliantly. Screenwriter Chris Terrio has done a good job with the writing the story for this movie. 

The Cinematography of the movie is quite good and Rodrigo Prieto has done a great job in showing the dark streets of Iran during those political unrest times and some of the sequences were really well presented. The Costumes worn by the actors in this movie are exactly what it should have been in those times, and the costume design team deserves some credit for that. The Background music which is given by Alexandre Desplat is quite brilliant stuff and although in some of the scenes there is sheer silence and people only talking, but in many scenes Desplat has shown his magical music as he has delivered so many different kinds of music in the film, and the background score really synchronises well with the scene's of the film.

There's little doubt that Ben Affleck is now a prominent filmmaker. As an actor he has always been somewhat wooden and reserved, but with his two first films, Gone Baby Gone and The Town (neither of them wasn't very good but well made nonetheless), he proved that his real skills might be behind the camera. But with Argo, he has once again made a film that can be called very well executed, but still not as good as it ought to be. Chris Terrio's screenplay (which is his debut in film) is a very fine one, with political thriller, satirical comedy and nostalgic period drama playing very well together. Affleck's direction is proficient, and during the last thirty minutes he manages to squeeze out some really nail-biting thrills without a single gunshot or explosion. John Goodman, Alan Arkin and Bryan Cranston deliver fine performances, while Affleck himself, in an act of George Clooney-ish smugness, has cast himself in the lead role, but is once again weary and wooden, a problem that isn't as exasperating here as it was in The Town, but still. With all of this promising surface (an interesting true story, good cast and loads of awards), Argo would seem like a must-see. But the fundamental problem with the film is its political narrow-mindedness. Every Iranian in the film is portrayed as a clamorous maniac, waving rifles in their hands and hunting down Americans at any cost. There is no attempt to explore this historical conflict from their side; instead we just get sentimental scenes of fearful Americans hiding in a house. Watching this, one can't help but be baffled by Affleck's recent, patronizing comments in Bill Maher's talk show, in which he accused Maher and author Sam Harris of "racism" and "Islamophobia" in a very controversial debate. Religion has nothing to do with Argo, but Affleck should look back at the film he made, and maybe realize that his accusations were profoundly indiscreet, and remember that his outrageously xenophobic thriller also just happened to win the Best Picture Oscar.

Historically accurate and beautifully told, Argo keeps you wanting more with its urgent continuity and a plentitude of humor, until you do finally reach those long, suspenseful moments of the film's end. Meticulously cast and thoroughly adapted, Argo is a pleasantly surprising follow-up for Affleck.

Argo confirms Ben Affleck as one of the most talented directors working today.  A thriller mixed with a bit of Hollywood satire, Argo tells the true story of how a CIA "exfiltration" specialist managed to smuggle six US Embassy officials out of Iran during the height of the Iran Hostage Crisis back in 1979-1980.  Affleck plays the specialist, who poses as a film producer for a big budget science-fiction film that is looking to film in Iran.  The film is a fake, an elaborate ruse created by the CIA with the help of a Hollywood producer (Alan Arkin) and a make-up effects expert (John Goodman).  Affleck and his filmmaking team do an incredible job of portraying the fear and tension that ran rampant through Americans under siege in Iran during the Iranian Revolution, including two harrowing sequence where Affleck and the Embassy officials, disguised as a location scouting crew, drive through a political demonstration to meet up with a government official to tour the bazaar.  The last hour of the film, in which the escape plan is carried out, is so intense and suspenseful, I needed to remind myself that the plan worked and the officials made it home alright.  Affleck also does a great job in employing lighter moments of comedy throughout the film as a way of breaking the tension and giving the audience a break psychologically before building up the tension once again.  Alan Arkin steals the show anytime he's on screen.  Expect him to receive all sorts of acting nominations come award time.  I expect the film will be recognized for many awards, and deservedly so.  Affleck delivers one of the best political thrillers in recent memory, and does so with the confidence and skill of a seasoned veteran director twice his age.  One of the best films of the year thus far.

So, ARGO really does succeed in my book.

The third directorial film from Ben Affleck ("The Town"), plunges those old enough to remember this time period, back into an air of nostalgia while edifying a vast mass of others on the attitudes of feuding nations and the realities of the Iran Hostage Crisis as seen by two nations during the Cold War. Also starring in this film, Affleck takes on the blank slate of Tony Mendez, a disheveled CIA agent with a shaggy haircut and a flippant backstory. The film shifts between historical fiction and thrilling caper, Affleck portraying a steely eyed spy, traipsing through the entire movie as a confident and reserved escapist. The film covers a touchy time in American history, as it centers on the Iran Hostage Crisis. Six employees of the embassy escape into the streets only to go into hiding. In comes Tony Mendez, a seasoned operative of the CIA and the only man who is able to save their lives in a time of public outcry. The main premise of the film is one that strikes interest immediately: Mendez must secretly promote and create a sci-fi film and smuggle out the escapees with fake passports purporting that they are a Canadian film crew, in Tehran for location scouting. Mendez accomplishes this with the help of a monster makeup expert and a washed up producer. Besides being thrillingly entertaining, it's surprising to note the level of historical accuracy that went into the making of this film. The soundtrack is a nostalgic throwback, though it doesn't aim to be pushy about the setting. Much of this was meant to look and feel like a seventies' political thriller. Not only did Affleck really think about the film's progression, but it's texture, including using seventies' style filming techniques when recreating scenes from real events, including a public hanging by crane and the organization of readings to the press. The historical framing and attention to detail were very specific. Even the casting was specific in reference to the look of the characters. Some amazing choices included John Goodman as Oscar winning makeup artist John Chambers, Bryan Cranston as CIA senior executive Jack O'Donnell, and Alan Arkin as the hammy award winning producer Lester Siegel. Though the premise may seem gimmicky, it never even borders on over the top. The film is far more about the fear of an entire country gripped in revolution and social unrest than it has anything to do with goofy sub-plots involving aliens and monsters. The violence that centers on the Iranian peoples' revolt is heart chillingly cruel and horrific while being vividly realistic. The reason it isn't the best, or even one of the best films of the year, is because Affleck skews the truth by using false starts again and again. It's not the facts that are being diverted, but instead the stakes of the film, heightened by situations that swell with the rise of Alexandre Desplat's score. The tension keeps building to achingly uncomfortable levels, but doesn't grip you, only heightens your fear to an anticlimactic plateau. It doesn't hurt the integrity of the story or diminish the courageous tactical planning of Mendez, the Canadian ambassador or the hostages' predicament, but it does lose credibility to an already fantastical feeling story. The lesser characters are mostly flat and revolve around the plot without evolving past vaguely interesting. Arkin is certainly the most interesting, providing the same shock humor in this film that he shown us before in "Little Miss Sunshine" and "Get Smart." Interesting enough Arkin isn't the only comedic presence in this film. Threaded throughout  are hints of dark humor, and the some edgier fair . More often than not you will be on the literal edge of your seat, either in anticipation of the characters' fate, or laughing at the well placed humor. Though it depicts some vague human cruelties and is obviously showing a nation strangled by oppression and violence, the film seems very keen to keep from having Iranians be outright demonized. While the CIA agent's dialogue and footage from American protesters in the film would say otherwise, it's really about peace between nations and saving lives. It's a taut thriller because the circumstances surrounding that time in history were unflinchingly grim, not because Affleck takes liberties with historical events. It's exciting to see what next this sophomoric director will show us.

Remember the days of Daredevil, Gigli, and Surviving Christmas? The days when Ben Affleck was everywhere, doing many films a year, most of which turned out horrid? Turns out all it took was for him to step behind the camera and start directing his own films to begin a new career as a person actually worth talking about again. With Gone Baby Gone and The Town, he met critical success, and with Argo his trend of successful films continues. Adapting a true-but-absurd story for Hollywood can be difficult, but its playful nature about it as well as tension-filled moments equate to another milestone in Affleckâ(TM)s career, showing that the director truly is a master of his craft. Contributed by an ensemble cast that never oversteps their role, Argo is what thrilling and entertaining cinema should look like: never boring the audience, and finding ways to keep them on the edge of their seat even when we know the outcome.

The film is based on a true story about a CIA agentâ(TM)s attempt to smuggle six American hostages out of Iran, which is currently in the midst of a revolution. Tony Mendez (Affleck) concocts a plan to pretend to make a science fiction film called â~Argoâ(TM) in order to extract the hostages out of Iran safely. As Bryan Cranston says in the film âItâ(TM)s the best bad idea weâ(TM)ve gotâ?, and Affleck does a great job at showing that. To not have the tone of the film too jarring between its ridiculous sub-plot and tense overarching situation, all of the comedic elements of the film take place in the beginning of Argo, and weâ(TM)re slowly worked up to the reality of whatâ(TM)s happening. The movie takes a lot of liberties with taking jabs at Hollywood during its initial set up of the Hollywood movie plotline and taking note of how ridiculous their plan is. Once Mendez travels to Iran to help the hostages escape though, the tone shifts from a âthis is absurdâ? mindset to âwe have no choiceâ? in a well-developed transition, as Mendez tries to get into contact with those he loves before he leaves, providing the gravitas of the situation.

Once the audience is brought into the thick of the plot, it becomes obvious just how dire it is to get all seven people out of Iran. Mendez now races against revolutionaries, attempting to perfect everything and leave before they piece together who the six Americans are and that theyâ(TM)re still in Iran. The final moments of this film become a massive game of cat and mouse, but itâ(TM)s also one of the most tense sequences displayed on the big screen in recent memory. Knowing the ending in no way took away from what was going to happen, and Affleck really shows that he knows what heâ(TM)s doing here. However, some people may take offense to the fact that they did change the perspective of the story to a more American one, basically saying itâ(TM)s all because of Americaâ(TM)s help that everything went successful and without them these hostages would never have been freed. Itâ(TM)s Hollywood though, and it definitely plays up the Hollywood elements of the film.

And Hollywood is definitely what this film is, supporting an ensemble cast that assist this film in so many ways. Bryan Cranston is great, Alan Arkin is hilarious, John Goodman is entertaining, and Ben Affleck is surprisingly reserved in his acting. No one outshines one another, and in a film that boasts such talent, itâ(TM)s definitely quite a feat for something like that not to occur. It also shows why this movie is great: Argo downplays actors that other Hollywood films would not be able to resist overusing, and it never takes the focus off of the fact that there is an important hostage situation happening. Even in the films first act where everything is making fun of how Hollywood works, the viewer is treated to cuts to the situation in Iran and how grim of a situation it is there. Itâ(TM)s also hard not to mention the use of old newsreel footage in the film (not sure if it all is genuine footage, but some of it for sure is) and how well itâ(TM)s incorporated into different scenes, just helping remind the audience that this is a true story.

There were many ways this film could have flopped, from being too political, too jarring in tone, too focused on itâ(TM)s talent, or just being a boring movie altogether. Fortunately, Affleck has shown in his previous work and continues to display here why he is a great director. Nothing in his repertoire has been even remotely close to average, and it will be interesting to see how he decides to follow-up Argo. And since awards season is officially here, Argo will definitely be a hot contender for best picture when the Academy Awards roll around.

A CIA hostage extraction specialist is called in to retrieve six US Embassy workers hiding out in the Canadian consulate in Iran after the civil uprising of 1979. Argo reminded me very much of The Bank Job, a British heist movie from a few years ago starring Jason Statham. They share a similar mix of humour, politics and history, done in a 70s thriller style format with a plots that seem extremely implausible and yet were based on actual events. Ben Affleck shows some excellent attention to detail in recreating not only the period during which they occurred, but the cultural and political climate and even casting actors who resemble their real life counterparts. The formula is almost a cross between Munich and Ocean's Eleven as the preposterous idea of faking a 70s sci-fi movie to smuggle out the would-be hostages leaves room for a lot of humour and the brilliant partnership of John Goodman and Alan Arkin is constantly laugh out loud funny. This light tone soon becomes darker as the real danger the six face becomes more and more apparent making for a nail biting finale as they attempt their escape. I also have to admire Affleck's candidness in describing the events which led to Iran's contempt for the west and once again his accomplished direction makes for a film that is consistently both entertaining AND intelligent.

The reinvention of Ben Affleck as film director took a big step forward with the critical and commercial success of the 2010 cops-and-robbers thriller, The Town. While I'd argue Affleck's first outing as a director, 2007's Gone Baby Gone, is still his best, The Town won over plenty of doubters. Here was an actor-turned-director who could deliver smart drama, intense suspense, and coax Oscar-caliber performances from his brilliantly assembled casts. Have you seen Blake Lively half as good in anything as she was as a tragic junkie single mom in The Town? She'll be able to get work for years just from the demo reels of that performance. But with two sturdy, complex, taut genre movies under his belt, Affleck still had doubters. The political thriller Argo takes Affleck far out of his Bostonian comfort zone. The creative stretching proves fruitful because Argo is a stirring, fascinating, and engrossing true-life story that should at last silence the remainng doubters concerning Affleck's talents behind the camera. 

In 1979, The U.S. embassy in Tehran was overtaken by a storm of Iranian protestors. Fifty-two Americans were held hostage for an exasperating 444 days. During the takeover, six Americans escapes through a back alley and found asylum with the Canadian ambassador (Victor Garber). There they waited for months, trying to work out a plan to escape. If caught by the mob, it's very likely they would be deemed spies and executed. Enter CIA agent Tony Mendez (Ben Affleck) and his scheme. His idea is to pretend the six American hostages are part of a Canadian film crew scouting locations in Iran for their sci-fi movie. His superiors seem dubious but Mendez gets the green light. He heads to Hollywood and puts together his team, a veteran makeup artist (John Goodman) and Lester Siegel, an established producer (Alan Arkin) on the outs with the industry. They settle on the screenplay "Argo" and have to build a credible cover story. From there, Mendez travels into Iran to meet with the hidden hostages to sell them his scheme. They were all coming out together or nobody was getting back home. 

Argo is a fascinating story that seems like it could only exist in the movies, and yet it's a true story and one hell of a story. It's a mission movie, so we know the familiar flow of the film even as the details seem fresh (unless you're Canadian). The very idea is one of those "so crazy it might work" plans; one State department official asks, "You don't have any better bad ideas than this?" Even though we know it was a success, that doesn't stop the movie from being engrossing. Argo flies by like a caper film as the CIA gathers the resources and experts to try and put together a ramshackle rescue mission. There's feeling out the Hollywood angle, gathering the pieces to create the illusion of an actual film production, and the urgency of the façade. Even though it's a bit outlandish, the fake movie plot seems worlds better than the other possible plans being pitched by the government agencies (smuggling in bicycles and maps?). I thought it was genuinely interesting just to be granted access to a room where people where debating rescue options and picking them apart. The film is consistently intriguing watching smart people come up with smart solutions to challenging problems.

Argo really is three movies expertly rolled together into one; a Middle East thriller, a Hollywood satire, and a D.C. procedural. It's a bonus that every one of these segments works but it's even more surprising, and rewarding, that the different segments all snap together without breaking tone. Credit Affleck the director for making sure his movie parts don't overpower one another. We can go from a tense Middle East sequence where the hostages might have just risked exposure, and then we'll cut to Hollywood and laugh at the cantankerous Lester. It's a delicate balancing act that Affleck superbly handles. The humor of Hollywood doesn't detract or minimize the seriousness of the Middle East chapters; it allows room to breathe, to let off steam. The D.C. segments are the biggest expository moments but they give scope and meaning to the danger. Each of these segments is compelling and each one could have been a captivating movie all its own. We're fortunate that Argo gives us all three.

Audience ignorance aside, we may know how this story ends but that doesn't stop the film from being completely nerve-wracking. Affleck showed remarkable skill in The Town when it came to building exciting sequences that felt like they would explode with tension. When it came to Argo, there were moments that literally kept me on the edge of my seat, a rarity with action films. The beginning sequence of the American embassy is rapt with suspense, as the security system deteriorates and the people inside realize the inevitable. They start destroying classified state evidence but really they just have to sit and wait, hearing the footsteps, knowing what is near. The sharp screenplay from Chris Terrio (Heights) does a tremendous job of developing clear suspense sequences. There's the tension of the precarious subterfuge, of the hostages hiding behind enemy lines, so to speak. If one wrong person were to discover their identity, it could quickly unravel. There's a whole team of children being paid to piece together shredded documents and photos like they were jigsaw puzzles. Knowing this, it makes the scenes where the group ventures out of the embassy thrilling. The group has to visit a marketplace as part of their cover and it's terrifying.  We know the steps of escape, and each one could easily blow up and get everyone killed. Just when you think you can breathe a sigh of relief we've moved onto the next challenge and the tension washes over you again. The climax is so tense that your audience will likely erupt in applause when the hostages eventually escape, relieved and proud of the accomplishment.

The maturation of Affleck as a bonafide directing talent continues. There's a growing confidence in his direction. The man doesn't have to rely on flashy visual artifice nor does he seem to be hewing to one notable style. He's directing each movie as its own beast, be it crime thrillers or true-life suspense story. The man knows where to put his camera in the thick of the action. Affleck also eschews the popular shakycam docu-drama approach that too many filmmakers automatically does all the work of establishing realism. Docu-drama visuals can work when properly utilized, but too often I find it to be self-consciously arty and an annoying distraction. Affleck's camera remains steady but holds on his actors, giving them space to emote. Three movies into his directing career, Affleck has established himself as one of the best men to direct actors. He's already lead two actors to Oscar nominations and might just earn a third for Arkin. Plus there's the fact that Argo, top to bottom, is cast with great character actors. You have people the likes of Michael Parks (Red State) who are there for one line. It also helps Affleck the actor to have Affleck the director. 

The only nagging problem with Argo is that it's rather light when it comes to character development. The caper is the star of the movie and sucks up most of the screen time. The film does an excellent job of recreating the anxiety that the hostages felt. I can't say we get to know any of them well as people. I can't say we get to know much about Tony Mendez either, beside the de rigueur parts of being a CIA agent like divorce, child custody, and long nights of loneliness. The best-developed character in the movie is Lester Siegel, and while he's terrifically entertaining, it's something of a misstep for the cranky Hollywood producer to win that title. He's a man who knows his value in the ever-changing currency of Hollywood; bitter, crabby, but hopeful of making a difference. Arkin (Little Miss Sunshine) is a natural fit for the character and brings more dimensions to the role. I wish the same care were given for the other people in the story, particularly those in harm's way. The nuanced approach to character with Gone Baby Gone and The Town is just absent. Thankfully, the story is so engrossing that it's not a mortal wound, but you do wish there was a greater emotional involvement in the film rather than a generic empathy of rescuing those in danger. Also, the Canadian involvement seems curiously downplayed even though their ambassador was the one hiding them for months. His role in the movie plays like he's Guy #8. I know we tackle the CIA's involvement but Canada could use more recognition for their integral contributions. 

Argo establishes Ben Affleck as a dependable, versatile, actor's director; someone along the likes of a Sidney Lumet or Sydney Pollack (I swear I don't have a "Sydney" thing going on in my brain). Affleck has proven to be a director who immerses himself into his stories, and his fingerprints are on every frame, every performance. He just nails it. The pacing is tight, the suspense builds to near unsustainable levels, and the tones are expertly juggled to prove complimentary rather than distractions. Best of all, Affleck lets Terrio's terrific script take center stage. The incredible true-story of Argo is the biggest selling point for the movie, and Affleck doesn't try to gussy up a whopper of a tale. The film has even more unexpected resonance given the recent spur of violent protests in the Middle East, notably the deadly attack on the U.S. embassy in Benghazi. Argo doesn't sensationalize the hostage crises for cheap popcorn entertainment. Nor does it glorify or denigrate the Iranian's outrage over the U.S. giving sanctuary to the deposed Shah. For a very political subject, the movie takes a very muted political stance, relying on the facts of the situation. The movie finds a rare poignancy in its appeal to the power of international cooperation. By the end of the movie, you might even tear up when you hear the actual hostages and government officials recount their struggle and ultimate triumph. Argo is that rare breed of a movie that seems to have everything. While it's not perfect, it's clear that Affleck is here to stay as a top-level director.
