"Gone Baby Gone," "The Town," and now "Argo," -- Ben Affleck scores a hat trick with three acclaimed films that exhibit his impressive command behind the camera. Producing the film with George Clooney and Grat Heslov, who worked with Mr. Affleck for the award winning "Good Night, and Good Luck," (2005) "Argo" is also based on history, with its fair share of dramatic license, that uniquely incorporates Hollywood during the tumultuous times of the Iran hostage crisis of the late 70's to early 80's.

"Argo" opens with a compelling re-creation of the takeover of the U.S. Embassy in Iran by militant students. It's November 4, 1979 and the world is about to change. Civilians force their way into the Embassy slowly, then, once the gates are forced open, in droves. Employees and diplomats rush to shred and incinerate all sensitive material before the building is completely overtaken. Six of them - Bob Anders (Tate Donovan), Lee Schatz (Rory Cochrane), Mark and Cora Lijek (Christopher Denham and Clea DuVall), and Joe and Kathy Stafford (Scoot McNairy and Kerry Bishe) - escape and make it to the residence of Canadian ambassador Ken Taylor (Victor Garber), where they are hidden for nearly 3 months.

The State Department, helped by the CIA, decides to mount a rescue mission. By mid-January, concerns are rising that, if the diplomats aren't smuggled out of Iran, they may be captured and publicly executed. The Canadian government, concerned about the safety of the ambassador and his staff, is also applying pressure. CIA director Jack O'Donnell (Bryan Cranston) calls in agent Tony Mendez (Affleck), an infiltration expert, to devise a plan to get the six people out. The primary problem is that there is no viable reason why a half-dozen North Americans would be wandering Tehran. With the help of Hollywood make-up artist John Chambers (John Goodman) and producer Lester Siegel (Alan Arkin), Tony establishes a fake production company for a cheesy sci-fi movie called "Argo," and devises a cover story that will hopefully allow them to pass through security at the airport and board a Swiss Air flight.

"Argo," is directed with flair and style by an admired actor/director, and as a period recreation it is just about flawless. There is a notable lack of on-screen bloodshed or violence, confident in its compelling story to invoke edge-of-your-seat tension. The movie has a surprisingly celebratory, feel-good tone rather than dwelling on any political overtones or commentary. The film is made to resemble something coming out of that era, integrating archive footage that lends authenticity to the retelling of the "Canadian Caper."

A closing-credits side-by-side montage shows to what lengths Affleck has gone to re-create the real-life places and people of "Argo," and its his impressive command behind the camera -- the staging, editing, and the calibrated progression of the story, especially its harrowing final moments -- that solidifies Mr. Affleck as a talented and formidable director. "Argo" deserves to find the discerning audience it has been made for: After all, if we buy tickets, it hopefully leads to more intelligent, sophisticated filmmaking.

Argo is a perfectly crafted blend of the classic pizzaz of the Hollywood heist, mixed with a covert thriller, topped off with a healthy dose of patriotism, and above all, once again marks Ben Affleck's legitimacy in the realm of film. 

   Argo follows Tony Mendez (Affleck), a CIA operative attempting to extract six Americans from Tehran during the Iranian hostage crises. When all other plots fail, Mendez suggests the CIA fund a fake movie in order to create six fake identities revolving around a movie production team. Backed by famous make up artist John Chambers (Goodman) and classic actor Lester Siegel (Arkin), Mendez must construct the the science fiction film "Argo" and pray that the six can learn their secret identities if they hope to escape Tehran alive.

   One of the film's most impressive feats is it's artful ability to transition back and forth from personal cameras and news pictures during the crises, along side film recreations of events. While I'm always skeptical of the accuracy of any "based on a true story", the real time clips give an aura of authenticity, no matter how close the calls are in the film. Film techniques also mimic those from the seventies, again giving a much appreciated attempt towards authenticity.

    The script at times is simple, especially with it's overbearing suspense. Despite easy plays at these points however, it maintains an edge of your seat intensity. Most refreshing about the film is possibly the Hollywood section, mirroring the glitz and, as Arkin refers to the "bs business" of the actual operation itself.

    Arkin is by far the only especially memorable character, but the rest of the cast does a terrific job together. I personally can't see any performances worthy of an Oscar nom, but instead the cast works as the perfect ensemble (again which gives the film that almost heist feel as opposed to solely CIA operative extraction).

   At times the film certainly plays to traditional patriotic gestures with a cliched yet fulfilling ending. But what truly makes Argo great is it's incredible use of historical and fictional footage, and the unique spin that only Hollywood can put on a traditional covert operation genre.

With the recent attacks on the American consulate in Benghazi and the latest presidential debates that feature an abundant amount of middle-eastern fear mongering & talk of nuclear diplomacy, it is no wonder that Ben Affleck's 3rd outing as a director is resonating with American audiences. Affleck does not exploit the looming threat of the Islamic world by setting up a world of American good squaring off against a foreign evil. Instead he carefully shows that America had a decisive hand in this violent uprising. But that in even in this mess, there is still a chance for heroics. 

Affleck really knows how to create an intense environment and effortlessly eases the viewer into the shoes of those held captive in this land beset by turmoil. I even really appreciated how in many scenes he doesn't subtitle the words of the Iranians. In those moments where even the smallest gesture could throw a monkey wrench in their whole plan, it effectively immerses us into the terror that the Americans must have felt during the operation.  

Affleck assembles quite an impressive cast who are all very good in their roles. Especially Arkin and Goodman who on top of being interesting characters, are just simply a joy to watch. I do think Affleck could have benefitted from having somebody else take the reigns of the lead role. He seemed to be doing his best George Smiley, but sadly just came off as a guy who is fighting his way through a handful of Xanax. 

Also, while I appreciate his ability to make a balanced & taut thriller out of a real historical event, there were times that I hard time believing what was taking place. Maybe the events were really that wildly coincidental, but I couldn't help but feel that maybe some facts were smudged in order to craft a more intense ending. 

Overall, Argo continues to prove Affleck's detractors wrong. While in front of the camera he may still have some kinks to work out, behind the camera he is an undeniable force to be reckoned with.

While there are some parts that are fictional, they fit right into the story and add to a climax that is already so tense you'll only think to yourself that it may not have happened exactly that way long after the credits are over and the story the film is based on is so bizarre you will have trouble pin pointing fact from fiction. To add to this, the film is perfectly cast; during the credits there are comparisons between the actors and the real people and it's stunning to see that the casting director not only found great lookalikes, but also people that could carry the material they were given. The film is funny at times and it's incredibly suspenseful when it isn't. The beginning starts a little slow, but this is to build up the story and really immerse the audience into the time period. Argo, is a chapter of world history, stranger than fiction. No one would believe the plot of this movie if it didn't actually happen. The CIA fakes a sci-fi movie with appropriate producer, script and press conference to create alibis for the six hidden Americans. And, it works.

My wife and I saw this movie last night and we're both shocked that it was reviewed so highly.  Even though this movie is based on actual events, Affleck's direction succeeded in making the whole thing seem utterly preposterous.  Considering that this was a true story, the fact that we were unable to suspend our disbelief speaks volumes about how poorly this screenplay was executed.  The movie is chock full of excellent actors, yet we were constantly aware that everyone was "acting".  While the real American citizens undoubtedly faced true life-or-death peril, the movie's attempt at building suspense felt amateurish, hollow, and manufactured. The characters were generally bland and uninteresting, especially Affleck's stone-faced protagonist.  I typically enjoy Alan Arkin and John Goodman, but their scenes in Hollywood felt silly and out of place with overall suspenseful tone of the movie.   I would have thoroughly enjoyed Goodman's goofy special effects guru and Arkin's old-school hollywood shark if this was a comedy.  Unfortunately their scenes just highlighted the farcical feel of the movie and made me begin viewing the movie as satire.  That is until the manufactured gravitas of Affleck's character made me realize..."Oh, they're trying to be serious."  Even the Iranian bad-guys seemed completely unblievable.  Somehow the Iranians were at the same time a decentralized haphazard mob, a group of gullable beurocrats, a small band of tech-savvy detectives, and an inexplicably well-oiled machine that could instantly mobilize a response using early 80's technology when the pieces of the puzzle were finally put together.  All in all, Argo is the movie version of Gangnam Style: a block-buster hit with the masses yet devoid of real quality with lyrics that are hollow and meaningless.  And, just like the Korean rapper PSY, Affleck takes himself extremely serously all the while delivering moves that just feel amateurish and laughable.

Ben Affleck directs and stars in this faithful recreation of actual events during the Iranian hostage crisis of 1979-1981, when six U.S. employees fled the embassy just as it was being stormed, and found refuge in the Canadian ambassador's residence.  After exploring and discarding various rescue schemes, the CIA chooses to set up a fake science fiction film (complete with a production office in Hollywood), designates the six as location scouts, and sends in an exfiltration expert (Affleck) undercover as a producer, to lead them out.  Affleck (as director) has chosen a very linear, procedural style for ARGO, but executes it marvellously, especially in terms of recreating period details.  (I am still in awe of the shots of airplanes flying above Tehran against the backdrop of snowcapped mountains.)  Halfway through the film, I realized it reminded me of ALL THE PRESIDENT'S MEN, and I later learned that Affleck actually studied that film to emulate its look.  While all performances in the film are respectable, Alan Arkin rises above the rest with an unforgettable turn that I expect to be rewarded with an Oscar nomination next year.

Argo is easily one of the best films of this year by far. The movie is gripping, intelligent, suspensful, dark, humourous, blunt, painstakenly crafted, well acted, well directed and well written. My heart was beating as the picture's climax rose steadily...Could Tony Mendez's plan work? Could he actually be capable of persuading and fooling the Iranian authorities by making a fake movie during the Iranian hostage crisis? Finding the six Americans who escaped, give them fake Canadian passports, instruct them to know their fake identites inside out so they won't be spotted, disguise the Americans as a fake film crew and quietly wield them out of the country? The odds seem highly impossible.

There is a scene where Mendez is with the fake movie crew at the airport and they're being held by hostile Iranian authorities. Through much speculation one of the Americans talk in Iranian of filming and making a movie project in Iran showing them fake storyboards and such which the authorities would later, humourously get to keep. At times I was wondering if the authorities would really pick up on the scheme and put the drop on Mendez and the Americans. 

The performances is top notch. There is no bad performance in this movie. Dear Ben Affleck,

With "Gone Baby Gone", "The Town" and now "Argo" under your belt, I don't think anybody (mainly myself) can deny your prowess as a top tier filmmaker any longer.  So, before I began with my actual review, I wanted to preface it with this short statement, which you should take as a letter of apology for every negative thing I've ever said about your filmmaking through the years, as well as a letter of forgiveness for "Gigli", "Jersey Girl" and "Daredevil"...well, maybe not "Daredevil".

Synopsis: Directed by Ben Affleck, "Argo" is a film which dramatizes the declassified true story (set in the late 70's/early 80's) of CIA agent Tony Mendez (played by Affleck) who spearheaded the insane plan to secretly extract six fugitive American diplomatic personnel out of a revolutionary Iran, by posing as a fake Canadian film crew scouting a fake Canadian film (a "Star Wars" rip-off by the name of "Argo").  And while this synopsis sadly may not sound like it would translate into a compelling Saturday night date movie (especially to those who didn't live through the actual event, or to those who think purchasing tickets to see the newest Silent Hill film is a good way to spend their money) what puts it over-the-top/makes this premise sing, is the undeniably engaging combination of Chris Terrio's screenplay, which perfectly balances comedic scenes with ones of gritty wartime events (maybe the toughest thing to do in scriptwriting) and Affleck's spot on portrayal of late 70's Iran and America (at times using actual footage) showcasing a devastatingly provocative parallel to that point in history and the post 9/11 atmosphere in the United States, as well as his startlingly brilliant ability to take a rather simplistic resolution (final 45 minutes) and mold it into one of the most suspenseful climaxes in recent years.

The only real flaw I could see in "Argo" is that with such a wealth of great actors, and the movie primarily surrounding Affleck's character, for long stretches of the film actors such as Bryan Cranston (who in my opinion, has overtaken Stanley Tucci as the best character actor working today) John Goodman and Alan Arkin (who are all excellent in their roles) aren't really given much to do.  My only wish (if this movie weren't already 2 hours long) would've been to see more scenes showcasing this strong supporting cast.

Final Thought:  Aside from the fact that "Argo" may garner him an Oscar nomination, what director Affleck has done with this film, is shown his incredible Spielberg-esque ability to take a historical event, that may have come off as dry or utterly uneventful in other hands, and make it so every second of what's on screen, no matter how seemingly mundane or complex, is impressively compelling.  If you haven't figured it out by now, what I'm saying is that everyone should go see "Agro" (as it is one of the best movies of the year so far) even if movies described as "historical dramas" immediately make you reply with the phrase: "so what else is playing?"

Ben Affleck has, over the past five years, proven that, while he's not always the most solid of actors, he has a bright future as a director. I know the net is full of ribald fanboys who still hate Affleck's guts for the awfulness of Daredevil, but, as a dramatic filmmaker, I think he's more than redeemed himself. Argo, like The Town and Gone Baby Gone (Affleck's prior films), is a straightforward drama, though there are elements of comedy thrown in, and, unlike his prior films, this one is based squarely in reality. The events of the film have been given a Hollywood spin and the suspense has been ratcheted up, but Argo never loses its' firm grip on reality (which the slideshow credits make painstakingly clear). Argo tells the story of six American citizens hiding out in Iran during the 1979 revolution, and the CIA's bizarrely conceived exfil plan, led by operative Tony Mendez (Affleck). Mendez's idea to sneak the civilians out of Iran involves having them pose as the film crew of a would-be Hollywood sci-fi blockbuster called Argo. Things do not go according to plan, and it's amazing how much tension Affleck is able to wring out of something as simple as a crowded market scene, a stroll through Tehran's airport, or an on-set holdup. The comedic elements provide some much-needed brevity, particularly after the incredibly tense opening sequence. Most of them are supplied by John Goodman and Alan Arkin (as the studio execs Mendez cooperates with), although Bryan Cranston (as Mendez's boss) has one of the film's best lines, which involves "those two old fucks from The Muppets". When Argo turns its' attention to the crisis in Iran, the film wisely eschews the comedic approach in favor of tiny dramatic flourishes, and a few tension-building scenes of the Iranians piecing together the identities of the American civvies. The performances are mostly subdued, with Affleck playing Mendez as a bit of a disconnected loner. Alan Arkin manages to steal every scene he's in, but the character never comes off as a stereotype of Hollywood producers. The best thing about Argo, besides Affleck's tense filmmaking style, is the attention to period detail. The movie was produced in 2012, but looks like it came directly from the late 70's or early 80's. Even Affleck deglamorizes himself with a thick beard and a foppy haircut. Watching Argo, I was reminded more of All the President's Men (another tense film with its' roots firmly planted in history) then more recent "period" films (The Conspirator springs to mind). The ability to recreate the time period and setting is one of the reasons Argo works so well. We're not just watching the story unfold, we're transported into the proceedings. This is an adult, intelligent film that requires the viewer's attention. Those taking frequent breaks or checking phones will probably be bored to death by Argo, but those willing to invest their attention will likely enjoy what the film has to offer. It's an excellent film with painstaking attention to detail that benefits the story immensely. As a director who's shaping up to be one of Hollywood's new-wave of greats, I'm pretty sure Affleck has now-redeemed himself for even Surviving Christmas. His next directorial effort cannot arrive soon enough.

What a difference a decade makes. Not long ago Ben Affleck was the butt of jokes in Hollywood and his career seemed to be going nowhere. Flopped films like Jersey Girl and Gigli solidified that notion even more. That was until he started directing movies. First, he debuted with the incredible mystery/crime drama Gone Baby Gone. Second, he conquered the sophomore jinx with one of the best heist films since Heat with The Town. Which brings us to his third film and its safe to say he has hit the trifecta! Argo, based on the unbelievable true story of the life or death rescue mission of six Americans during the Iranian Hostage crisis, is not only Affleck's best film to date but its also one of the best films of the year. One of the tricky things about films based on true stories is trying to keep the audience engaged in a film about an event that mostly everyone knows how it'll end. In the case of Argo, you've got a political thriller that was a classified mission that was eventually declassified and made public during the Clinton administration. Somehow though, Affleck pulls it off with flying colors and by the film's climatic ending you'll find yourself on the edge of your seat. For starters, the screenplay and editing is very tight and keeps to your attention with a brisk 120 minute runtime. Secondly, the film is anchored by some veteran actors. Alan Arkin, John Goodman, Bryan Cranston and yes, the film lead Ben Affleck all give great performances that give it that added touch of credibility to its belt. However, the most important aspect I found to towards the movie was its tone! With most political thrillers, they always seemed to have a hidden agenda of trying to prove something or make a statement. Amazingly though, political thrillers, whether its the truth or not, work best when they simply just try to tell a good story. Argo not only passes this test with flying colors but also gets gutsy by adding a little humor to the film which surprisingly works in this situation. In fact, Argo harkens back to classic political thrillers of the 70s/early 80s with films like All The Presidents Men, Taxi Driver and Blow Out. Along with a great story, great acting, and great direction, Affleck has produced not just one of the best films of the year but one that should receive many nominations come Oscar time. Indeed, what a difference a decade makes! 5 out of 5 stars!

In the midst of the Chicago Film Festival I squeezed in the highly touted and commercially successful "Argo", a film that captures the explosive and traumatic events revolving around the Iran hostage crisis; November 4,1979, the American embassy in Tehran, was stormed by Iranians, posing as students, the saga lasted 444 days; six escaped and found refuge in the Canadian embassy. "Argo" is the enactment of those who got away and the ruse perpetrated by the C.I.A. to accomplish their incredulous salvation.

Instead of judging "Argo" on its historical veracity I chose to view it solely on its "film" attributes, and it shines. Ben Affleck (admittedly, I have always been a fan, even liking the catastrophic bomb, "Pearl Harbor") stars and directs this scenario, buried until President Bill Clinton declassified it in 1997. From the onset "Argo" is true to the times: sideburns, ubiquitous smoking, 1980 technology; in today's world this endeavor would have backfired, immediately and profoundly.

Affleck is brilliant in creating a narrative where the conclusion is known but the process cloudy; commencing with historical information about Iran, the Shah and America's involvement in the region, culminating with the Ayatollah's triumphant return, masterfully incorporating film footage of the horrific debasement of the interned Americans; youthful David Brinkley and Ted Koppel ambushing the communication limelight with their iconic, daily reporting.

Affleck is "Tony Mendez" the C.I.A. operative who executes the preposterous plot of rescuing 6 Americans (disguised as Canadian filmmakers) making a movie in hostile "Iran"; levity and humor inform the creation of "the best bad idea" with John Goodman giving a sensational, jovial portrait of Academy Award winner "John Chambers" (a makeup artist par excellence); Alan Arkin as producer "Lester Siegel"  gifts audiences another palliative, perspicuous performance.

"Argo" careens hypnotically from one nerve fraying moment to another; a ride worthy of the price; ultimately remembering, revering those who escaped and the heroes who implemented their survival.

Could anyone have predicted ten years ago the path that Ben Affleck has taken? To go from being the butt of countless â~Benniferâ(TM) jokes, prancing around Hollywood in terrycloth jumpsuits, to being one of the most interesting, well-composed film-makers working today? Audiences love a comeback story, and thatâ(TM)s precisely what Affleck has given us, with three excellent films under his belt, the best of which, Argo, is a genuine front-runner for best film of 2012.

Itâ(TM)s possible that Ben Affleckâ(TM)s skill as a director and (as his fantastic work in Argo can attest) actor, owes a great deal to his time right in the centre of the public eye. Rebuilding his credibility as an artist to be taken seriously must have been no mean feat, given the ridiculous level of tabloid exposure he had, but by turning his attention to slow-burn thoughtful fare such as Argo he has all but removed himself from public life and simply lets the quality of the work speak for itself.

Argo is a fascinating story, so absurd that it can only be true. Concerning a covert mission to rescue six American citizens in hiding during the Iranian hostage crisis of the early 1980s, itâ(TM)s deeply serious material, but with an almost farcical edge. And while Affleck certainly takes many opportunities to inject humour into the film, the stakes are so high that when the extraction actually begins, the level of suspense stretches the limits of endurance.

Bizarrely, the film makes an interesting counterpoint to last yearâ(TM)s suspense highlight Mission: Impossible - Ghost Protocol. Where that film relied on outlandish stunts and huge suspension of disbelief to perch us on the edge of our seats however,Affleckâ(TM)s languid pacing works perfectly for Argo. Creative license is assumed, but the realism permeates every frame. M:Iâ(TM)s Ethan Hunt is for all intents and purposes a superhero, whereas Tony Mendez (Affleck) is simply a man, albeit an expert as his specific vocation. He appears to take everything in stride, right down to his troubled home life, and Affleckâ(TM)s enigmatic performance is easy to overlook, but absolutely grounds the film.

Itâ(TM)s character work that gives nothing away yet says so much, and if he appears to take everything in stride, itâ(TM)s simply because he must. This is a man who prepares for the worst so he wonâ(TM)t be caught unawares when it happens, and as such he seems a little distant, aloof as to whether the mission succeeds. Yet small moments give him away, betraying his intense investment in what he does. Itâ(TM)s not flashy, but itâ(TM)s a very well pitched performance.

As good as Affleck is in his dual role as star and director, this is by no means a one man show. Alongside a mightily impressive cast including Bryan Cranston, Alan Arkin and John Goodman, the film is beautifully shot with wonderful period detail, and Alexandre Desplatâ(TM)s clever, lively score adds the exciting spy film atmosphere that is absent from the script.

Argo is a triumph, an old-fashioned example of how to make tense, exciting adult drama, and itâ(TM)s not unreasonable to assume that Affleckâ(TM)s film will be a key player on the coming award circuit, and deservedly so.

In the wake of two previous successful directorial features, "Gone Baby Gone", and "The Town". Ben Affleck was already proving he was on his way to something cinematically monumental. "Argo" is that result, and what a result it is. Back in 2005, Steven Spielberg "Munich" was a bold picture with a beautiful representation of it's time period. Like Spielberg, and along with studying this film, Affleck perfectly uses very ounce of talent in capturing the look, and feel of 1979-1980. "Argo" is not as deep of a film as "Munich", it's something else. It's a perfect straight story about something the world was watching, and yet did not know the measures taken in how it all really happened. I remember a time when hearing Ben Affleck was in a film or making a film, was not exciting at all. Now I am hooked for whatever he directs next.

"Argo" opens with a powerhouse of a scene, the siege of the US embassy in Iran, where 52 Americans were captured and held hostage. However, six managed to slip away and found refuge in the home of the Canadian ambassador, in the hopes to escape Iran before found and executed. The opening scene is executed in a fashion true to the real events and sights which unfolded that day of November 4, 1979. This is also where the film's gripping suspense begins and very very rarely quits.  Ben Affleck plays CIA specialist Tony Mendez who after hearing numerous bad ideas of how to get the six out of Iran, including a six with bicycles and make them bike 350 miles to the border. In the wake of Hollywood sic-fi films like "Star Wars", "Star Trek", and "The Planet of The Apes", Mendez comes up with  "the best bad idea" of pretending to film a sci-fi film in Iran called "Argo" as the cover for the six Americans being there and then flying them out on a commercial flight. In order to prove it can be done, Mendez looks to Hollywood Oscar winning make-up artist John Chambers (John Goodman) to help set up Black Op mission by pretending to make a fake film with a real cast, a real script, a real studio, and a real producer. They turn to Lester Siegel (Alan Arkin) to put up his own money for the movie in order to save the six Americans. In a film filled with pulse pounding suspense, the Hollywood scenes add a lot of humor and relaxation to the film. Goodman and Arkin are perfect as the film's comic relief, but the comedy isn't based on slapstick, it's based on the way Hollywood works. The film is quick in it's energetic pace and soaking with great old fashion cinematic suspense. Affleck wisely uses every inch of research and resource he had to make this picture right, and get the story right. This day and age most directors would of neglected the little details of the story thinking they're not important. Affleck is on a completely different level of masterful filmmaking with "Argo". He is not only showing history, he's got the edge to show history to the world for the first time. The Argo operation stayed top secret until Clinton declassified it in 1997.

Simply put, "Argo" is the best film I have seen in the theater since "Inception" , which goes all the way back to summer of 2010! I urge people to see this film, even if you know the outcome. It is just like "Apollo 13" where you may know the outcome, but the telling of the suspenseful events leading to it's dramatic end make the film a must-see. Believe me "Argo" is probably the first film since "Apollo 13" to have the same overall feeling in the end as "Apollo 13" had. Unlike a period piece, this is a rare modern film which never for a minute feels modern at all. "Argo" is a incredbly smart and bold film that has Affleck in line for a best director nomination and best picture nomination. The story is real, the people are real, the events happened. This is how Black Ops are carried out. In most Hollywood films, an armed group of Special Forces, like "The Expendables", would've been sent in to save the hostages in heavy gun fire and explosions. "Argo" is way too smart to be that kind of a film, and to all those films I have to say, 'Argo fuck yourself'.

The film shows great attention to details with stunning late 1970s realism and succeeds in recreating the subdued and understated mood of 1970s great classics such as Sydney Lumet's Network or All the President's men. It's produced by Affleck and George Clooney and it shows. Great acting all around, especially from Affleck and Alan Arkin who have created very strong characters. John Goodman has a small role and is great too. The only slight small negative point is the last 5 minutes where the pursuit is over the top. It didn't need that addition to be great. Overall this is very entertaining and intelligent storytelling. The film is partly based on an article published in 2007 in Wired magazine chronicling the CIA's mission:

'Argo'. Ben Affleck, take a bow. A magnificent achievement in pacing and tension, bringing an unbelievable true story to life.

There's a line towards the beginning, when they're trying to sell The Hollywood Option, that goes something like, "And everybody knows they'd shoot in Stalingrad with Pol Pot directing if it would sell tickets." 

This cynical undercurrent that still permeates through Hollywood today, arguably more so, grounds this film in a believability that would be hard to artificially create solely for this film. It's one of the many cheeky shots the film takes, having a go at acting, directing and everything in between. 

Affleck's camera movements are frenetic and clear all at once, swooping, circling and darting rapidly on occasion, most noticeable in the opening hysteria at the embassy. 

The last twenty or so minutes, where 'Argo' ratchets up the tension, is owed in large to some brilliant editing, switching between the four parties involved, while never needing to cheat the audience in taking them down a false path. There was an audible sign of relief in the theatre when that plane finally takes off!

Then there's Ben Affleck the actor. First things first. I have a large man-crush on his beard. Affleck doesn't overplay his character, but he nails the emotional moments, and I was totally on board his crazy plan, with his heart very much in the right place. 

The supporting cast is insane, but Bryan Cranston and Alan Arkin shine the brightest, getting the killer lines written by Chris Terrio.

I loved 'Gone Baby Gone' and 'The Town'. It gives me great pleasure to see Affleck stretching out from his familiar Boston, making something completely different, and getting it so right.

Ben Affleck's third film as a director, "Argo", about the 1980 Iranian hostage crisis and the fake film created as a ruse to facilitate the rescue of six Americans, is undoubtedly his finest and most sure-handed offering. That he has been once again blessed with a slew of extremely talented actors is just an elegant spice on top of this superb cinematic treat. It's a Hollywood winner that is stylistic and suspenseful in ways that so much of the boring box-office sure-bets grossly lack. Even if it lacks some of the intense bite of his "Gone Baby Gone", it's still Best Picture nom quality for sure, and a Best Director for Affleck, as well as a handful of other guaranteed nominations. And if I'm not mistaken, nothing seems destined to stop it from actually winning in all of these categories.

Argo tells the story of the Iranian revolution, and hostage situations that were involved with it. On November 4, 1979, the Iranian revolution reached its boiling point, the U.S. Embassy in Tehran was stormed by militants, and Americans were taken hostage. During this revolution, six American citizens manage to escape and find refuge in the home of the Canadian ambassador. It was only a matter of time before the citizens' cover was blown, or they were rescued. A CIA (Central Intelligence Agency) specialist, Tony Mendez (Ben Affleck), concocted the best bad idea the CIA had to rescue the citizens, and get them out of the country with their lives.

This was a covert operation that wasn't known to the public eye until the 1990s. The story is amazing, and extremely memorable. This story was back in 1979 and 1980, so it definitely makes for an early 80s atmosphere. It's nice that this revolution gets revisited, it brings knowledge of something that happened a fairly long time ago. The impact it had on the world at the time seems large, but, apparently, not large enough for me to hear of it in this day and age.

It's sort of fascinating how Affleck made it feel more like the 80s, and he did it in quite the innovative way: according to IMDb, he shot it on regular film, cut the frames in half and blew those images up to 200% to increase their graininess. The viewer can also tell that they're in for an older styled atmosphere because of the old Warner Bros logo which was to match the time of the 80s.

Ben Affleck's pure Hollywood acting career may be dust in the wind (or at least starting to feel a bit like that) but his directing career isn't going South anytime soon. He has a real knack for making great and memorable films.

It's an extremely thrilling and captivating film experience, and is the most riveting film of 2012 thus far.

There are history and politics thrown in here, but politics only crossed my mind a few times. It feels more like a great CIA rescue mission more than anything else. It's intense and there's some great comedy thrown in there. There's one great joke that gets used a few times, but doesn't get overused because it's thrown at you at times you least expect it.

The rescue mission is a great gamble, because Affleck's character is both risking his life and theirs.

The characters are fine, because they are real and none feel expendable at all. Affleck's character has a son and a wife; and some of the Americans stuck at the Canadian Ambassador's house are married. Each actor and actress wonderfully capture emotions of stress, anxiety and intense worry.

One of the most captivating things about Argo is the boiling suspense of the situation, and the viewer can just feel it build throughout. It also really is quite nerve-racking.The pacing is great, and it doesn't feel slow in a lot of places. There are a lot of memorable scenes, and then others just build up the plot. There aren't any bad scenes, though, so that's great. Argo sort of plays out like an assassin giving you his first choke-hold, he's inexperienced and you may feel the grip loosening from time to time, but then it strengthens again and doesn't let go until the very end.

Something that annoyed me is the odd time when there wasn't any subtitles when the Iranians spoke their language (Farsi, maybe?). Still, you can tell the emotions that they are feeling, so I guess it doesn't matter very much, now that I think it over more.

The use of old footage really interested me some. It worked into the film well and didn't feel out of place at all.

The film does live up to its hype, and to its trailer. The use of Aerosmith's song Dream On, was extremely effective and amped it up about ten times as much. I wish they didn't use some of the film's best lines in the trailer. Yet again, studios do that a lot. They still were great when I heard them during the film though.

Phil.                      ARGO
It's quite something to see a director at the height of his powers (eg. John Boorman when he made 'Excalibur').   Ben Affleck, who has had a strong beginning to his career as director, reaches the same height of complete and skilled control with his latest film, 'Argo'.
Beginning with ten minutes of the most terrifying footage, seen from inside the American Embassy in Teheran, which is being overrun (in 1979) by a tidal wave of crazed Iranians, Affleck never takes his foot off the pedal.  Six of the embassy staff escape to a safe house, and, astoundingly, the almost suicidal plan to liberate them, under the guise of their being a production crew for a sci-fi movie, actually took place.  However, it was a story that could not be told until some ten years later, when the facts were declassified.
The name of the phony film project is 'Argo' and Tony Mendez (Ben Affleck) is the CIA operative with the responsibility of master-minding the audacious plan.  Affleck, who turns in a very restrained but focused performance, is possibly best directed by himself, these days. However, the rest of the cast is also impressive, especially Bryan Cranston (who has made his own mercurial career leap, from the loopy Hal of 'Malcolm in the Middle').  As Jack O'Donnell, one of the CIA top dogs, he delivers a powerful and intense performance.  No doubt, when the Oscars roll around, his name will be thrown into the arena, as best supporting actor.  In addition, there is great support from Alan Arkin and John Goodman, who contributes some snappy humour. 
Many films suffer from a middle third 'sag'.  Not so with 'Argo' where there are no lapses into 'sit-com' romanticism or swathes of cliché-burdened dialogue.  The suspense, in fact, never really lets up and, in the final scenes, involving a madcap race at the airport, the tension is stretched to breaking point.
Despite demonising the Iranians (difficult to avoid when seen only through Western eyes) the film does present archival material explaining the people's source of resentment.  In addition, and to its credit, the film avoids political proselytising, keeping the focus firmly on the excitement of the heist.  As a slice of history, then, the film is informative.  As a political thriller, it is a cracking good yarn that will nail you to the edge of your seat.

Loosely based on the rescue and exfil operation of 6 American diplomats who were taking refuge in the Canadian Ambassador's residence during the midst of the Iranian Islamic revolution. Tony Mendez (Ben Affleck) proposes a preposterous plan to CIA to rescue the six American diplomats. It was so farcical that they all believed no one would suspect it and it worked. The basic plan is to setup a fake production of a middle-eastern themed science fiction movie titled 'Argo', pose the diplomats as location scouting crew and get them out. The operation is planned to the T with the help of his trusting superior Jack O'Donnell (Bryan Cranston) and ably supported by his Hollywood acquaintances Lester (Alan Arkin) and John Chambers (John Goodman). 

Talking of humor I just couldn't control myself laughing for no reason in John Goodman's introduction scene without him even saying a word. Bryan Cranston fits the role perfectly with a new look since the only other role I have seen him and so often is his egotistic manipulative Mr. Hiesenberg. The Hollywood script reading exercise could have been a little toned down, CIA hierarchy and method of general operations felt too generic. In some parts, the urgency and dramatization felt a little forced to elevate the thriller element. Ben Affleck thankfully was superb with no special histrionics and brings a sense of calm which was so required. The actors who play the diplomats were well chosen and bring in their best at the right moments. Last but not the least is the high attention to detail in regards to the gadgets, clothing, sets and location of the period bringing in a highly authentic feel to it. People playing the Iranian guard were also very intense and believable.

Darkly funny, toned down performances and attention to detail makes this a winner.

Where the film transcends its story and has something to say about current day is the context of the film on the domestic political front in the last days of the Carter administration. Carter was pictured as impotent and weak for not freeing the hostages. When these hostages got out the true story was kept secret and stayed secret. It was feared that if the US trumpeted the achievement that the other hostages might be killed. It might have turned the election if this was leaked to the press. Its hard to see either US political party not trotting this out to turn its political fortunes in current times.
In the comparison with real events this is not even loose with the truth: its more fiction then based on true story. The Canadians were instrumental in saving the hostages: splitting them up and moving them regularly around Teheran. Nearly all the ratcheted tension at the climax is wholly invented. Thats not a criticism but a good to know afterwards before people view this as a documentary.

Ben Affleck, the filmmaker, has proven twice before that he is a force to be reckoned with, but with this, his third film, he shows that his relationship with the director's chair is a marriage, not a fling. Many are calling this Affleck's first "serious" film, and while I'm not sure I agree with that claim, one can see the point. It is a film tied to politics, and to real events; its stakes go worldwide and its scope and craft seem far larger than in 'Gone Baby Gone' and 'The Town'. The three films together show a clear evolution, a learning process, and if whether this is his best movie yet or not, it is certainly his most polished. Chronicling an event that most Americans have heard of but little know much about (I admit I was one), the film centers around a terrifying moment in history involving a hostage situation in Iran, and the necessity of a unique strategy for getting six Americans out of the country- right under the noses of the Iranian government. The plot is masterminded by Tony Mendez, played here by Affleck himself: he, with the assistance of some Hollywood muscle, would plan a fake film shoot in Iran and get the six out as supposed members of his crew. The whole idea is so silly that it could only be reality, and while it starts out in L.A. as an in-joke funny plot, it ends in powerful and affective drama. Stellar performances by Affleck, John Goodman and Alan Arkin (and the whole cast, really) keep this film funny, emotional and thrilling, and Affleck's confidence as a director keep the look and feel of the movie tight, stylish and efficient.

What's he thinking? Looking at Tony Mendez (Ben Affleck) in "Argo," it's hard to answer that question. And that's not just because of the masklike beard Mr. Affleck wears. As he walks into danger again and again, his eyes sometimes seem to flicker with dry fear but otherwise, he is impenetrably still, almost drained of life.

He has to be. In real life, Mr. Mendez was a CIA agent who successfully rescued six fugitive Americans during the Iranian hostage crisis. The year was 1980 when Mr. Mendez, posing as a Canadian film producer, flew into Iran and passed the Americans off as members of his crew. Together they escaped and the rest, of course, is history.

At first, it's difficult to tell what kind of history Mr. Affleck intends to pass it off as (he also directed the film). After a fragmented introduction filled with smashed glass and burning flags, we follow Mendez to Hollywood where begins building his cover identity. 

Yet, marketing to the contrary, "Argo" spends very little time under the clear California sun (and thank goodness--the one-liners delivered in this portion, like "You can teach a rhesus monkey to be a director," are alarmingly tacky). Instead, it whisks Mendez to Iran, where he informs the government that he's scouting locations for a science-fiction epic. "You came at a complicated time," one official tells him. No kidding.

It is these complications that the film is interested in. Through montages replete with television clips (in which angry Iranians rage against the United States), "Argo" captures an international mood of violence and unease. And Mr. Mendez has to walk right into the middle of that violence, not only to help the Americans escape, but to help them build their cover identities. It's not enough for them to show up at the airport and declare that they're Canadian--they have to be seen in the crowded streets of Iran, preparing to shoot their "film."

I knew from the start that the hostages escaped. And yet "Argo" is terrifying suspenseful. The threat of death hangs over the movie so prominently that even after the initial musical swooping when Mendez and company are safely home, an air of fear and grief lingers. That seems to have been Mr. Affleck's intent--he wants us to appreciate the safe rescue of the hostages, but he doesn't want to end on a note of triumphalism either. He could have shown Mendez's reunion with his young son, but instead he chooses something simple: a shot of them lying together on a bed, not speaking.

Argo begins with the events at the Iranian US embassy on November 4th, 1979, when protesters-incensed by their country's inveterate political and societal turmoil-broke through the embassy gates and held the residents there for what would become a 444-day hostage situation. Serving as both setting and character introduction, this opening sequence is one of the most indelible and disquieting beginnings I have seen in the theater in a good long while, and provides us with a trove of useful info, both within the movie and without. Superficially, it pulls us headlong into the story, introducing characters and circumstances in a meticulously edited prologue, while building to a truly frightening climax that sets the whole picture in motion. Incidental to the exposition the scene provides is the realization that this is a seminal moment for Ben Affleck as a director. Argo is a strong film in many ways, yet this opening sequence suggests a caliber of talent not just absent from his first two titles, but altogether unaccounted for. It seems that Ben Affleck the Director is the real deal.

That same terrifying November morning, when the eyes of the world were on the Iranian embassy, six Americans slipped quietly out the back door, and fled to the house of Ken Taylor (Victor Garber), the Canadian Ambassador. And here we arrive at the crux of Argo: these six Americans, their detention, and the plan to get them out-an elaborate ruse dreamed up by CIA extrication specialist Tony Mendez (Affleck) centered around the bogus production of a fake film entitled Argo. Mendez enlists the help of two Hollywood acquaintances: Makeup Artist John Chambers (John Goodman), and Producer/Director Lester Siegel (Alan Arkin), utilizing their connections to legitimize his phony production, before making his way to Iran to meet up with the stowaways. Mendez provides them with new identities, adamant that they have precious few hours to memorize them before they face the gauntlet that is the Iranian airport. They will be a Canadian film crew, come to Iran to scout locations, now on their way out of the country. And they will be met with resistance.

I haven't seen Gone Baby Gone, but I remember The Town as a particularly tense film. Affleck wanted to create a heist film built on suspense, which he did, and he did with impressive skill. In Argo this skill has been honed and refined, resulting in a film that dictates the emotional experience to its audience. There's no ambiguity in Argo-from the first shot of frenzied protestors to the hero's final redemption, you know precisely how you're supposed to feel based on the camera's focus and the film's soundtrack. This emotional manipulation can be a double-edged sword. Guiding your audience to feel and react the way you want them to is an exceptional talent, and vital to being a noteworthy director. Antithetically, this style of artful filmmaking doesn't give your audience any room to think, or even breathe, and can result in a memorable experience but a forgettable film. It also simplifies the heroes and villains, and while the world may not have been attuned to political correctness in the early 80s, Affleck's depiction of the Iranian people often veers towards one dimension-evil. Regardless, the storytelling on display here speaks volumes about what Affleck has picked up in his Hollywood years. It's easy to picture him as the guy standing over Director X's shoulder, listening and learning while his co-stars nap in their trailers. You don't glean this kind of skill simply through connections, and Affleck should be applauded for the work he's put in to get here.

On second thought, I suppose he could be commended for said connections, as Argo is a talent parade. Certainly the first tier of characters is filled out with strong and marketable talent, and guys like Goodman and Arkin, and Bryan Cranston as Mendez's boss have made the director's work a whole lot easier. But there are also distinctly recognizable actors getting 30 seconds of screen time in this film. Having friends in high places can do wonders for your movie's overall quality, and as much as this contributes to the film's ultimate success, Affleck's maturing talent as a director is undeniable.

Unfortunately, herein lies the difference between Argo being one of the best films of the year and merely being a strong film from a young director. While Ben Affleck's third film is undoubtedly successful in articulating his voice, it's also clearly the product of many hands. This isn't a knock, and it certainly doesn't suggest that Affleck has maxed out; as I said before, Argo is definitive proof that he is going places. It must, however, be taken for what it is, and not what it could have been. While the peaks and valleys of Argo are surprisingly well executed, they don't hide the director's uncertainties and bad habits. Only time can do that.

Argo, based on a true story. Is a political thriller, which chooses to cut out the political aspect and existence in the story. It's there, but it's not the focus. What we get is a story about a rescue mission, a mission which sounds so ludicrous that it's fun, but carries such a high stake that you're forced to take seriously. Argo does a fine job of giving the script a minor comical feel, it's mainly delivered through John Goodman and Alan Arkin's characters.

Ben Affleck plays Tony Mendez a C.I.A agent, who specializes in exfiltration, exfil meaning in a nutshell, evacuations or rescue missions. He is brought in to bring back 6 American escapees from the U.S. Embassy in Tehran. They are holed up at the house of the Canadian Ambassador. The conditions are rough in Iran, political upheavel is present, citizens are looking to kill any American souls, for what they did to their country. 

The film begins with a beautiful narration, which literally throws the audience in the midst of terror in Iran, at the U.S. Embassy, it's being raided. Six Americans manage to escape. Boy, they sure did a fantastic job of making their character look authentic. They looked like they were in the 70's, early 80's. The mustaches, big glasses, flat top hair. It's very believable. Although, some of the exterior shots in both the United States and Iran look like they were shot in present day. 

The situation is so bad in Iran, that a regular exfiltration will not work. A plan, a risky plan, a plan so ridiculous and over the top, you would think it's a movie. That's where the 1st act hits, and it's fantastic. Tony's watching a movie on his television, the camera slowly dollies into to his eyes, and it hits him. They'll be making a fake movie, the six Americans will be posing as film crew members. The proposed film is named Argo. A sci-fi adventure in the Middle East, it works out like a charm. I wish we could've seen more of them posing as a film crew, but I guess since it's a real story, that's what really happened. It's riveting, when you see them make mistakes, and often nail biting too.

Argo goes into overdrive mode in it's 3rd act. It is absolutely brilliant, parallel action from one place to another, tense music and throw in fantastic acting too. Everyone is on top form. Ben Affleck as Tony Mendez, John Goodman as legendary make-up artist John Chambers (did make-up for Planet of The Apes), Alan Arkin as Tony Seigel and Bryan Cranston as Jack O' Donnell. Cranston does a mighty fine job, switching from a powerful person to a helpless one with his eyes and voice. Affleck as Tony Mendez fits the role perfectly, a soft spoken but driven expert in his field. People might say he's trying to throw his name in the film, not at all, this role was tailor-made for him, and it feels less forced than his last outing in his own film, The Town (2010).

Argo has some absolutely brilliant technical work. The cinematography by Rodrigo Prieto is fitting for the film, they had cut the frames in half and blown it up by 200% to give it an authentic 70's look to the film. Not only the look, but the camera movements, the placement is all fantastic. Goes hand in hand with the editing, sometimes the place the shot ends, makes it so much easier for the editor - William Goldenberg, who also does a fine job. The film has many instances where there are 2-3 actions taking place at the same time, parallel action we call it, it's seamless and very easy to follow and hard not to appreciate. The film paces very well too, as I said when you're in the 3rd act, you're glued to edge of your seat, hoping everything ends out well.

When I saw this film, I said to myself. There is no such thing as a perfect film, but Argo is the closest thing you'll see this year which is extremely close to a perfect film. An excellent job, one of the best films of the year.

A CIA operative ushers six Americans out of Iran during the 1979-1980 Iranian hostage crisis by pretending to make a science fiction film. This is a tense, understated thriller, drawing its drama from the ever-present threat that the protagonists might get caught and killed. It's the only film I've ever seen that can make going through customs seem like a dramatic experience. For the most part, Argo succeeds in ellicting a heavy tension. The film begins with fast-paced, witty dialogue as writer Chris Terrio channels his inner Aaron Sorkin. Alan Arkin and John Goodman are fantastic as Hollywood moguls building the CIA cover story; they spit out witticisms with such aplomb that I was reminded of the best scenes from Wag the Dog. But when Affleck's character, Tony Mendez, takes over the film, the mood changes, the pace slows, and I found myself missing Arkin; if only his character went to Iran too ... The pace picks up in the third act, but the second act lull is almost too steep a hill to climb. As the film progresses, we don't get to learn much about Mendez. There is one scene in which Mendez grills the six entrapped Americans about their identities, and it's Affleck at his Chuckie-from-Good-Will-Hunting best. But the remainder of his performance focuses on his tense, worried face. Actors say that playing drunk is hard because one has to pretend not to be drunk; the same goes for "worried liars." One has to pretend not to be a worried liar, and Affleck and the rest of his clan look like worried liars. What's more, the last shot of the film fails to compel because not knowing enough about Mendez, we don't know enough about the set-up to be inspired by the reunion. Overall, I liked Argo because it is a well-made thriller and a fine, harrowing story, but the poor pacing and its inability to fully explore the main character made me want more out of the film.

'Argo' presents maybe the greatest, if not the most absurd, account of American foreign policy espionage widely unbeknownst to the greater majority. The story, which falls perfectly into the category of you-can't-make-this-kind-of-thing-up, is based upon Tony Mendez's rescue of six isolated US diplomats out of Iran, during the time of the Iranian hostage crisis of 1980, through the means of creating a fake film production as cover.

Director Ben Affleck proves here just how incredibly mature and restrained a filmmaker he's become, molding what is inherently a political story, yet wisely setting aside the politics. He masterfully handles the changes in tone very fluidly, from one moment being edge of your seat tension, to the next of inspired comic relief. It brings back memories of 70's thrillers, when craft and entertaining went together hand-in-hand.

The cast of veteran character-actors is worth the price of admission alone. Nearly every speaking role is occupied by a recognizable face, with the likes of Philip Baker Hall, Bob Gunton, Michael Parks, Kyle Chandler, John Goodman, Bryan Cranston, Alan Arkin, and more. This is easily one of  the best casts of 2012 (right behind The Dark Knight Rises) and, better yet, they all brought out there A game.

"Argo fuck yourself"
Do you see what they did there? That line of dialogue, repeated several times in the film, is a simple yet very effective play on words to help open up the film to some darkly comic material; an added dimension to an extremely tense and exciting film about a mission to rescue 6 Americans in an Iranian hostage crisis. How can you possibly rescue 6 Americans in Iran without a possibility of hostage exchange or being noticed by Iranian officials? Well, it's simple. You come up with the "best bad idea" that a government agency can: making a fake movie on foreign soil. 
The power of the film industry is astounding. Even in the most hostile of countries where war and violence are so prevalent, Hollywood can still find the permits and make its way into such a dangerous environment. Of course, they would never allow Americans to do so, though. Ben Affleck, who plays Tony Mendez, is a CIA exfiltration specialist who flies to Iran to make sure that the 6 Americans he is going to rescue are able to keep there cover as part of his Canadian film production company. It is surely a dangerous mission for everyone a part of it. It requires a director, producer, and all the rest of a crew. The movie needs a script, it needs story boards, and it needs an exact location to shoot. A whole lot of stuff has to go perfect in order for the mission to be a success. Amazingly, the story is true, making the story one that is hard to forget. 
Let's not forget that this mission took place in 1979 and was classified until, as the credits teach us, Bill Clinton declassified the mission. Thanks Bill. It is a fascinating mission that had to be put on screen. Of course, the mission surely did not play out exactly as the film tells it, especially in the final act of the film when its basically a race to get the plane home in the air before the Iranians realize there really is no movie. But it provides incredible thrills. 
Ben Affleck has really established himself as a director. He knew his niche right from the beginning with "Gone Baby Gone" and following it with "The Town." He knows how to create tension and excitement without sacrificing artistic quality. In "Argo," he mixes film textures to create a documentary style feel to certain moments to remind audiences just how real this mission was. This is not simply a made up Hollywood story, this was real (for the most part), and Affleck wanted to reinforce that idea. 
The film opens with the 6 Americans in Iran on the verge of being in a disastrous spot. A huge mob of angry locals are storming the U.S. embassy in Tehran but they manage to hide out in the home of the Canadian ambassador. This scene establishes a tension right from the beginning without introducing any of the characters in depth, an impressive feat. It is understood that these 6 people are in trouble. It is understood that they need to be saved. So, operation Argo is a go. 
Ben Affleck's character does not show a whole lot of emotion in the film. I'll assume this is purposeful. I think Affleck has solidified himself as a better director than he is actor, but this role was opportunistic for Affleck because it wasn't too demanding. He just had to make sure his fake film crew understood the importance of their cover to make it home safely. He does so in a very serious and effective manner. The best two roles of the film belong to John Goodman and Alan Arkin who knock it out of the park in very limited screen time. Both act as comic relief during the pre-production for Argo, the film within the film, sequences.
There was a part of the story i did have a gripe with. Mendez has a son and a wife.  While it is always an important background to establish for a character if he or she does have a family, it felt like the family dynamic was just thrown in there. Yes, in real life, Tony Mendez may very well have had a wife and son. However, for the story, it didn't seem necessary. It was sort of just added on emotion. While Mendez was in danger in Iran, I never really thought about how his son and wife would react if he didn't come back for some unknown reason (the mission was classified, even to them) and while Mendez was surely thinking about them while doing the mission, it was never really demonstrated. 
One other gripe I have had to with the pacing of the pre-production part of getting the Argo film together. It felt rushed. It felt as if "alright we just have to get this part out of the way so we can get to the exciting stuff again." This may be pushing it, even for a critic like myself, but it's how I felt. 
Argo felt like an episode of "24" (never a bad thing if I do say so myself) without all the ridiculous subplots the show featured. It was tense, exciting, and appropriately funny. I am excited for the next Affleck directorial piece. It will be interesting if he decides to direct something in a different genre. Or he may just tell anyone who wants to throw him a different genre "Argo fuck yourself."

Synopsis:  In 1979, when Iranian militants seize the American embassy, six Americans slip into the Canadian embassy for protection, prompting the CIA to concoct an elaborate plot to rescue them by pretending that they are filmmakers rather than diplomats.

Often there is a huge schism between what the general moviegoing population want to see and what awards firms like the academy choose to nominate.  In general, people want to see fantastical worlds, events, and characters, even if they do not realize it.  What do The Hangover, Twilight, and virtually all the biggest hit movies of the past ten years have in common? Most of them are relatively ridiculous and fantastical.  And if you want to get some love from the academy of motion picture arts and sciences your movie better have a firm foot on earth.  In other words if you want a prestigious award, your going to have to make the kinds of films that for some reason or another, do not attract the same kind of mass population as the former.

Ben Affleck seams to be on a mission to destroy this fact.  His last film effort, The Town, was rooted in fantastical elements but chose to hide these elements until the endgame.  The result was a film that felt much more mature than it had the right to be.  With Argo, Affleck has found a story that satisfies film snobs requirement of maturity in storytelling and depth of craftsmanship.  And although the film itself isn't rooted in the fantastical (it's about the Iranian hostage crisis of the 1970's) it's seed is very much oriented around the concept of a heist film.  Probably a big reason Affleck accepted to direct it, a wise decision as it could very well be the finest of his trilogy of directorial efforts.

I only wish there was a more standout performance from one of it's actors.  The Town was filled to the brim with some of it's year's very best performances (Jeremy Renner was even nominated for best supporting actor).  There is no such acting tour de force here with Argo.  John Goodman and Alan Arkin team up for the standout performances, though in actuality their characters feel too much like comic relief to put much praise into their portrayals.

But not having one of the best performances of the year is a little too much to ask of a film in the first place.  Especially when a film is directed with as much precision, acted with such sufficiency, and written as well as Argo has been.  It's undeniably one of the years best pictures.

It is nail biting, re-creates the mood precisely, and features great non-performances from the cast - it almost plays as a documentary in Iran, but that is down to the skill of the cast and Affleck.

They are funny, sharp and add the spice that the rest of the film deliberately avoids like poison. The script is exemplarly, tight, believable, and compelling.

Films this good never win Oscars. They are not flashy enough, emotional enough, and they never do great box office. But they do win Blockies - my own awards.

I have long said that the only time I can stand Ben Affleck in a film is when he personally directs it. Or he has a very large hand in the films creation. Or if he dies within the first twenty minutes (Thank you Smokin' Aces). Because Ben Affleck, is a great director. Not just good, not just talented, but great. Gone Baby Gone could have been a fluke. The Town meant that there had to be another reason besides a fluke. And now Argo confirms it, Affleck knows what he is doing.
	Set amidst the political turmoil of late 70s and early 80s Iran, Argo is the story of six American embassy employees who were rescued through a hilariously sitcom like plan and international cooperation. If you remember your history correctly, you will remember that under the Carter administration the U.S. Embassy in Iran was taken over by a very anti-U.S. Iranians. About 40 or so Americans were held captive for over a year in Iran. What most people don't know is that six of them escaped before the place was overrun and took shelter at the Canadian Ambassador's home.
	Enter CIA agent Tony Mendez (Ben Affleck). A specialist in exfiltration, Mendez was assigned the responsibility of getting them out. After running through plan after plan that just didn't seem to work Mendez got a crazy idea: pretend the Americans were a Canadian film crew working on a sci-fi film that they wanted to film a part of in Tehran. Mendez flies into Iran pretending to be Canadian, and gets the Americans to do the same so that they can all fly out together.
	And it's all a true story! Mostly. But the story that we have, however Hollywoodized is wonderful. The opening scenes of the movie, the gathering crowd outside the embassy, the horrified employees inside quipping, "it looks bigger today," are so tense, everyone is waiting for the pin drop. And drop it does when the protestors finally decide to climb the wall.
	Tense is the name of the game. The opening scenes, the walk and drive through crowded squares of angry Iranians and the final harrowing airport scene where one slipup of identity results in probable death for all involved.
	The superb acting by all involved, especially Bryan Cranston, Ben Affleck, John Goodman, and Alan Arkin, coupled with both fantastic writing and pacing provides for a very entertaining film that does almost nothing wrong.
	There are a couple of things I noticed. One, is the Iranian girl who looks like she might betray the Americans but instead risks her life for them. When she crosses the border to Iraq, we see nothing more of her. She isn't explained in the credits which leads me to believe she was an entirely fabricated character for an interesting plot point.
	And that is a real detriment throughout. There's a nagging thought that reappears, "how much of this is real?" And for me, after doing some quick wikipediaing, enough of it is to disappoint me.
	But the spirit of the film is still all there. The tension is through the roof and the sharp writing is both entertaining and dramatic. I'm sad I didn't see it sooner.

Ben Affleckâ(TM)s third film as director, Argo, tells the declassified story of the mission to rescue six American diplomats from Iran as the Iranian hostage crisis unfolds. The film is loosely based off the account of Tony Mendez, a CIA specialist whom Affleck portrays.
In 1979 the United States embassy in Iran was attacked by anti-American protestors, and employees escaped as the mob breaches the building. The CIA then worked to find a way to rescue them without risking the safety of the hostages.
After many ideas were trashed, Mendez came to a solution while watching Battle for the Planet of the Apes that an agent and the diplomats pose as a film crew location scouting for a movie. The movie had to be real, but it would never actually be made. The script selected is entitled Argo.
Everything about this movie is gripping and entertaining. Every scene holds the viewersâ(TM) attention whether through laughs or suspense. Even if you know how the situation plays out, the fact that this is a true story grasps viewers.
There is not nearly as much violence as expected in Argo. While there are disturbing images, there is no graphic violence. There are very few gunshots in the movie, which simply builds the intensity. However, there are several portrayals of violent protests and civil unrest.
John Goodman plays John Chambers, the makeup artist from the Planet of the Apes series, who has helped the CIA in previous operations. He convinces a movie producer, Lester Siegel, to produce the fake movie and assist in the operation. Goodman shines on screen for the few scenes he is in, but he is almost overshadowed by Alan Arkin.
Arkin plays Siegel, and he simply steals the show in every scene he is in. Almost every line he has is either quotable or will have you laughing out loud. With either flat out vulgarity or a witty remark about Hollywood, Arkin will keep the viewersâ(TM) attention.
Bryan Cranston from AMCâ(TM)s âBreaking Badâ? plays Mendezâ(TM)s CIA supervisor, Jack Oâ(TM)Donnell. Cranston is not in the movie as much I expected him to be. If he were more present in the movie, I would say Cranstonâ(TM)s performance was Oscar worthy. The pressure the character is under is clearly visible to the audience.
The movie is propelled by the true story aspect, so there is little room for character development. Surprisingly, as little as we know about each character, we feel the stress of all of them. Ben Affleckâ(TM)s character is solemn but not wooden. If there are any characters you connect to in this movie, they would be the diplomats being rescued.
I was surprised to see little to none of President Jimmy Carter. The film uses footage from the events, including a couple of glimpses at President Carter. This was actually a good thing for the movie, because many films involving government operations such as this tend to involve too much of the president. If Carter were to be in the film, he would be a part of another story arc the audience has to follow.
In short, Argo is one of the best movies of 2012. I expect Affleck to win best director, if not- he should at least receive a nomination for an Oscar. I would recommend this movie to anybody who likes historical films or a good thriller. The movie is rated R for strong language, smoking and drinking throughout, and some disturbing images. I thoroughly enjoyed Ben Affleckâ(TM)s work in this film, and I look forward to his next project.

After thinking his first directorial effort 'Gone Baby Gone' was a one shot masterpiece, he followed that up three years later with 'The Town', a film that should have saw Oscar praise. Now, two years after 'The Town', Affleck surely presents us with probably the best film of the year: 'Argo'. I am hoping that his next project is sooner rather than later based on his consistent maturity and growth as a filmmaker.

There is a trick to making a film based on ACTUAL events (as opposed to INSPIRED by true events, which essentially means the only grain of truth to the story is something in the premise); how do you make a film thrilling, tense and engrossing when most of the people viewing it already know the outcome? Affleck handles this deftly by giving the film a documentary feel that is rich in detail with actors that eerily look like the people they are portraying and by sticking to the true situation rather than a fictionalisation of events. When Affleck does (as he goes for several feel good moments) the film falters a bit, but only a bit and it does not take away from the films near perfection.

'Argo' is based on the true story of CIA agent Tony Mendez (Affleck) and his mission to free six American citizens during the 1979 Iran Hostage Crisis. As the US Embassy in Iran was being overrun, these six citizens, workers within the embassy, were able to escape and remain hidden in the home of the Canadian Ambassador.  As the CIA fumbles with insane plans of using bicycles to get the trapped US citizens to Turkey, Mendez, who specializes in extraction, develops the idea to pose as a Hollywood producing scouting Iran for a science fiction movie shoot and sneak the six out posing as the film crew.

Mendez partners with his old friend (and make-up artist who has helped him in past missions) John Chambers (John Goodman, as strong as always in a fantastic role); together they enlist the help of a producer, Lester Siegel (the hilarious Alan Arkin) and put together a completely believable, fake movie cover for the Iranians to buy. Amazingly so, the humor works well in the scenes shot in Hollywood bringing a much needed rest from the tension building in Iran. Affleck handles this well and his cast treats the script perfectly. Bryan Cranston as CIA lead Jack O'Donnell once again proves why he is one of the best character actors performing today. Victor Garber as the Canadian Ambassador is as amazing as always.

Affleck's touch here is nearly flawless, from the late 70's Warner Brothers logo during the credits, to the grainy film stock used, to the hand held documentary feel, to the use of period strong music; Affleck submerges us into the situation. You will walk out of the theater exhausted from the ride, but you will feel good about the ability of governments to cooperate in the desperate time of a nation gone mad. Affleck pulls no punches in portraying the students and the Iranain goverment for what it was, people who wanted to kill Westerners simply because they did not believe as they did. It's no surprise that while majoring in film studies, Affleck also majored in Middle Eastern studies.

Affleck is quickly building the reputation of an Oscar winning director; justifiably so with this 4 star effort that should be seen by the entire nation.

Hailed as Ben Affleck's best directorial effort, Argo chronicles the incredible rescue of six U.S. embassy employees who found refuge at the Canadian ambassador's private residence during the Iranian hostage crisis of 1979. The film revolves around Tony Mendez (played by Affleck himself), an intrepid CIA agent who comes up with "the best worst idea" to rescue the refugees: creating a fake Canadian film production and sending a crew to Iran under the guise of scouting locations for a new Sci-Fi movie - the eponymous Argo. Once the Brechtian plan is approved, Mendez flies to Hollywood to recruit the wizard of disguise, John Chambers (John Goodman), the legendary makeup artist who received an Oscar for "Planet of the Apes" - and the old school producer Lester Siegel (Alan Arkin).
If it were not based on real events, the only possible adjective for this movie would be 'grotesque'. And yet, meticulous attention to detail, an aesthetic evocative of the 70s, a bunch of striking lines and a memorable soundtrack (Dream On by Aerosmith sticks in the mind for days) make of Argo one of the favorite candidates in the running for the Oscars.
With an opening gambit that is worth the whole movie, the helmer hooks the audience by crosscutting images of the angry Iranian revolutionaries outside the U.S. embassy with those of the besieged Americans stuck inside, in a pulse-raising sequence that quickly plunges the spectators into a nail-biting spy story that will turn out to be surprisingly funny. The director, in fact, shrewdly mingles elements of action and humor, giving birth to a brand new genre which is a cross between a thriller and a dark comedy. Perfectly orchestrated, Argo finds the right balance between humor and suspense. Indeed, the Hollywood farce serves as a light counterpoint to the tension, bringing levity when the pace becomes breathless.
Although more on the comedy side, Argo makes room for criticism of Iranian society. Affleck, better behind than on camera, zealously depicts a country with all its contradictions through an emblematic sequence of images: a crowded street in Tehran where a woman in a chador eats Kentucky Fried Chicken (a symbol of the previous pro-American Shah's regime), a dead man hanging from a crane as people walk beneath him amid general indifference.
That's Affleck's final statement on the Iranian revolution and its paradox. Such uncanny images echo recent political turmoil throughout Maghreb. This reference to the so-called 'Arab Spring' is more than a coincidence. The never-ending conflict between Islam and the U.S has never been so alive, and Affleck is aware that one of the secrets to please the Academy is a certain kind of reference to current events. The race for the Oscars is on.
