This is Ben Affleck`s third film as a director and he`s made yet another brilliant film. Not everyone may agree that he`s a good actor, but I think we can all agree that he`s one of the top directors of this century. His first film Gone Baby Gone was a huge success, and he followed that with an even greater hit: The Town. Both these films were set in Boston (Affleck`s home town), but now Ben went out of his comfort zone and directed a film set in Iran in the late 70`s. The general look of the film felt so real and authentic; it was as if Affleck transported us into the past and we were really there. The film has an authentic 70`s vibe that reminds us of other great films from that period. I had my doubts about Argo considering the subject matter. I didn't think it would keep my attention for long, but I was wrong because Affleck was able to create so much tension and suspense that I was at the edge of my seat during most of the film. He also mixed that tension with some humor and movie industry satire. Arkin played a movie producer and Goodman an Oscar winning makeup artist; the scenes between both these actors were hilarious and they were on top of their game. Those scenes were probably among my favorite of the movie, I don't know if I would`ve enjoyed the movie as much as I did if it weren't for those two supporting actors. I still think Gone Baby Gone and The Town were both better films than Argo, but this will surely have more success with the Academy voters. Argo will be nominated for Best Picture and could be one of the favorites to win the Oscar.

The film is based on true events that occurred during 1979 while tension arose between the United States and Iran when Iranian revolutionaries invaded the American embassy in Iran and took several American hostages. Six American employees managed to secretly escape during the turmoil and found refugee in the residence of the Canadian Ambassador. The CIA then plans a secret mission to try to take them out of the country before the Iranians realize that six of the employees from the Embassy are missing. Tony Mendez (Ben Affleck), a CIA exfiltration expert, comes up with a risky plan to bring them back home safely. He creates a fake Canadian film project and travels to Iran with the excuse that he is looking for locations to shoot his sci-fi film titled Argo claiming that Iran is the perfect spot. In order to make his plan believable the CIA begins to collaborate with some trusted Hollywood people: Lester Siegel (Alan Arkin), a film producer, and John Chambers (John Goodman), a make-up artist. Together they prepare to produce the best fake movie Hollywood has ever made and has everyone in the industry fall for the lie. Meanwhile at the residence of Canadian Ambassador, Ken Taylor (Victor Garber), tension is beginning to rise as the revolutionaries are beginning to suspect that there might be some Americans hiding there. These Americans are Bob (Tate Donovan), Cora (Clea DuVall), Joe (Scoot McNairy), Lee (Rory Cochrane), Mark (Christopher Denham), and Kathy (Kerry Bishe). Tony Mendez provides them with Canadian passports and a fake identity and has them each passing for crew members of the film he`s producing. Bryan Cranston plays Affleck`s supervisor in the CIA who gives him the green light for the highly risky mission.

Saying that Argo is based on a true story doesn't mean that everything that happened in this film was real. Of course you have several things that were made up in order to build up the tension. This isn't a documentary and if you want to read about the real story there is plenty of information about what happened in Iran. The film is based on the article written by Joshua Bearman and the screenplay adapted by Chris Terrio. People familiar with the story already know the outcome, but Affleck is able to maintain the suspense and tension nonetheless. His real success here was the way in which he was able to recreate several scenes in such a believable fashion. The amount of attention he put into small technical details can be seen during the end credits where we have pictures of the real events along with the scenes from the film. Affleck also took a huge risk by mixing movie industry satire with suspense and tension, but it paid off really well and was the highlight of the film in my opinion. Argo is a truly satisfying film and without a doubt one of the best films of the year thanks to the technical aspects of the film, a strong performance from the cast, and the thrilling storytelling all supported by the great direction of Ben Affleck.

Remember ten years ago when everyone was making fun of Ben Affleck? Remember when he was one of the biggest jokes in Hollywood who no one in pop culture thought could act? The ten years that followed proved all of them wrong and I am certainly grateful for it. I took part in making fun of him because I was twelve and didn't know any better but had anyone watched anything he did before Gili? Was: Good Will Hunting and Shakespeare in Love not proof enough that he's actually a good actor? Of course Pearl Harbour and Armageddon were awful and Affleck was awful in them but we had proof beforehand that he is a very good actor.
 
But how we didn't expect to be surprised by Affleck was his astonishing skill as a director. His directorial debut came in 2007 with Gone Baby Gone, which is a damn good movie with a great story and interesting characters that excellently developed suspense. Three years later Affleck returned to the director's chair with The Town and had Christopher Nolan's Inception not come out the same year Affleck's sophomore effort would have been the best movie of 2010. It had great and complex characters with greatly shot action set pieces which were surprisingly intense. Affleck's third trip to the director's position is Argo which is supposedly based on a true story. Not only is this a fantastic movie which you should all see immediately, its climax was the most intense pieces of filmmaking I've seen in YEARS. 
 
The "true story" is the aftermath of the Iranian revolution where angry Iranian students capture several workers at the American embassy in Iran and take them hostage. What they didn't know as that six embassy workers escaped capture and were taking refuge in the home of the Canadian ambassador Ken Taylor (Victor Garber). CIA specialist Tony Mendez (Ben Affleck) comes up with the idea to help these six escape Iran to try and pass them off as filmmakers who are doing location scouting for an elaborate science-fiction movie. Tony must get these six to know there parts so they can escape the country without being executed by the students who had stormed the embassy initially. 
 
What makes Argo one of the best films this year is the way it tells the story. It never doubts for a second the severity of the events and consequences these characters could be facing but still eases the audience in via comedy without ever coming across as quaint. This is because the characters responsible for the fake production company John Chambers (John Goodman) and Lester Siegel (Alan Arkin) are hilarious. The dialogue given to them by screenwriter Chris Terrio, is witty, hilarious, vulgar and endlessly quotable. 
 
But after this introduction and Mendez is in Tehran to help these embassy workers escape, the audience is reminded again just what the stakes are. Itâ(TM)s the use of simple shots of violent protesters or a body hanging above the streets that provide the audience with this information and we as a result take it to heart. We care about those people and want them to get home alive and safely but we know just how difficult it's going to be and the suspense is that much more tense making everything else in the movie that much more exciting. It's the "show don't tell" rule of filmmaking in practise and proof that it's the most effective way of telling a story with this medium.
 
Argo is worth seeing because it's a very intelligent, tense and exciting espionage thriller with great characters, outstanding direction and even has the ability to be hilarious in moments as well, but I don't think I can finish this review without addressing the elephant in the room. The film has received some controversy in Canada because of the way the film downplays the Canadian role in the real life mission, especially in the case of Ken Taylor himself. Based on the research I've done about the actual history the people with these complaints do have a point.  The Canadians did play a much larger part in the actual mission than the film gives them credit for. 
 
That being taken into account, do I care, or am I offended as a Canadian, or does this make me think less of the film? NO! Not in the slightest because I'm aware what I saw is a MOVIE and not a tool for history education. I went to see it because I wanted to see a well told story and I got exactly that. The idea that a lot of it wasn't true or some of the things that were true weren't shown is irrelevant to me. The only thing that I would say bothered me about the omission of certain truths surrounding the event is that the real Tony Mendez is a Hispanic man who was played by a white actor. I will criticize the film for that because it's hard enough for non-white actors to make it big in Hollywood because of how few roles are available to them and changing races like that doesn't help the issue. 
 
But even that misnomer didn't decrease my enjoyment of the movie at all. This is a great one folks, see it!

The premise of 'Argo' is simply too nuts not to be based on a true story. Set during the Iranian Hostage Crisis of 1979, Argo stars Ben Affleck as Tony Mendez, a CIA operative, charged with the unenviable task of rescuing six US diplomats hiding out at the Canadian embassy in Tehran from Iranian militants. Inspired by a glance at the then-new Battle for the Planet of the Apes, he creates a front to sneak them out: they are Canadian filmmakers out shooting some desert scenes for a science fiction movie. Directed and co-produced also by Affleck (alongside George Clooney, of all people), 'Argo' has been receiving widespread acclaim. Is it justified?

Yes. There can be no mincing of words: this film is awesome. The palpable tension combines with superb acting and storytelling to create a vividly detailed and absolutely unforgettable film. That such tension and anxiety can be generated in the viewer, even though they know the outcome, is impressive.The darkly goofy inside-Hollywood comedy contrasts with the grimy themes of terrorism and overly-zealous religious mania marvellously. What would seem like two genres completely at odds with each other are brought together seamlessly and the end result is immaculate. In theory it shouldn't, nay, couldn't work, but Affleck has struck gold here.

Being based on a historical event always leads to the same question: is it historically accurate? While it does take some liberties, for the most part this movie stays true to the actual events (a nice little nugget of context is given at the beginning, which preps the viewer on Middle-Eastern history), while simultaneously providing a near-obsessive attention to detail. The 70s dÃ (C)cor and cultural references are spot on. The actors and scenes resemble the real deal to a tee, and the closing slideshow of photos which pre-empts the credits illustrates this. Affleck has clearly poured a lot of effort into this project, and it shows. This makes 'Skyfall' look decidedly average by comparison.

The artistic licence that the film does take is subtle enough to add to the overall experience without undermining its authenticity. In fact, certain events which actually happened were deemed too silly to include: one of the men kept calling his friends by their real names instead of their aliases, for instance. The added drama, such as the cars chasing the plane as it takes off at the end, didn't ring quite as true for me as the rest of the film did; once it begins to rely on traditional action movie tropes, it jars slightly with the established realism of the film. This is a very minor complaint and takes nothing away from the overall experience, however.

Of course, 'Argo' is an undeniably political film, and as such it raises several questions. Does it portray the USA as the heroes, and the Iranians as villains, as is the typical West vs. East scenario? Not quite. The frustrated plight of the Iran people is clearly explained at the start, though their frankly barbaric and animalistic behaviour certainly puts them in a negative light. 'Argo' endeavours to emphasise the importance of international cooperation in world politics, as well as the redundancy of war in general. Though this film packs such a dramatic punch that all of the above could be ignored and the movie would still be thoroughly enjoyable.

As opposed to his mediocre reputation as an actor, Ben Affleck has become a more successful film director following his debut feature Gone Baby Gone in 2007 and more recently The Town in 2010. Next on the agenda is Argo, another thriller set in the complex, political world. However, Affleck provides a sense of genius with Argo as it is not only a thriller about rescuing American captives from Iran, but also about the usefulness and charm of film. Sure, when you look at it that way, the plot is extraordinary but Argo has still got a hint of intelligence behind it. Therefore, Ben Affleck's latest feature is not only about the complicating world of politics and the creativity of cinema, but also represents themes of bravery and commitment.


Considering his long filmography of mediocre on-screen performances and following only three features as director thus far, we have established Ben Affleck is more gifted when behind the camera. His direction in Argo is sublime! The opening sequence immediately sets up the forthcoming narrative of the film and, therefore, sends the audience into a suspenseful, gripping mood. After a very long and occasionally slow build-up, the nail-biting tension rapidly heats up upon arriving in Iran. In addition, Affleck illustrates the creativity of cinema in a more political way as opposed to a visual representation of the art like we saw in Martin Scorsese's Hugo. With this in mind and being a true story, Argo indicates the complexity of politics and government with the fascination of cinema in a reality form of art.


Let's face it, Ben Affleck may have had the odd few decent performances throughout his career but he has never truly proved himself worthy as a talented actor. He appeared as the central character in his own film The Town, but Affleck returns as a leading actor as well as director to portray protagonist CIA specialist Tony Mendez. This character is leading the whole idea behind the fake film Argo as well as being the one to enter Iran to rescue the 6 hostages. However, although Affleck sparked as a leader at a satisfactory level, he slightly lacked the heroism and courage that symbolizes the character and what Tony Mendez himself had done. 


Meanwhile, the majority of supporting cast in Argo were in roles playing characters that specialize part of film production. First, Alan Arkin portrays producer Lester Siegel in a performance that mixes the occasionally light humour and makes the film, at times, hilarious to watch. This makes Arkin the stand-out of the film and he deserves another opportunity at Oscar glory. Furthermore, John Goodman makes an appearance as make-up artist John Chambers. Goodman who ironically had another role playing a character part of the film industry in 2011 Best Picture winner The Artist, delivers a solid performance that is not quite as brilliant as Arkin's but is still impressive enough to appreciate.


Argo may look your traditional boring and complex political feature but it is important to note that, alongside cinema, it is a film of creativity and skill. It is a film that can be seen as just plain Hollywood entertainment but Affleck's marvellous direction proves that there is more to Argo than that. Therefore, it is a remarkable feature from Ben Affleck, who outshines himself by overlapping his gift as a director with his vintage satisfactory performance, and deserves critical acclaim and recognition at the upcoming Academy Awards.

In 1979, the American embassy in Iran was invaded by Iranian revolutionaries and several Americans were taken hostage. However, six managed to escape to the official residence of the Canadian Ambassador and the CIA was eventually ordered to get them out of the country. With few options, exfiltration expert Tony Mendez devised a daring plan: to create a phony Canadian film project looking to shoot in Iran and smuggle the Americans out as its production crew. With the help of some trusted Hollywood contacts, Mendez created the ruse and proceed to Iran as its associate producer. However, time was running out with the Iranian security forces closing in on the truth while both his charges and the White House had grave doubts about the operation themselves.

Affleck And Arkin Excavate Americans

Argo is a movie that has been showered with critical acclaim, with 5 stars and other perfect ratings being openly handed to it, so why has no one gone to see it?

As always, timing is everything, and it truth Argo's timing is nothing short of horrific! It's been released so close to Skyfall there is almost no room at all for it at the cinemas and no time for publicity. It's almost as if Ben Affleck wanted to hide his own project about a hidden American mission. But I suppose the real question is, will Argo just be Argovation?

Argo is the true (ish) story of a declassified mission revolving around 6 Americans, an Iran rebellion and a fake film made to look real.

I'm conscious of giving away too much of the plot in this review, however I think Argo is best enjoyed with minimal knowledge. That's not to say there are any twist endings to the movie, like it's all a dream. This is after all based on a true story, however one of Argo's real strengths is that it takes what could have been boring and mundane, and makes it gripping, right from the outset.

When you think about it, that's high praise indeed for Ben Affleck (as he directs and stars in the movie), there isn't a moment in Agro where we as the audience are not engaged nor interested in, when you consider this is a movie where for chunks of it, the people in "jeopardy" do nothing more than sit around in a house, you can understand the achievement.

Those sequences fail at being boring because Affleck pumps every scene with tension, there is a feeling at all times that these people could be killed at any given moment, they are not safe, even in a safe house. It's more than that though, Affleck successfully maintains conflict in every relationship, between the hostages with each other, between the husband and wives for what they should do, between the government and Iraq for withholding their demands, with Affleck and his superiors for their misjudged plans. In Argo there are battles everywhere.

Argo is a movie that really highlights to us what really happens behind all the closed doors, in extracting people. In our heads it's the likes of Jason Bourne and Ethan Hunt swooping in guns blazing to save anyone from any situation no matter how badly they are outnumbered, the truth is much more ordinary then that. The truth is, it is people in a room, making suggestions. That's it. So much of the movie is eaten up by the planning stages of the operation that when it comes to the actual moment of truth, everyone is not bored and emotionally engaged.

I don't think it's the people we care about as such, I don't think it's the 6 Americans who the mission is to save, I think who we care about is the moral stability, and emotional welfare of Tony Mendez that really grips us as an audience. Mendez is a man who clearly holds himself accountable for whatever may happen to these people.

What else is distinctively impressive about Argo is that it uses raw footage to it's advantage. Affleck splices in moments that were shot at the time at the scenes in his own movie. But then the question mark always hangs over a movie like this for accuracy, how authentic is it? Well I can honestly say that Argo is one of the most authentic movies I've ever seen in that regard. During the credits we are shown images from the original events put side by side with the images from the film and they look identical.

All of the cast are convincing and dedicated in their given roles no matter how big or small, of course the headliners are the people putting in the most work. Alan Arkin, Bryan Cranston and John Goodman all steal the show, however it is Ben Affleck himself who gives the most to Argo, it's clear that this is his baby, and he should be a proud father indeed.

Argo ultimately, is an old school spy thriller with both its head and heart in the right place, Affleck's strongest work yet from behind the camera.

Affleck directs Affleck for the third time in Argo, after the excellent (if fantastical) Gone Baby Gone and the earnest (but average) The Town. The good news is that, all in all, Argo hits many more times than it misses, with Affleck's good eye for what makes a tense thriller coming through in spades. Add to that a decent ensemble cast and an intriguing recent historical backdrop and you've got one of the winter period's best crowd pleasers, so best to bring popcorn.
After an attention grabbing story-board style opening giving the context, the film opens with the American embassy in Iran being ransacked. In many ways is symptomatic of the film; the politics are declared early and afterwards fade into the background. Despite the factual framework, it is a film that is more about a group of people trying to survive under pressure. This style of the film is both its greatest strength and weakness. Tackling the hostage crisis is heavy duty stuff, but by drawing attention away from the actual hostages themselves and focusing on a small group of escapees, the film manages to avoid much of the controversial political intrigue. Instead, the film is a direct CIA thriller, depicting attempts to remove the escapees from Iran. No spoilers; the plan for escape is novel, and all the more entertaining for being true. Still, while not necessarily a flaw, this approach may leave the viewer hoping for something more sophisticated. Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy this isn't.
Still, the film is at its best when it has your pulse racing. There are scenes that are genuinely seat-gripping, made more remarkable for their simplicity. A walk through a crowded market place, questions over loyalties, concerns over the odds of success: all these moments are superb, paced perfectly to maximise heart rate. When the action gets a touch overblown you may feel your engagement slipping, largely because the film is in many ways better than that. It is convincing before the limits of plausibility are pushed; by making it more of an action movie it cheapens the rest of the experience.
Some small niggles aside, if you take the film for the thriller it is there is much enjoyment to be had. All round, the cast are excellent. John Goodman never disappoints, and Breaking Bad's Bryan Cranston adds another arrow to his rapidly growing quiver. The cast of escapees is well chosen, and Kermode's suggestion that casting lesser known actors allows us to empathise with them rings true. Finally, it is great to see Affleck's acting continuing to develop after his decent turn in The Town; it would seemthe unfortunate episodes of Gigli and Daredevil really are behind him. Argo is very good and, thankfully, Affleck's return to form is beginning to look rather permanent.

Quick Review:

Argo is a film that takes place during the Iranian hostage crisis.  After the US granted alyssum to the Shah, a brutal dictator who ruled with an iron fist a mob overran the US embassy demanding his extradition.  52 embassy staff were captured and held hostage for over a year.  

However, this story  involves six workers who were able to escape the overrun and fled to the canadian embassy.  The six spent months Anne Frank style hidden in the home of Canadian ambassador.  Ben Affleck plays Tony Mendez a consultant for the CIA who helped get many of the Shah's people out of Iran during the overthrow.  

Argo is excellently casted with a plethora of talent.  It also does a fairly good job splicing together its well done cinematography with  special effects shots and footage of the actual crisis.

The film pace loses some steam in the middle but the end ramps up tension very nicely even though it was probably "hollywooded" up.  Everything so last minute and in the nick of time with car chases and such.  

Ben Afflecks character doesn't really shine but the film doesn't really bank on his performance.  It's a good film and another great addition to Affleck's directing resume.
Argo is a visually convincing period piece and its subject is always conveyed artistically. There is always enough tension to keep us interested but not quite enough shock value to truly thrill us.

"Argo" opens with a brief and desultory history of Iran leading up to 1979, at which point the movie begins in earnest with some very pissed off Iranians storming the American embassy in Tehran and taking 66 people hostage. During the commotion, six manage to sneak out the back door and end up hiding out in the Canadian ambassador's house. As the weeks tick by with no end in sight and with the Canadians themselves wanting to evacuate, the CIA scratches its collective head trying to come up with a plan to free them. After discarding such gems as having them bike to safety in Turkey and pretending that they're teachers at a school that's actually been closed for months, an "exfiltration" expert named Tony Mendez (Ben Affleck) is brought in.

Tony's idea comes to him while watching "Planet of the Apes" in his hotel room. His plan, which falls squarely into the "so crazy it just might work" category, is to set up a fake production company shooting a fake science fiction movie in Iran, and to pretend that the six escapees are members of a Canadian film crew who were flown in to scout out scene locations.  An actual screenplay is purchased (the movie is named "Argo"), promotional materials are created, and publicity is generated in order to give the plan an air of credibility. 

This would all seem patently absurd if it weren't for the fact that it actually happened.  Tony Mendez is a real guy and the CIA really did go along with his crazy-ass fake movie idea to try to free the six trapped Americans because, as someone in the movie points out, it was the best bad idea they had. 

Despite the fact that I and probably everyone else knows in advance how this movie turns out, it still manages to be a real nail-biter. There are a lot of extremely close calls - a ringing phone answered just in the nick of time, plane reservations made just in the nick of time - that aroused both tension and annoyance in me.  Annoyance, because even though I know "Argo" is based on a true story, I assume most of these tension-building sequences were invented by the writers for dramatic effect.  But despite my brain repeatedly alerting me that poetic license was being taken in order to manipulate me, I was powerless against this manipulation, kind of like when that ASPCA commercial comes on showing one pathetic abused dog after another as Sarah McLachlan wails about angels in the background and I have to change the channel to avoid calling the toll-free number and emptying out my IRA account. 

Which is to say, "Argo" succeeds quite well as a thriller.  And if you're into edge-of-your-seat, crowd-pleasing rollercoaster ride types of movies, you're going to love it.
 
My personal preference, and I know that I'm in the minority here, would be that this story, as well as the stories upon which most other docudramas are based, be made into documentaries instead. Sure "Argo" might be less thrilling and entertaining without all of the contrived near-misses, but the reality at the heart of this story is interesting enough to stand its own.
  
As is the plight of abused dogs even without a sad Sarah McLachlan soundtrack.

	Argo starts with a provocative premise: In the revolutionary Iran, a CIA agent tries to rescue six hostages with the pretext of doing a (fake) movie in the Middle East country. 
	However, the intriguing premise becomes a romantic story in the end, being too emotional. Let's summarize it with few words: a work hard CIA agent with familiar problems (his wife abandoned him and the son is out of reach) engages in a tremendous deadly journey to help the American hostages (and save the American's honor). He accomplishes everything he set out to do. In the end, he reattaches with his spouse and can be closer to his beloved son; moreover, he receives a secret congratulation for his services.
	I also watched this movie with the eyes of someone who have basic knowledge about the Iran-America crisis in the 70-80s. The conclusion I made is: in a psychoanalytic perspective Argo is laughable. It seems to me an attempt of treating a past trauma caused by the Iranian revolution effects. 
	Therefore, Argo is less ambitious than it intended to be and more dreamlike than it should be.

Ben Affleck is shaping up to be a phenomenal director. Argo is a taught, well written thriller. The opening ten minutes are some of the best to come out of Hollywood in years. The last twenty minutes unfortunately resort to every cliched trick in the movie playbook to ramp up the stakes. While Affleck does a good job with this as well, it's so overdone that while you are sufficiently caught up in the action, you are also inwardly rolling your eyes at the ridiculousness of it all.

What Argo does best, however, is manage to remain mostly objective. It takes a tone of presenting the facts. It doesn't present the Iranians as the enemy or evil and does a fantastic job of setting up the situation surrounding the hostage situation without glorifying the Americans or vilifying the Iranians. This was a situation where both sides shared some of the blame for the results and Argo acknowledges that. The one area where this objectiveness is compromised is in the Canadian role in the rescue of the Americans. While never completely ignored, the role of the Canadian ambassador is relegated to the fringes with the focus given to the CIA operative sent to get the American's out. This is mostly forgivable as it is an American film so of course they'll tell the story from their point of view. This skew of facts is also somewhat rectified by the use of archival footage from just after the rescue detailing the Canadian's involvement.

All in all, Argo is a film that manages to keep you involved and on the edge of your seat through its entire run time, even when the outcome is never in doubt. The direction is solid as are the performances and the use of archival footage is expertly done, blurring the lines between the fictional diegetic world of the film and the reality of the event in question.

Although the film deals with heavy content - military extraction and political tension, it flows lightly mostly due to its comical relief by Arkin and Goodman as well as the fact that a not-so-great-but-best-worst-rescue-plan was portrayed so convincingly and seriously. Directed by Ben Affleck, who has proven himself magnificently as a director with Gone Baby Gone (2007) and The Town (2010), this is a taut and suspenseful thriller which also happens to be an unbelievable true story too. A rescue mission which you would never have believed have worked, but it did. Set within the lion's den of the most dangerous country on Earth, it captures the mood and feel of the time. On November 4, 1979, the U.S. Embassy in Tehran, Iran was ambushed by militants. Most of the embassy staff were taken hostage, but six of them managed to escape down a passage and they found refuge in the house of the Canadian Ambassador Ken Taylor (Victor Garber). Weeks pass, and the situation hasn't gotten any better, and the CIA are trying to think of a way to get them out of Iran, CIA specialist Tony Mendez (Affleck) comes up with a plan so crazy, it might actually work. With help from special effects man John Chambers (John Goodman) and producer Lester Siegel (Alan Arkin), they go into Iran as a Canadian film crew, scouting locations for a sci-fi film called Argo, and try and get them out. It's on-the-edge of your seat stuff, but it's absolutely amazing, and it might even be the best film of 2012. Affleck shows professionalism as actor and director, with great support from Bryan Cranston as Mendez's boss at the CIA, who is watching what's happening.

What really scares me is that this film is somehow going to become a base standard against which other films will be compared in terms of greatness, or that studios will only (yes, ONLY) aspire to make films as good as this and no better, because that would be a real shame.  Hollywood has made and certainly should still be able to make films of a much higher caliber than this one.  First of all, Ben Affleck has never been much of an actor, he has never shown an audience that he can inhabit and become a character like much more accomplished and talented actors (Sean Penn, Kevin Spacey, Don Cheadle, Daniel Day Lewis, to say nothing of classic actors of Hollywood-past), and now he wants to be a director?  This is a solid outing, but he's got a lot of improving to do; I'm convinced he was only able to create this solid a film because he based it on actual events.  Despite the film being "loosely" based on actual events it seems that the inaccuracies stem not from added material (or at least not added plot device material) but from information excised from the original situation as would be expected when you make a film out of real circumstances; you can't put everything in.  Argo also suffers from the conflict inherent in not knowing exactly what it wants to be: the funny parts are funny, the tense parts are tense, but like mixing ice cream with pasta, two good things combined doesn't create an exponentially better ... anything.  Now that I've vented about the film's weaknesses there are several things I very much enjoyed about Argo: the stock footage gave the film a solid grounding in reality, even if Affleck borrowed this technique from countless directors who came before him (Scorsese?); the casting (aside from Affleck casting himself in the lead...) was excellent, Arkin and Goodman are solid character actors who pull off excellent performances and the hostages cast as unknowns was a smart choice; and the story is interesting, engaging, and highly entertaining to watch.  Like I said above, this is a good film, but this isn't the best we can expect, even from today's bullshit Hollywood money factory...

It's tough to define "Argo." Is it a thriller? It's certainly exciting like one. Is it a comedy? It certainly is hilarious, isn't it? Is it a drama? There are a lot of dramatic moments, too. I think the only thing you can really say about it is that "Argo" is "Argo." And that is a great thing to be.

Argo is a thriller (very loosely) based on a true story, which seems a bit like an oxymoron. How exactly does one make an exciting film where the ending is pretty much a foregone conclusion? The answer to that is: I don't know.

I can't explain it. I can't explain why this movie works, it just does. The liberties taken with the story (and there are many) are almost entirely for the better; they add tension, pathos or comedy to a story that would have been not nearly as fun to tell without them. The only change that feels unnecessary is the fact that they changed the race of the protagonist, Tony Mendez, but Ben Affleck gives a good enough performance to justify it.

Speaking of changes, can we just thank God that Chris Terrio invented the character of Lester Siegel (Alan Arkin)? He and the real-life makeup artist John Chambers (John Goodman) really steal the show, providing the biggest laughs, and even a bit of pathos here and there.

Which isn't to say that the film is an entirely humorless affair without them. Bryan Cranston gets a lot of great lines in as Jack O'Donnell, Tony's boss, and even the refugees get their moments of levity in there.

The film is also a thriller, and the movie never pulls punches when it comes to what's at stake. The taking of the hostages at the embassy is shown as unflinchingly brutal and terrifying.

Honestly, I could talk for hours about "Argo", but I could also sump up how I feel about the movie in just four words: "Go See Argo. Now."

Argo

Espionage, secret operations and clandestine missions are an integral part of any nation on the face of this earth. As we relate to their individual foreign affairs, covert activities tend to form the "the first line of scrimmage" as it pertains to security and countryship. Most of these operations and individuals might not look right in general public view, but when lives are at stake there's no point of good vs. bad. It's plain necessity!

In modern world "Survival of the fittest" has rendered itself to be an incomplete theory though it may seem senseless and futile.

Plot:

It's 1979 Iran - the days of extreme civil unrest with burgeoning and bludgeoning angst and furore against western policies primarily the US. The US embassy in Tehran is mobbed and five officials manage to escape.

Burrowed for their lives, they secretly camp out at Canadian Ambassador's residence while rest of their colleagues are held hostage. Rest of the film is about US government's plan of action in plucking their citizens out of Iran putting an end to their scarily bizzare survival before they fall back as hostages.

Analysis:

The punch lines - The movie was fake. The mission was real and The mission was a movie sum up the story in as simple a manner as possible. First off, its a damn real story directly out of CIA case files and some amount of appropriation might have crept in.

But as the trio (Ben Affleck, Alan Arkin and John Goodman) famously mouth "ARGO **** yourself" - it doesn't really matter. "Argo" is the 3rd directorial feature from Ben Affleck (Gone Baby Gone and The Town) and it is his best yet.  Set during the 1980 Iranian Hostage Crisis a man comes up with a solution to get six American fugitives out of the country.  Based on a true story, Tony Mendez, a CIA agent comes up with an idea to get these people out from a country desperately trying to find them.  He teams with a couple movie producers (played by John Goodman and Alan Arkin) to create a fake movie that they will use to dress these people as a fake film crew on a scouting mission in Iran.  It is a crazy idea, many feel it will never work, but Affleck and these two producers have made convincing case.  Mendez must go deep into enemy land to teach these people how to act in order to save their lives.  The slow suspense in the final act is the only part that truly feels untrue while the rest of the film feels authentic, real, and powerful.  Add in some comedic scenes from Arkin, Goodman, and Brian Cranston and you have a really good movie.  This has started all Academy Award buzz and could bring one to Affleck for director.  Learning the true story as the credits role really helps put in perspective what you just spent and hour watching.  Never was there a dull moment and the old saying "its just so crazy it might work" sure did, not only in the event itself but in this movie as well.

I know I originally disliked ''Argo'', and with very good reasons I must say. But then I had just come out of the theater, I was with a very annoying audience that night and the screening was mostly impossible to appreciate due to a failure in projectionist skill. But now I happen to own a copy of the film in Blu-ray, and I've come to closer observation of it due to a recomendation of a professor, and I intend to argument why the film's highlights overcome its fails.

''Argo'' is a film that, most noticeably, intends to encourage diplomacy, against impossible odds though. Its intentions are well-meant. Even if the film is obviously biased, shows partialized versions of this historical occurence, and focuses too much on the normalization of clandestine operations to be believable enough, director Ben Affleck and crew make a solid effort to propel ''Argo'' with enough credibility and impartiality to both sides of the story. Nonetheless, I believe this movie should have focused a little more in the Iranian people, rather than just showing some period footage and angry mobs shouting in the streets and assaulting the American Embassy. Had this project been in the hands of David Fincher, I'm sure it would have been more satisfactory on that sense. However, Affleck does try, and his attempt doesn't go unnoticed when the film is over. What really screwed up the experience for me the first time was the final scene of Americans escaping Iran while Revolutionary Guards chase their plane in trucks and police cars: a very stupid scene I may say, and that shatters most of the film's thoroughly ellaborate authenticity. 

Nonetheless, as I said before, ''Argo'' does account for its flaws more than it originally seemed to me. The Hollywood cover is interesting, even though as a student of political science, I could not buy it for one minute. This operation was successful because there was strong negotations between the United States and Iran. In fact, the event itself is one of the main happenings of the 20th Century that go on profound discussion by polithologists. Not to say it is widely considered a pinnacle in international relationships during the Cold War era. The film itself lets you know that, and I understand that's why it came to be of such appeal. Afflect's Tony Mendez is an agent who contributes in a great deal to operate through a more peaceful way than his superiors prefer. At one point, he is called from Washington to cancel the operation and take on a military agenda. Upon the possibility of invading Iran, Mendez would rather continue his work and let peace talks continue without disrupting the country's seek for a populist government after overthrowing the dictatorial Sha. 

Director Ben Affleck accomplishes a very tense and captivating atmosphere in the film that does evoke the toughness of the event with utmost skill, while presenting both sides of the aspects, such as where exactly was the U.S. wrong by harnessing a violator of human rights and how was Iran wrong by occupying the Embassy and therefore leaving no room for diplomatic solutions. I understand this works better as a thriller than as a truthful account of events, but even so, it is still throughly satisfying, engaging and mostly, dynamic. Acting is not the film's very best. I'll go with the production design and cinematography as some of the film's greatest achievements. Particularly the score, by Alexandre Desplat, is freaking amazing. Some tracks are beautifully describing of Iran and the mission, specially the one ''Scent of Death'', as well as the beautiful Chilean lullabi ''Hace Tuto Guagua'' at the end.

After a second viewing I'm glad I cleared most of my issues with ''Argo''. It is an excellent thriller film that prefers intelligent resolutions to action sequences, with plot focus at the top of its reservoir.

Audiences love to hypothesize how or why certain films ever got made: Ego? Marketing strategy? Financial gain? Adam Sandler's pool cleaning bill? But it's safe to say seldom has a film received the green light in order to free Middle Eastern hostages. It's a premise that sounds even too far fetched for even Hollywood standards, but it's precisely the truth-based tale on which "Argo" is based.
"Argo" is the third directorial effort from Ben Affleck, and perhaps his most commercially polished yet. Based on the Iran hostage crisis in 1980, "Argo" enlightens us on a part of the release that was not played out on the nightly news: six Americans who managed to escape a seized U.S. Embassy in Tehran, found covert asylum in the Canadian ambassador's home and were  ushered out in a most unorthodox fashion.
Tony Mendez (played by Affleck) is a CIA operative whose job it is to find opportunities in otherwise hopeless situations. Before he arrives to the scene, the best the agency could devise was getting the hostages bikes to pedal a few hundred miles across the border to safety. Mendez enlists the help of one of his contacts in the film industry (a special effects artist played by John Goodman) to create a phony flick that would allow the escapees to pose as filmmakers on a simple location scout.
While Affleck dresses up the film in appropriate period attire (including the old-school Warner Bros. logo that opens the film), itâ??s heart is firmly in the â??70s, when names like Friedken, Scorsese and Lumet were cranking them out. Thatâ??s right. I said it. Affleck is fast proving himself to be in a directorial league with those powerhouses. Sure, heâ??s learned a thing or two from other directors over the years (the conclusion feels on par with Ron Howardâ??s â??Apollo 13,â?? in which every conceivable second that ticks away pulses with life-threatening urgency).
What helps â??Argoâ?? connect is its focus on the humanity of its tale. Thatâ??s no small task for the director, as the cast with which he is working is huge. Everyone from the agency staff back in the office, to the hostages hidden in their safehouse, to the high-level staffers in the White House, thereâ??s a a ton of story heâ??s packing in the flick. Each of the actors feel as though they lived through their roles and are merely recounting them in front of the camera.
He brings just the right amount of humor amidst the tension, like occasionally letting the air out of a balloon that you can see is about to pop. Much of those moments are courtesy of Goodman and his producer-buddy (played by Alan Arkin) who believe more in the plan for their faux film than they do the entire film industry in which they work.
If there is a weak link, it would be casting himself in the lead. Not known for his ability to carry heavy narrative, Affeck is particularly pensive here, which may be part of his characterâ??s nature, but it would help as entertainment to punch up the emotion if Mendez is chosen as its primary focus.
That is not enough to deter what is otherwise a superlative effort from all involved. It realizes that film is â??escapismâ?? (in the truest sense of the word, here), and Affleck masterfully clicks his stopwatch in the last act as we sit edging ever closer on the theater seats.
If a decade ago you were to tell me that Affleck and acclaimed director Paul Thomas Anderson (who recently released the comically confounding â??The Masterâ??) would both release films aiming for the Oscars and that Affleckâ??s would be the far superior film, I would ask for a hit of what you were smoking.
Some snobs may argue otherwise, but I will take the precision of â??Argoâ?? over the pretension of â??The Masterâ?? any day.

At the base of this movie is an absolutely incredible true story about a covert operation to get six Americans out of Iran in 1979. The group escaped the US Embassy as militants stormed the building and took everyone else hostage. Knowing it was only a matter of time before the they were found out and executed, CIA specialist Tony Mendez (Ben Affleck) dreamt up a risky plan to get them out. He pitched the idea of the six posing as part of a Canadian film crew location scouting for a sci-fi blockbuster 'Argo' and enlisted the help of special effects make-up artist John Chambers (John Goodman) and producer Lester Siegel (Alan Arkin) on the ground in LA. I love that this included a launch party and an ad in Variety for a film that was completely fake. Genius.

It's such an outrageous way to try and rescue these people and even more outrageous that it was true. While the hostage situation is a well-known news event, their story remained classified until 1997 and director Affleck did an amazing job digging it up and sharing it with the world. Of course it has been given the Hollywood once-over, complete with thrilling suspense and a pretty unbelievably close-call of an ending. Nonetheless the story really appealed to me and the film did a wonderful job telling it.

The juxtaposition of the magical land of Hollywood with the brutal regime in Iran was striking - not only visually, but in the sound, the dialogue and the camera work. The parts shot in LA were smooth, well produced and quite airy, while in Iran the camera was often handheld and shaky. Goodman and Arkin were absolute standouts and I felt we got to know their characters more than the six stuck in Iran, which probably shouldn't have been the case. Affleck put himself in the hero role and although I find it a little narcissistic and cringy when actors do this (cough.. Tom Cruise.. cough), I still think he gave a strong performance. 4/5

Of the high-profile movies that have come out this year, this is one of the best at good old-fashioned storytelling. This film, right from the beginning, takes off in a way the previous two didn't, and becomes one of this year's most purely engaging films. It's gripping, entertaining, and smartly-made.

Based on a true story, this film is about a particular CIA mission relating to the 1979 Iranian hostage crisis. After Iranians storm the American embassy and take everyone there hostage, six embassy workers manage to escape and hide out in the Canadian ambassador's house, where they are effectively trapped. Back in America, CIA agent Tony Mendez (Affleck) comes up with a crazy scheme to exfiltrate those six: go to Iran, pretend to be part of a film crew doing location-scouting for a Star Wars-ripoff called Argo, and then leave with the hostages posing as crew members. To do this, he enlists the help of actual Hollywood people, including cynical old producer Lester Siegel (Alan Arkin) and Planet of the Apes make-up artist John Chambers (John Goodman). 

The acting is generally very good throughout the film. Affleck's own performance is quiet and reserved, but I think it works well for the character. Arkin, who's always been a lot of fun to watch lately, is very effective comic relief in his scenes. Having John Goodman in your movie is always an easy way to score automatic bonus points with me, and this movie does indeed have a fine role for Goodman. Bryan Cranston is also very good as Mendez's boss at the CIA. And the actors playing the hostages, though their roles mostly consist of looking scared or worried, are all utterly convincing.

The movie doesn't really linger on its performances, though. There's nothing quite like a good suspense film for holding the audience's rapt attention, and this movie excels at fingernail-biting suspense. The opening sequence, depicting the storming of the embassy, is just fantastic, and the climactic scenes of the mission are almost unbelievably tense. Indeed, I'd be willing to bet that the ending is where the film veers the furthest away from the facts in favor of heightening the suspense, but it's like the thing Spielberg said about the shark at the end of Jaws: Affleck's had us for this long, he can afford to do whatever he wants with the ending. The audience I saw the movie with, who were mostly very talkative before and after the movie, were completely silent with attention while it was playing.

In a smart move, Affleck decided to make the movie look like a 1970s thriller itself, which almost made it look like we were watching a found document of the mission rather than a high-budget film made decades later. The film has the slightly faded colors of many 1970s movies, and generally goes for a gritty, realistic tone that works perfectly for the material. As a bonus for me, I saw the movie projected in somewhat scratched actual film at a small second-run theater, which happened to add to the retro vibe of the whole thing. Overall, while no single aspect of the movie stands out as obviously as does, say, the acting in Lincoln or the cinematography in Life of Pi, the whole thing works beautifully as a cohesive, old-fashioned movie experience. I was totally caught up in it.

ARGO is an anomaly as it is a very "Hollywood" movie that offers up sharp satirization of the film industry while also saluting it.  On top of that, it a remarkable mixture of political thriller, witty comedy, harrowing drama, socio-political commentary and crowd-pleaser triumph, and it works.  Affleck's talented direction performs the incredible task of guiding the film through these wildly shifting tones with astounding steadiness, while he also stars, and though his onscreen performance isn't as impressive as his behind the camera work here, it's apt and nonetheless worthy.  As I said, it is a very "Hollywood" movie, so great deal of liberties have obviously been taken with the material, and history buffs will have plenty to gripe about, but who needs a history lesson when you can have a great movie?  Of course, history is fine, but this film is obviously taking liberties, so it entertains fully, but leaves you wondering about the real details of such an odd bit of history.  Of special note here, is the flawless art direction of the film, made to emulate the look and feel of a political drama from its time period of the 1970's.  The retro Warner Bros. logo opens the film, the picture is sometimes a little bit grainy, and the whole thing has that sort of solid, grounded, clinical aura about it, while attention to visuals based on the real events and people is superb; during the credits they get the chance to brag when they show archival photos and footage alongside counterparts from the film.
It's well made, well acted, and well directed, but it misses that special thing that makes movies so great.

Ben Affleck's third directorial effort recreates the events from the famous Tehran Embassy hostage crisis and how six American diplomats who managed to escape the America Embassy were extracted from Iran. Despite being quite loose in terms of being close to the actual events (mostly all the suspense is based on Affleck's screenplay changes), the movie seems incredibly realistic. It is not only the cinematography and the costumes, but also the overall recreation of the political background and events, that make this absurd and sometimes even comic story unbelievably realistic.

For two hours Ben Affleck manages to fully engage his audience and to actually make the audience wonder whether this mission would succeed. The "main" character and hero in the movie is not Affleck himself, but Hollywood and the whole movie industry depicted by the wonderful duo John Goodman and Alan Arkin. As the main tool for extracting the six diplomats, Tony Mendez (Ben Affleck) is comfortable with the environment, emotionally restrained, devoted to his country and above all vulnerable. Totally different from the super hero spies (Bond, Bourne, etc) and other action-related field agents, Ben Affleck's character adds up another realistic touch to his movie. Another wonderful decision has been the casting of non A-Hollywood actors for the supporting roles. With nobody from the Tehran cast known to the broader public, Argo's director increases further the dramatic load in the story. JOSH SORELL: REVIEW: ARGO
	Ben Affleck seems to be trying really hard to make up for the all the crappy performances he made us endure, but he has pulled it off. Argo, his most recent since The Town, is probably going to catch a lot of awards in the next few months for its disciplined storytelling and the way it manages to balance all the pieces of this political thriller just right.
	The film begins with a series of drawn segments, based on photographs of the Iran Revolution of 1979, the deposing of the Shah and the formation of the Islamic Republic under Ayatollah Khomeini. Explained in quick summary, the renderings display the close ties between fact and fiction in the world of international espionage, as we are quickly drawn into a scarily intense story.
	Five members of the American consulate in Tehran manage to escape the building as militants outside the embassy break the gates and take the rest consulate hostage. They manage to escape to the Canadian ambassadors house, but with death squads and revolutionary guard on the streets immediate escape is impossible. The CIA begins planning for extraction routes; starting only with bicycles.
	Ben Affleck, as extraction expert Tony Mendez, eventually comes up with a scheme; disguise himself and the hostages as members of a Canadian film crew scouting locations for a science fiction film. This is where the film really gets going. Part of the 2nd act is dedicated to showing the development of the fake film, Argo, as a way to properly sell the disguise to the Iranians. Enlisting in a series of Hollywood contacts Mendez begins to build an intricate façade. John Goodman and Alan Arkin bring the most levity to the film as a makeup artist and producer who have to fool their Hollywood colleagues, putting a constant spin of espionage even into the most mundane of scenes. There is even a fake script reading of the film complete with a cast and costumes seemingly borrowed from Buck Rogers and Battlestar Galactica. Although some of the Hollywood associates were made up for the film, most of them were real professionals, including an unnamed storyboard artist who in reality was comic book legend Jack Kirby.
	There is a particular kind of strangeness to the story, and not just because it involved the CIA not doing something completely cynical for once. The film crafts the narrative of liberation through parallels with the fake film, elaborating on the kind of bizarre constructions we use in fiction not just as a way of entertainment, but as a way of reflecting the kinds of overwhelming changes and circumstances that people in a mundane society can't always come to grips with. Is the science fiction movie just a cheap mask or does it show how we as a culture always have to make fictional constructions around the real world?
	The parallel of the science fiction film brings a kind of romantic levity to the overarching story, but the film's presentation is determined and tense. There is a particular shot when Mendez enters Tehran and he sees a man killed by the revolutionary guard hanging from a crane in the middle of a road. Photographs during the credits confirm the accuracy of the events depicted. Although there are artistic liberties taken with the amount of danger the hostages were in during the final days of their crisis, these liberties allow for Affleck and crew to depict the kind of immense terror that swept through Iran during the Revolution. Scenes of Affleck and the hostages moving through the streets of Iran as protestors and militants are all around them are exquisitely built with high tension.
	The shot photography and camera movements are crisp and smooth even during the massive break in at the embassy in the beginning of the film. Affleck uses the advantages of wide shots to show off the aesthetic beauty of Tehran even under the insane and violently horrible conditions of the Revolution.
	There have been complaints about the historical accuracy of parts of this film. The role of the Canadian embassy has been greatly diminished and certain orders made by the CIA are not accurate, but honestly, it's sometimes hard to make bureaucracy exciting. Granted having the director of the film as the main star (who in real life was Hispanic) is often problematic but despite that, Affleck manages to give a solid performance without letting any kind of egotism break his stride.
	Was the film completely accurate? Like most artistic adaptations, no. Did it make a damn fine film? Yes. Argo wins hands down for the "really solid and not boring or stupid political thriller" of the year award, as well as the "screw you, Iran" award. All right Ben Affleck, you have my trust now, don't let me down.
Argo is a rollicking yarn, easily the most cohesive and technically accomplished of Affleck's three films so far, but a part of me wishes the director hadn't cast himself in the lead role.

Argo had me on the edge of my seat for pretty much the entire two hours. It was very tightly directed, had a lot of engaging moments and in general was a fantastic film. However, I feel compelled to take a couple of stars away for compromising historical truth for a tale glorifying the part of the US while diminishing the role of Canada and even Britain and New Zealand. 

The movie claims, in its opening scenes, that the British and Kiwi embassies turned away the diplomats, while in fact, they helped them greatly. The Canadians hosted them at their own peril and at great risk and were involved in the plan the entire way, yet, nowhere in the movie is this mentioned. Instead, what we get, are patriotic Americans, the CIA, coming up with an ingenious plan to get the diplomats out of Iran, and then 'allowing' Canada to take the credit to protect the rest of the hostages. 

I'm sorry, but this level of distortion of fact, only to satisfy the egos of an entire country does not do the real operation any justice. It would have been possible to take just as compelling a movie without compromising on Canada's involvement. The ultimate irony is when Affleck throws them a bone at the end, saying that the CIA complemented Canadian efforts in the rescue operation, when the film spent two hours painting it as an entirely CIA operation.

The Iranian hostage crisis is an international episode ripe for cinematic portrayal.  Unfortunately, the best part of the story revolves around the fact that the hostages were released the day that President Ronald Reagan was sworn into office.  This would make for a good movie, but Hollywood doesn't like to glamorize our 40th president.  Instead, they're all atwitter about director-producer-star Ben Affleck's (The Town) telling of a CIA mission to get six Americans out of Tehran during the calamity.  It was a promising venture, with Affleck starting to come into his own as a director, and story that was a lot less serious than his last two films.  However, dealing with such a subject doesn't bode well for viewers who understand that films aren't exactly the most historically accurate ways to convey a story.  
In November of 1979, Iranian militants stormed the US Embassy in Tehran, taking the staff as hostages.  Just before the takeover, six Americans escape the embassy and take refuge in the house of the Canadian ambassador.  Weeks pass, and the state department becomes aware of the six, so they plot an extraction with the diplomatic mess at the embassy continues to unfold.  The state department enlists the help of CIA agent Tony Mendez (Affleck), who balks at all of their plans.  Instead, he pitches the idea of extracting them by posing them as a Canadian film crew in Tehran on location scouting.  He gets approval for the mission, but has to enlist the help of a contact in Hollywood (John Goodman, 'Trouble with the Curve') and a movie producer (Alan Arkin 'The Muppets') to help sell the story.  When Mendez finally arrives in Tehran, more obstacles arise in his plan.  All the while, the militants realize that they don't have all the Americans that work at the embassy accounted for, and begin a manhunt to find them.   
The whole movie feels like one very long, drawn out "for your Oscar consideration in all categories" commercial.  For one thing, the movie is a love letter to two things, Hollywood and Jimmy Carter - so right there, you've got Oscar voters willing to throw their support behind the film, no matter how good it is.  Secondly, it tries to highlight Affleck's direction over starring role, prop up Goodman, Arkin, and Bryan Cranston's (Rock of Ages) supporting roles, and then basically plead with the Academy during the credits for nominations for the makeup and production design departments.  Oh, and Affleck and his writer, Chris Terrio, made sure to throw in a completely uncalled for abortion analogy and plenty of anti-American demonstrations to thrill the far-left Academy voters.  Oh, and it casually leaves out that the Iranian hostage crisis was solved when America elected a competent president - something that didn't happen this election cycle.  
One wants to like the movie.  The trailers promised solid direction - in the wake of Affleck's last confident but flawed film - a cast with game - sans Affleck, who should stay behind the camera - and a premise that allowed for comedy and thrills.  Though his career careened off a cliff called 'Gigli' almost a decade ago, audiences have begun to forgive that cinematic atrocity due to his redemptive efforts behind the camera.  As a leading man, however, he doesn't quite succeed with this venture.  Sure, it's an ensemble piece, and he's not entirely unlikable, but he just doesn't have tremendous gravitas.  Plus, the movie never really takes off (pun intended).  It seems like elements of the story were overblown just to instill a sense of danger, but never really leave the characters in peril.  It also doesn't develop characters very well.  On top of the borderline cheesy subplot with Mendez's personal life, there was a promising introduction of Kyle Chandler (Super 8) playing White House Chief of Staff, Hamilton Jordan, but his character gets almost no payoff.  
Well, it looks as if the Academy has the last laugh when it comes to legitimizing Affleck's ascendance into directing.  He's picked Golden Globes and other awards, stemming from the voters loving movies about Hollywood, in lieu of him actually accomplishing something substantial.  Has the man got some skill behind the camera?  Yes, but he's got nothing on the likes of the perennially-snubbed Christopher Nolan, so he shouldn't feel so left out.  This is not an unwatchable movie, but it's not one that will stick with you when you leave the theater.  There's not a single performance that is worth writing home about, and the story isn't terribly moving.  Fortunately, this has some closure, so it's not your typical Oscar film.  But it won't be terribly surprising to see this one pull an upset win over other historical films in the race due to its homage to the assumed power of Hollywood and a failed president who is still trying to conjure a legacy.

Intrigued by what he can do, maybe, but not that much. But this time around, count me in as one of them converts; "Argo" is indeed an insanely great film. 
     
Being a regular inhabitant at Cracked (a very intelligent comedy website), I was able to constantly scan through numerous well-written humor articles that tackle relatively obscure historical/political facts and stories. One of them, obviously, is the very story of "Argo" itself, which has fascinated me (and made me laugh at some point, naturally) to high heavens when I first read it. Yet weird enough, when "Argo" was released, I haven't the slightest idea that it is indeed about the said 'Cracked' article. Instead, what I thought the film will be is something akin to a mere stylistic copy of Roman Polanski's "The Ghost Writer". But boy was I wrong. 
     
Packed with just the right amount of endearing characterization, tense sequences and moments of genuine humor, "Argo" is easily one of the best films of the year specifically because of how it has managed to be both politically compelling and entertaining at the same time, with great supporting performances by Alan Arkin and John Goodman (as the legendary Hollywood make-up artist John Chambers) to boot. As for Affleck's performance itself, it is, in no way, very memorable, especially when he's in scenes alongside Walter White, er, Bryan Cranston, who's just perfect in that bureaucratic CIA role. But even though Affleck's acting is not much of a revelation (his first choice for the role was not himself but Brad Pitt), the real star in this film is his inspired directorial effort; that and the beauty of 'science fiction' itself, which the film was able to subtly highlight. 
     
Of course, with "Argo" being a politically-charged film, its closeness to the truth is surely a great question, especially in its depiction of the Iranian populace and the real role of Canada in the accomplishment of the rescue mission. But for me, "Argo" is really not much about politics. Instead, what I think the film is actually all about is how seemingly contradictory forces (the Hollywood and the Government; Canada and the USA) can do an almost miraculous difference, all with the help of a make-believe planet and some storyboard aliens. 
     
Like 2011's "Hugo", "Argo", although very sublimely at that, is a tribute to the power of movies, and how it's not just a medium where we're able to discover the intricacies of life, but one which can also save some. And who would have thought that it will be some cheaply-imagined science fiction tale that can do such? "Argo", despite its heavily political nature, is an understated celebration of the imagination. 
     
For the longest time, the science fiction genre has been widely considered as the ultimate form of 'escape'. Indeed, in many cases, it actually is, what with its abundance of colorful interplanetary creatures, silver-clad heroes and interstellar adventures. But let's not forget that, for once, it was also instrumental for actually pulling off quite a literal one. "Argo", a stunningly inspired sleeper of a film, will forever remind us of that fact.

Ben Affleck's seamless direction of this otherwise bland and shallow portrayal of the real life exodus that took place in the Carter era is so noticeably well done, it almost convinces you that this is a near perfect film. It is not. The most apt description of Argo would be "boring".

I've come to really appreciate Affleck as a director. He knows exactly what he wants and executes it with more conviction and slickness with each film. Unfortunately, the more ridges he's learned to smooth in theses neatly packaged films, the less heart they have. Gone baby Gone, although overlong and drained by the third act, is still my favorite of his films.

What that film has that this one lacks is an understanding of character. We have an interesting story here, a great blend of Hollywood insider comedy with some real world political tension, pitch perfect tone and swift pacing. It's an ideal film for the idea it presents, but it's so "filmy" and wrapped up so aptly that we miss the humanism in it. The only reason we seem to care about the bored hostages is that they are Americans lost in the horror of the always villainous Middle East. A true story doesn't make for true emotion just because its basis is in the real world, and that's where the film loses its touch.

There is not one person, other than the amazing Brian Cranston, that breathes life into their characters. I know it won best ensemble, but I don't see why. They had nothing to work with. It is because this lack of empathy for any person in this film that the story suffers. The music is Hollywood typical, and the last act is (although we know the end) completely predictable and ludicrous. All the last minute "oh nos!" and near misses seem thrown in for the sake of suspense and could be called out before any of them happen. It becomes stereotypical in this sense and loses it's shot at greatness.

Beyond all the potential and hype, there is a man who is letting go of the grit that gave him the chance to create the things he has. Let's not reward Affleck just yet. Starring in his own movies requires much better acting than the lifeless gazes that sink scenery, and I don't want to see his movies become like his former celebrity: A raw talent that succumbs to being an idolized star. Ben, keep the movies and yourself human, and you'll have your reward.

Like Zero Dark Thirty this is based on true events, but unlike that movie, also nominated for Best Picture alongside this, Argo has the knowledge that there is another side to this story.  Ben Affleck, maturing as a filmmaker - perhaps becoming one of the best ones in America today - shows how American intervention in countries and conflicts beyond its cultural and religious understanding has led to violence in those countries - and it is that violence that traps its citizens in a siege and facing death.

Argo is not without its flaws, however.  Affleck's Tony Mendez, is the CIA operative sent into Tehran to recover six civilians hiding in the Canadian embassy - he is well-drawn, a man trying to do good even when his superiors think contrary to him.  The six civilians he is sent to recover all remain one-note, though - I'm not sure I even knew their names - and this works against the effort Affleck and writer Chris Terrio have put into making sure Argo remains engaging - it makes Tony Mendez more like an action hero, riding into dangerous territory to rescue his men.  The Canadian embassy's maid gets more characterisation than the six.

The final 30 minutes of the film are as nailbiting as anything in recent thriller cinema.

That this has been nominated for Best Picture is not a surprise: it might even be read as Hollywood saves the day, and appealing narrative for an industry that love to backslap.  This is not Affleck's best film as director - he is more comfortable in Boston, I think, and in Gone Baby Gone and The Town - but it is a fine film, and one of the best up for Best Picture this year.

A terrific and tense spy-thriller based on true events, Argo is absolutely engrossing and mesmerizing delivery of Ben Affleck. With steady tension-building, convincing cast and a glimpse of political satire Argo is among the smartest spy-thrillers of recent years. 

Ben Affleck's third directorial effort recreates the events from the famous Tehran Embassy hostage crisis and how six American diplomats who managed to escape the America Embassy were extracted from Iran. Despite being quite loose in terms of being close to the actual events (mostly all the suspense is based on Affleck's screenplay changes), the movie seems incredibly realistic. It is not only the cinematography and the costumes, but also the overall recreation of the political background and events, that make this absurd and sometimes even comic story unbelievably realistic.

For two hours Ben Affleck manages to fully engage his audience and to actually make the audience wonder whether this mission would succeed. The "main" character and hero in the movie is not Affleck himself, but Hollywood and the whole movie industry depicted by the wonderful duo John Goodman and Alan Arkin. As the main tool for extracting the six diplomats, Tony Mendez (Ben Affleck) is comfortable with the environment, emotionally restrained, devoted to his country and above all vulnerable. Totally different from the super hero spies (Bond, Bourne, etc) and other action-related field agents, Ben Affleck's character adds up another realistic touch to his movie. Another wonderful decision has been the casting of non A-Hollywood actors for the supporting roles. With nobody from the Tehran cast known to the broader public, Argo's director increases further the dramatic load in the story. Here is Affleck's great craftsmanship as he brings everything to the question of live and death, even without spending a single minute on any of the six character in particular (families, dramas, dreams, etc). The only thing he focuses on them is his camera for their facial emotions and the fear they feel during the moments when they are in the streets of Tehran or at the airport. 

Argo is one of those movies, which would never have reached its Award-worthy level if it was directed by somebody else. Affleck puts the best of his heart and soul in this movie and he takes further step (after Gone, Baby, Gone and The Town)to the dreamed Best Director Oscar. He would probably not win it, but with these terrific two hours of hypnotizing entertainment, he is clearly on the road to becoming one of the major Hollywood directors.
