One of the best movies of 2012, if not the best, Argo proves that Ben Affleck is the fantastic director that his last two movies made him out to be and that he isn't as bad of an actor as many of us thought either.

Bravo, Ben Affleck.

He scored big in his first two directorial efforts Gone Baby Gone and The Town, and it appears that Argo will be no different. His attention to detail and instinct as a director is apparent in his latest feature, which chronicles the classified "Canadian Caper" CIA operation that took place in 1980 during the Iran hostage crisis.

The film opens up with the Iranian Revolution at a boiling point, as young revolutionaries storm the U.S. Embassy in Tehran in retaliation for America's sheltering of the Shah. As most of the staff is taken hostage, six evade capture and find refuge in the home of the Canadian ambassador.  The opening scene takes a good ten minutes to play out, but the attention to detail is worth it. The anger and frustration of the Iranian people is palpable, as is the danger to the Americans inside. It's this early scene-setting that sets the tense mood for the rest of the film and really glues you to your seat.

The escapees' situation is kept a secret, and the State Department begins looking into extraction options. CIA specialist Tony Mendez (Affleck) is brought in on a consulting basis, and quickly exposes the weaknesses of the proposed ideas. While watching Battle for the Planet of the Apes that night, Mendez slowly puts together a cover story for the escapees, in which they are Canadian filmmakers scouting exotic locations in Iran. After consulting with his supervisor Jack O'Donnell (Bryan Cranston), the two contact Academy Award-winning make-up artist John Chambers (John Goodman), who in turn puts them in contact with film producer Lester Siegel (Alan Arkin).

Thus, the fake film "Argo" is born. Mendez is to extract the six escapees under the guise that they are all scouting for the movie. Chambers and Siegel set up a phony production studio, and the plan is put into action as the entire State Department holds its collective breath.

Argo works not only as a thrilling rescue flick, but also as a sort of period piece. It captures the fear and resentment of the time, both within the U.S. and Iran. These two worlds are carefully connected through radio broadcasts and TV newsrooms, using actual footage to heighten the realism. The escapees are well written and they act accordingly - I found myself unwittingly gripping the armrest and silently pulling for the six scared Americans. The use of montage and quick cuts helps keep some of the slow scenes interesting and your attention focused, which really says something about Affleck's ability as a director. Goodman and Arkin do a great job as the make-up artist/producer duo, and provide some comedic relief that compliments the somber tone that the film carries for most of its run time.

In the end, Argo was what I expected it to be. There might not have been that "wow" factor to Argo, and there might have been a few underdeveloped characters, but perhaps that's what makes it such an awesome and inspiring tale. These were regular people whose lives were on the line, and all parties involved pulled off the improbable. These were fathers, mothers, husbands, friends, who simply wanted to make it home in one piece. I feel this was best exemplified by one of Mendez's last lines, as O'Donnell tells him that President Carter says he's a "great American." Mendez responds, "A great American what?" O'Donnell simply replies, "I dunno, he didn't say."

This has been my most anticipated movie since I first saw the trailer for it sometime last year, and I finally went and saw it after waiting a few weeks so I wouldn't end up in a crowded theatre. I kept my excitement from rushing me into it early by reading a few of the less spoilerific movie reviews about it, and to my surprise it was a favorite of both fans and critics. My only worry was that by the time I saw it I had ruined it for myself by building it up in my mind and setting my expectations unfairly high.

Here is the thing about unfairly high expectations: when you exceed even those, you have Argo.

First of all, as usual, the score. Magnificent. There is no other word for it. Half star.

Characters: Absolutely organic. They were based on real people and they felt like real people because they talked and acted like real people. I'm condensing three sections into one here because I'll just keep repeating myself about how well it is written, acted and spoken. 1.5 stars for the writing, acting and characters.

Theme: This is where I expected to have issues with the movie, simply because historical adaptations are always so full of making people into heroes, etc. Much to my surprise and delight, the film does NOT feel jingoistic, and it portrays all sides pretty fairly. You don't love the Americans and Canadians, more importantly you don't hate the Iranians. Everyone is just people, and they are living their lives how they can in shitty circumstances. Half star definitely awarded.

Cinematography: This film is phenomenally well shot. I generally don't like shaky cam, but thats because it usually appears in action scenes and makes them hard to see, which removes their one decent reason for existing. Shaky cam is used here alongside steady shots to create a very organic feeling world. I'm not even being hyperbolic at all when I say some of the footage looks like what a war correspondent would get filming a riot. The main point is that it looks great without looking cleaned up, studio great. I would see a film on mo other recommendation than that it had the same Director of Photography as Argo, that's how well it was shot. Half star given.

The Pacing: I'll admit, it starts slow. The first few minutes are pure exposition, the buildup drags on, and it's hard for maybe the first half hour. On purpose. The slow beginning feels like a news story because it was based on, and for all I know incorporated, real news stories of the time. An undefinable amount of time after the half hour mark however, it's like Ben Aflek magically flipped on the "You will now care about these characters" sign, and suddenly they are real people. People that you know. You have met, talked to, hung out with, been taught by these people. After that, pacing is irrelevant. The movie flows, and your body and mind are riding it. Half star granted with no reservation.

The Story: If someone had made this up you would absolutely call bullshit on it, and I would agree with you. However, I researched it a bit before I saw it, and this shit more or less actually happened, give or take a few details that are irrelevant to making a great and entertaining movie. If you are a person that insists that something be a perfect mirror image of the source material and will just hate anything over a small error, just save yourself the trouble and never see any movie ever again. For everyone else, there's this. I can only imagine what it would have been like if I hadn't spoiled the ending for myself. Half a star given for a stellar adaptation.

If you bother adding it up by category, that makes 4 stars out of 4 on the current edition of the Ted Scale, along with the strongest recommendation I will probably ever give for seeing a movie. If you haven't seen it yet, see it before it leaves theaters, it is worth it.

In  Ben Affleck's Argo, there are some grand-scale untruths, most notably the fact that it was Ken Taylor who took the hostages to the airport and not Affleck's hero, an intrepid CIA agent named Tony Mendez. Yet this - and a few other moments CIA-boosting 'truthiness' - didn't bother me while I watched the movie, probably because I didn't know about them at the time.
Now. In real life, the hostages went to the airport and got on a plane without a hitch. Naturally, this doesn't make for much of a 3rd act, so Affleck had to invent what are known as the 'stakes-risers.' For example: just before they go to the airport, president Jimmy Carter cancels the whole plan, leaving the hostages stranded. This impasses is solved by one of the CIA directors (played by Bryan Cranston) throwing a crimson-faced hissy fit, causing the entire White House to reconsider with just seconds to spare. It's all so ridiculously lifted from a Film-101 textbook that, as a viewer, you roll your eyes and move on, only to feel doubly cheated when the Iranians, realizing they've been hoodwinked, launch a runway car-chase just as that hostage's airplane is leaving the ground. 
Ironically, I think I would've like the movie a lot more had it been a flat-out fiction, as the 3rd-act suspense-builders wouldn't have bugged me so much. With it being a true story, however, I couldn't help but feel insulted by what the movie expected me to believe, and nothing kills a story faster than feeling like you're being patronized.
Yet here's the rub: if Affleck had stuck to the facts, the end would've been a snoozer. So. Is Hollywood's fondness for movies 'based on real events' an impediment to good film-making? After seeing Argo, I'm tempted to think so....

Neither as Good Nor as Bad as I'd Heard  

In the last week, I have seen three Best Picture nominees in the theatre.  All three started with a history lesson, even if it was as brief as a title card.  However, I think this one was the most important of the three.  Oh, the information we've been given for [i]Lincoln[/i] was brief, and I think the average American should have known all of it.  However, I do think we should be a little more aware of what our country has done, especially if we're going to be spending all that time wondering why people don't like us.  Ben Affleck lays out why the Iranians don't like us, why the Revolution had such great hatred of the American government.  It explains a lot about why Iran is the way it is today, which is something that is very important if we're going to understand our place in the world--and theirs.  That said, this movie was an awful lot more suspenseful because I couldn't remember any of the real-world details of how it ended.

The story really picks up in 1979.  The Shah (stock footage) has escaped to the United States, where he is undergoing cancer treatment.  The new revolutionary government demands that the US return him to be tried and executed; when the US refuses, Iranian students overrun the embassy and take the staff hostage.  The only people able to escape are six staffers who work in the visa office, the only building directly connected to the street.  They are finally able to find sanctuary at the home of the Canadian ambassador (Victor Garber).  However, that is not a situation that will last.  The State Department tries to come up with various plans to get the six people out.  However, CIA agent Tony Mendez (Affleck) does not believe any of them will work.  He develops a seemingly crazy plan that he insists is the only one that will work.  He will go to Hollywood and set up a fake movie production, and then he will go to Iran and bring out the six escapees as "crew" for the fake movie.

Most of the changes Affleck made in the story are for the purposes of heightening suspense.  Arguably the greatest sin is in failing to acknowledge the role the British and New Zealand embassies played in the escape.  Some people also took away from the movie that the Canadians barely did anything.  However, even if Ken Taylor and his wife, Pat (Page Leong), had just hidden their six house guests for all those weeks, that would be quite a lot.  Oh, and of course, there were the forged documents--the cover identities wouldn't have worked without the full support of the Canadian government.  I also felt that the CIA and the State Department were shown to be at best short-sighted.  After all, Mendez is the only one who suggests that perhaps claiming people are going to inspect crops doesn't work when there's still snow on the ground.  And, no, those last hours weren't quite so dramatic, but the story works better as a movie if you build suspense.

There are any number of places to the film that are better if you know film.  Oh, maybe not as well as Alan Arkin and John Goodman, or even their characters, but still.  Alan Arkin's Lester Siegel makes a throwaway reference to a lie sold to the public by Rock Hudson; in 1980, it's possible that Tony Mendez wouldn't have been sure what lie Hudson sold.  The Hollywood sign had actually been fixed by 1979, but only just barely, and I do think there's a certain symbolism to the sign's decay.  Goodman's John Chambers was a real person with his own honourary Oscar (1968; he did the makeup for [i]Planet of the Apes[/i]), but Chambers is shown making some terrible space opera with a minotaur in it.  Heck, Affleck even used the period-appropriate Warners logo.  It is also true, incidentally, that as producer, Mendez would be the one in charge.  Most people don't know that, though, and would assume that the director is the one in charge.  After all, the [i]auteur[/i] theory never mentions producers!

On the one hand, I am seriously impressed with this film, especially given how new to directing Ben Affleck is.  (I also thought his performance was considerably better than a lot of other people seem to believe.)  On the other hand, I really don't think that it's better than [i]Lincoln[/i].  Affleck seems a little enamoured of the Steadicam, and I'm not as fond.  The middle, the building of the background, is the strongest part of the film.  The beginning is weak, and the ending makes it a little too obvious to me that the chronology isn't quite accurate.  I like how the movie shows many examples of bravery above and beyond the call of duty; Sahar (Sheila Vand), the housekeeper at the Canadian ambassador's house, manages more strength than even some of the CIA characters.  Even the fact that the embassy staffers send the Iranians out first is a quietly brave moment.  They know all those people can be killed for trying to get to the US.  It would be easy for Affleck to center the film around his own character's bravery, but he makes it clear that there is enough to go around.

When George Clooney made his political thriller The Ides of March last year, I thought it suffered from too much cautiosness, with Clooney's imposed, seventies inspired finesse never quite finding the appropriate edge within the subject matter. Now comes Argo, originaly intended for Clooney, but later transferred to his directorial descendant Ben Affleck on his request. Some friendship!

Like The Ides, Argo covers the world of big politics, though some would argue that there is nothing more significant then the American presidential election. One big difference - Affleck doesn't want to be a political comentator like Clooney. More than a political thriller, his picture uses the aftermat of a serious political situation to draw out tension. A little irresponsibe? When you look at what event he has chosen as a setting and how he dealt with it, yes, definitely!

In the late seventies, as cute historical lession at the beginning points out, the Iranians overthrew Shah Mohamed Reza Pahlavi imposed by the USA and Britain some 25 years earlier. It was the starting point of Iranian Revolution, led by Ayatollah Khomeini, a classic example of evil regime replaced by something not many people wanted as a substitute. The shah was given shelter in the USA, something not met with approval back in his home country, where he has done some unworthy things during his time in charge.

The response was quick. After some verbal exchange between two authorities, the radicals decide that the convenient response would be the takeover of American embassy in Teheran. Before the military got in there, six of the employes managged to flee, and find shelter with the Canadian ambassador. A quick action from Washintong is required if they are to be saved before the information about their escape expands How to do it? Victorious proposition is one which includes filming a fictional film called Argo in Iran.

The amount of praise this picture has been getting is a true sign of the times. If the standards for pure popcorn entertainment have been sistematically lowered over the years, it would be futile to expect anything else in the area of "criticaly acclaimed films". Affleck deliberately shuns from establishing  a clear point of view. He is more than satisfied to just create an impression he has enough knowlage accumulated, and leave it linger somewhere between his oh so well constructed shots. It all comes down to the lines you pick up on the way, present more to show the wittiness of the writers than serious political stand. Since when have well crafted, tense thrillers devoid of any human interest or, in this case necessary poitical sharpness, become something to rave about?

Affleck doesn't measure the weight of making a film about a country he's never visited. Like many things in his picture, he just lets it be. The revolution was at the centre of turbulent times for Iran, bringing a shift in politics that was all but progrssive, and with the strong opposition from local intellectuals. Based on this, a viewer is tempted to think it can only be reduced to the hostage crisis. The sad thing is that the filmmakers can not be accused for bad intentions; just lack of bravery. That fact really bothered me, and note this comes for someone who greets historical adjustments if used tastefully within a context. Also, would emphasizing the cynicisam of using a money making machinery of Holywood in dealing with issues as large as these be too much to ask, even if shown in a film aiming for easy entertainment as this one does?

Few mention Affleck's participation as an actor. Being a lead player in a story this humanly numb, he doesn't need to act in a strict sense of the word, just lead us through the motions. This post contains plot spoilers for Argo.

Predictability can be an unpredictably lazy criticism. If a film feels too safe, if the plot's on rails from which it can't deviate, if you know the end from the beginning not because of omniscience but because you know the reality the film is based on, if it's simply evident from the start what's going to happen - all of these can be appropriate reasons for criticising a film. Not always, though; certainly not in the case of Argo.

The film is the third directorial outing for Ben Affleck; his first (Gone Baby Gone) was, for me, one of the most underrated films of recent years. Argo is taken from the recently declassified true story of the rescue of six fugitive American diplomatic staff from the chaos of Iran in 1980. The cover story under which the rescue was undertaken by a CIA-Canadian partnership was that of scouting Iran for locations in which to shoot an entirely fabricated movie production (the fake movie being 'Argo').

This isn't a story I knew. I knew some of the broader context, but nothing of the details - for me, that's a period of history that often falls into vague ignorance on account of being too young to take an interest at the time and it being too recent for much study.I thought I knew how the story would play out - I assumed some predictable plotting, my reasoning being that if this hadn't ended well the film wouldn't be made. In fact the reality is, on one level, even more predictable. The mechanics of the plot play out with precious few of the clichés you'd expect under fictional circumstances. If that feels like a spoiler, don't let it put you off - with all the predictability, it's funny, insightful and razor-wire tense.

The cast's performances are low-key and self-effacing - Affleck especially, whose role demands a kind of broken anonymity which he pulls of brilliantly. It's with these performances, and a script which gently sets context and propels plot that tension gradually creeps up on you. You feel - in a good way - like the proverbial frog in a kettle - only latterly aware that for two hours you've been in the grip of a slowly rising tension from which you can't escape even if you know what's coming. That included me and my wife with our lightly educated guesses at the conclusion and the unknown couple next to us who evidently knew the story well if their pre-film conversation was anything to go by. The script peppers wit throughout the film without ever breaking the dramatic moment. My favourite exchange? CIA strategists discussing if they're going to approve the fake film ('The Hollywood Option') plan to gain the fugitives' liberation:

Boss  - 'Don't we have a better bad idea than this?'

Employee - 'This the best bad idea we have, sir. By far'.

Economic, plot advancing, and I'm still chuckling to myself about it 2 days later.

The most moving aspect of the film snuck in under my radar in the closing minutes. Ben Affleck's character receives the news he's going to be lauded with the Intelligence trade's highest honour for his efforts to rescue the diplomatic staff. There's a catch  - because the mission still, even after completion, bears such a high degree of secrecy he'd receive the award at a ceremony with no-one else present, and would immediately have to return the award. No-one could know. No-one would then have known that President Clinton would be able to declassify the story; the story could easily have remained untold indefinitely. As his boss tells him, 'If we'd wanted applause, we'd have joined the circus'.

It struck me to the core. Wouldn't he want recognition from the country he'd served so bravely? Even if applause isn't granted, surely he'd have longed for it? As a Christian and as a leader, there are times when I feel the need to do (or not do) something. Sometimes I do the right thing, sometimes I don't. On the occasions I do get it more right than wrong, my heart suddenly yearns for approval, applause, recognition, validation. I can't talk about it though - to ensure confidentiality, to facilitate growth or simply because gaining recognition would defeat the purpose of doing it in the first place. I can suddenly move into a horrible version of jealousy at those who seem to get more recognition for doing the opposite (forgetting, of course, that I have no idea what God may be calling them to). Then I'm reminded of the audience of One who sees everything - my soft seduction into sin as well as my occasional good deed. To the One, I'm invited to keep open accounts. To confess, to tell things to, to ask for help and understanding. The words of my Biblical namesake help me. David - God-seeking, God-pleasing, adulterer, murderer, leader, David:

Search me, God, and know my heart;
    test me and know my anxious thoughts.
 See if there is any offensive way in me,
    and lead me in the way everlasting. 

(Psalm 139 verses 23-24, NIV)

David, a leader not of 60 people in a service on a Sunday morning, but millions in battle and politics; David, a broken failure who pleased God, kept clean lines with God, knows he's been heard, been seen, is forgiven and receives divine approval. David, for whom, on good days, the applause of One was enough.

May we who follow Jesus, may we who try to help others do so too, may we all have similar good days.

Ben Affleck the "director" is something of a new thing, he has just two other feature films under his belt, but "Argo" demonstrates a particularly seasoned approach to film-making that is a bit of a rarity these days.  The performances are fine, but the story-telling and especially the pacing of the film are, I hate to say it, examples of near cinematic genius.  Yes, the star of some of the worst movies ever made ("Daredevil", "Gigli", "Pearl Harbor") might actually be a genius behind the camera.  If Argo were merely a suspense/thriller/action film then this would be hyperbole, but Argo is considerably more than that.  Argo has comedy, feel-good patriotism, tension and a narrative that flows easily.  It's textbook story-telling/filmmaking that doesn't come off as manipulative.

Affleck stars as Tony Mendez, a CIA exfiltration expert who's called upon to try and figure out a way to exfiltrate 6 embassy workers trapped in Iran during the 1979 revolution.  The workers have been hiding at the home of the Canadian ambassador, but the revolutionaries are closing in on them.  There are several schemes for their escape floating about, from giving them bicycles and having them ride 300 miles to the border, to having them pose as crop inspectors (although as there was snow on the ground, it would be difficult for them to inspect anything).  Mendez' implausible, yet logical plan involves posing the six as a canadian film crew, out scouting locations for their upcoming sci-fi star fantasy, "Argo".  Mendez realizes in order to fool the Iranians, his bogus film must appear to be completely legitimate, and with the help of make-up specialist John Chambers (John Goodman) and producer Lester Siegel (Alan Arkin), Argo begins to take on a life of it's own.

Great films aren't necessarily about having a deep message, or discovering some profound truth, sometimes it's just about being very well made and unabashedly entertaining.  A great director like Hitchcock made populist films that were funny and suspenseful, but above all entertaining.  With Argo, Affleck seems to be following in those legendary footsteps.

Ben Affleck is now 3 for 3 as a Director. Argo may be the most boring movie Affleck has directed but it is probably his best. Argo hits on all cylinders, acting, directing, writing, cinematography, score, and even set design.

Affleck really put us into this semi-true story and made it come alive on screen. No cheap special effects or 3D bullshit, just a film the way it should be made. What I like about Affleck-Directed movies is they are so well-written and put together that no one actor sticks out, they are all fantastic and that shows that he gets the best out of all his actors, not just one.

You have got to hand it to Affleck for acting well in his own movies. He has always been known as kind of lesser actor in Hollywood but I have to admit he acts a hell of a lot better when he's behind the camera too. I guess the only Director who could truly tap his potential was himself. When he directs I find he is free as an actor to be better which is a really odd thing I don't think we've ever seen in Hollywood before.

I will say though Argo may be Affleck's best film on paper but it was by far the most boring of the three. I rank them Gone Baby Gone 1, The Town 2, and Argo 3. But that being said Argo feels more like a better polished Oscar-caliber film than the other two.

If you would have ever told me 10 years ago Affleck would become known as one of the best Directors in Hollywood I would have laughed my ass off but he's proving to be everything but the joke he has been considered for years. He has made 3 of the best films over the last few years and cannot be dismissed as a top 10 Director.

Now off Affleck for a second, the supporting cast was fantastically put together and on top of that they performed well. Whether it be Arkin, Goodman, Cranston, or even Affleck himself, everyone brought their A game to Argo. Also, I have to point out the writing by newcomer Chris Terrio. This was his second credit as a screenwriter and it's safe to say it was a coming out party of sorts. The writing was spot on which is so important with a period piece such as this.

Argo can be capped by saying it's one of those rare films that doesn't just have one strength to point out, it brings everything all together perfectly into one big mold.

Ben Affleck returns to the directors chair and stars in Argo, a groundbreaking film that documents the true events of one CIA agent's task of resucing American hostages from Iran in 1979. Affleck has proven his talents as director before with Gone Baby Gone and The Town, both films are nearly flawless in their own rights; but with Argo, Affleck has cemented himself as one of Hollywood's best with what may be considered as his masterpiece. Everything in this film is just done so expertly and delicately that it all just clicks in its own way. Every shot of the film is blended together perfectly with the footage shot for the film and footage from the actual news reports about the Iranian Hostage Crisis in 1979. Affleck just pieces them together to keep up the intensity and suspense. The suspense of this film is arguably the best part that should have gotten Affleck an Oscar Nod. Some part's of this film are more nerve racking than some of the scariest horror films ever put on screen. When the extrication of the hostages is occuring it seemed like my heart stopped for the rest of the film. We also get treated with some well placed comical relief to ease the stress and once again this is all credit to Ben Affleck. The script by Chris Terrio is so practical and simple that the film just flows naturally. Some films have these ellaborate scripts that off set the story and the characters because you don't believe they would say those things, but in Argo there is none of that. The simplicity just conquered and the film reeped all the benefits. The cast of this film is nothing short of top notch. Ben Affleck also steps in front of the camera to star as CIA agent Tony Mendez, the main character. Affleck really shows that he is capable of taking on both roles in a film. We saw that in The Town but we see it better here. The supporting cast of the film is absolutely outstanding with Alan Arkin leading the group. He adds the comedy where the film needs it and delivers arguably the most memorable one liner since The Hangover in 2009. Arkin simply delivers and almost steals the show. John Goodman plays John Chambers and really captures the man that inspired the role. His performance here ranks among some of his best in years. Rounding out the pack is Bryan Cranston as Jack O' Donnell. Cranston has become well known for his grit thanks to Breaking Bad and it carries over into Argo. When O' Donnell is mad you can feel the intesnsity and when he is glad you can see the joy. Cranston just reminds us that he can do just about anything in Hollywood. I really do not have many complaints about the film. If I was nit picking I would say that the film seemed to drag in the beginning and the pacing was off, but in all honestly, there really isn't that much wrong with this movie. It is smart, enticing, simplistic, genuine, and all together memorable. This is one of those films that you will hear alot of buzz about but this is also one of those films that is fully deserving. See this film as soon as possible.

But when all is done, I found "Argo" less than memorable. One point of contention is how it appeared to discredit the roles of other parties in the rescue mission. Still, I wouldn't be too displeased if it won, since "Argo" is an engrossing and dependable film.

Ben Affleck's latest bit of Oscar bait effectively balls up the tension, drama and political tripwires of the Iranian hostage crisis without feeling overly dense or inapproachable. An impressive, authentic collection of '70s wardrobe and scenery is partially to thank, with bad hair and cigarette smoke billowing about freely, and goes a long ways toward immersing its audience in the era. "Gone Baby Gone", "The Town", and now, "Argo". Ben Affleck scores a hattrick with three acclaimed films that exhibit his command behind the camera, and you'll probably find it tough to find anyone not convinced he makes a better director than in front of the camera as an actor. Producing the film with George Clooney and Grat Heslov, who did the award winning "Good Night, and Good Luck", "Argo" is also based on history (with its fair share of dramatic licence) that uniquely combined Hollywood's role during the tumultuous times of the Iran hostage crisis of the late 70's to 80's. 

In 1979, the American embassy in Iran was invaded by Iranian revolutionaries and several Americans are taken hostage. However, six manage to escape to the official residence of the Canadian Ambassador, and the CIA is eventually ordered to get them out of the country. With few options and with great concern, exfiltration expert Tony Mendez (Ben Affleck) devises a daring plan: to create a phony Canadian film project looking to shoot in Iran and smuggle the Americans out as as a production crew. Once the operation gets the green light from Washington, "Argo" goes to Hollywood, where a makeup man played by John Goodman and a producer played by Alan Arkin, advise Tony on how to set up a phony movie -- a shockingly easy feat in a town where, as Arkin's character observes, "people lie for a living." Like "Wag the Dog" before it, "Argo" takes full advantage of the overlap between trade craft and showbiz, depicting the movie industry as deceitful and vindictive. 

Working from a well-crafted script by Chris Terrio, Affleck threads viewers through the dauntingly geopolitics and tonal shifts of "Argo" with an utterly flawless sense of control, starting with an efficient, boldly graphic prologue explaining the roots of the Iranian Islamic revolution and putting viewers inside the U.S. Embassy in Tehran when it is stormed in November 1979. From the chaos of those moments and ensuing days, he moves to the home of Canadian ambassador Ken Taylor (Victor Garber), who has agreed to house six Americans who managed to escape the takeover. He then smoothly shifts back to Washington, where the State Department and the CIA weigh rescue options. 

There is a notable lack of on-screen bloodshed or violence, confident in it's story, plight and characters having the strength to invoke the thrills and edge-of-your-seat tension that makes it such a compelling view. Throw in the injection of humour, grounded as they are by being based on actual events. A surprisingly celebratory, feel-good tone that rather than dwelling on any political overtones or commentary, instead focuses on the spirit of camaraderie and co-operation. Technically, the production values are fantastic demonstrating great attention to detail paid in recreating production sets. The film quality is made to resemble something coming out of the era, relying also on archived footage to lend that documentary feel to the retelling of the "Canadian Caper", as it is known. 

A closing-credits side-by-side montage shows to what lengths Affleck has gone to re-create the real-life places and people of "Argo", but it's his command of his craft -- the staging, editing and judiciously calibrated unfolding of the story, especially its harrowing final moments -- that solidifies Mr. Affleck as a talented and formidable director. "Argo" deserves to find the discerning audience it has been made for: After all, if we buy tickets, that means more smart, sophisticated filmmaking.

Considered by both (American) movie goers and critics as one of the best movies of 2012, it is something of a propaganda piece but then a pretty good/honest one, reminding viewers American grievances against the Islamic regime in Iran over the last generation -- the taking of diplomats as hostages was something simply unheard of in the modern era until Iranian hostage crisis of October 1979- January 1981.

Though remembered largely in the United States as a time of, above all, humiliation, this film focuses on one of the few "bright spots" in this terrible episode ... the successful extraction of 7 American diplomats who weren't captured by the Iranian government organized mob that stormed the U.S. embassy but took refuge in the Canadian Ambassador's residence.

How to get the seven out? Well it wasn't easy. A cover story had to be concocted. The story that the CIA settled on was having an agent Tony Mendez (played by Ben Affleck) come to Tehran posing as Canadian film-maker looking to scout locations for a fake science-fiction movie called "Argo." The seven Americans would then be pulled out of Tehran under the guise of belonging to his "film crew." Was it a "lousy plan?" Yes, but it was the "best lousy plan" that the CIA had and it played on the Iranian regime's desire to portray itself as "normal," that is, eager to accept foreigners, if _not_ Americans, coming to their country "do business" even perhaps "making films."

Anyway, the film's based a true story and it offers a bright spot in an episode in American history that most of us Americans would probably want to forget.  -- Fr. Dennis at the Movies (http://frdennismoviereviews.blogspot.com/2012/10/argo.html)

The true star of this stunning political drama-thriller is Ben Affleck, the director.  Growing more assured in his third outing behind the camera, Affleck effectively exorcises the Ghosts of Shameful Blockbusters Past (Pearl Harbor, Gigli, anyone?) in proving to the world that he is a whip-smart, cast-iron filmmaker of class, wit, depth, vision and craft - and that he's here to stay.  Taking an unbelievable true story from a declassified 1970's CIA operation, Affleck tells his story with tension, politics, humour and an acute understanding of the politics of the time.  Deftly mixing America's political climate with its immediate storyline - the extraction of five American Diplomats hiding in Tehran's Canadian embassy during the Iranian Hostage Crisis of 1979 - the film is tense without being laborious, pacy without sacrificing content and time-sensitive without being incongruous.  Argo is a thriller that is sensitive and critical at the same time, moving at a deft, nimble speed, aided in no small measure by the cinematography of Rodrigo Prieto, who creates muted, hushed tones in recreating the 70's, Sharon Seymour's sensitive production design and the editor William Goldenberg's insightful, perceptive movement between scenes.  Affleck also shines in front of the camera as Tony Mendez, the man tasked with bringing in the five, who must pose as a film crew looking to make a Star Wars rip-off with Iran as its main location.  Bryan Cranston, Alan Arkin and the always dependable John Goodman also put in stellar work, but in the end, it is Affleck the director's show - a tour de force of pacing, tension, politics, and agile storytelling.  He would be well within his rights in dismissing anyone insinuating otherwise with the most unforgettable quip from the film: "Argo fuck yourself!"

Since bursting onto the Hollywood scene with 1997's "Good Will Hunting" (and winning an Academy Award for writing it), Ben Affleck has had a bit of a spotty career as an actor.  There were some good movies ("Dogma," "Changing Lanes," "Boiler Room") and there were some bad movies ("Pearl Harbor," "Phantoms, " "Surviving Christmas").  It's been up-and-down, but leaning more towards down.

As a director, however, he's 3 for 3.  In 2007, he directed his younger brother Casey in the complex, provocative "Gone Baby Gone."  In 2010, he delivered a crime thriller in the vein of Michael Mann's "Heat" with "The Town."  Now he's helmed his best film yet with the masterfully suspenseful and fact-based "Argo."
 
Like fellow Best Picture nominee "Zero Dark Thirty," we already know the outcome before going into the movie.  Also like that film though, "Argo" somehow manages to inject an extreme amount of tension into the proceedings, despite this.  Affleck displays an almost Hitchockian ability to create feelings of unease and wariness.  The fact that the movie also contains some rather humorous moments makes it an even bigger triumph.  I loved that I could go from wringing my hands in one scene to laughing out loud in the next.  This is a great film, perhaps the best of the Oscar nominees, along with "Django Unchained."  There's been some  minor controversy over the fact that Affleck did not get a nod for Best Director and now that I've seen the film, I can see why.  He most definitely got snubbed.
 
The backdrop of the film is the 1979 Iranian hostage crisis of the U.S. Embassy.  A bit of history: Iranian militants stormed the U.S. Embassy in Tehran, Iran and took its staff hostage.  They were demanding that the U.S. return their recently deposed Shah so that he could "stand trial" for the crimes he committed against their country.  Six employees managed to make it out of the embassy during the siege, and they took shelter in the home of the Canadian ambassador.  Knowing that it's only a matter of time before the militants figure out that some personnel are missing and begin conducting door-to-door searches, the CIA desperately tries to come up with a way to get the six Americans safely out of the country.
 
Enter Tony Mendez (Affleck), an exfiltration expert.  He comes up with a seemingly insane idea: he'll fly to Iran with paperwork for the embassy employees, and the seven of them will pose as a Canadian film crew on a location scout for an upcoming sci-fi movie.  In order to make this cover story as convincing as possible, the CIA actually had to commission this imaginary movie to be made.  They buy a script, entitled "Argo," and recruit a Hollywood producer (Alan Arkin) and special effects man (John Goodman) to assist in the process.  They hold casting calls, submit press releases, and create a film poster.  The lengths they went to to sell the cover story are astounding, but they were also, as it turns out, very necessary.
 
When Mendez arrives in Iran, the film really kicks into gear.  The suspense is ratcheted up in scene after scene, with the most intense arguably being the one in which the Americans actually go out in public to make it appear like they are scouting locations for their "movie."  This movie is filled with those white-knuckled, grip-the-theater-chair-arm-rest-as-hard-as-you-can moments.  What a life Tony Mendez must've lived; at one point, he tells the embassy staff, "This is what I do" and "I believe my cover story is the only thing between your head and a gun."  To come up with exfiltration missions and then carry them out as your daily job...I can't even imagine.
 
Affleck is very good in his understated performance as Mendez, but the real gems here are Arkin and Goodman, who inject the very welcome comic relief in between the scenes of almost unbearable anxiety.  "If I'm going to make a fake movie, it's going to be a fake hit," Arkin crows at one point, with one of his many funny lines.  The rest of the supporting cast is also strong, with a who's-who of reliable character actors such as Bryan Cranston, Victor Garber, and Phillip Baker Hall.
 
"Argo" tells the kind of story that, on its surface, seems too preposterous to be true.  How could anyone have pulled off such an insane scheme?  It's humorous to note that even the CIA knew how crazy the whole thing sounded.  "They're all bad ideas," states Cranston, as Mendez' superior, "but this is the best bad idea we have."  Perhaps the lunacy of the whole thing worked out in its favor; perhaps the Iranian officials just couldn't believe anyone could be so reckless.  Also, when considering how far Mendez and his crew went to portray their movie as the real deal, perhaps it's really not as surprising as one might think.

The irony of this whole thing is that the story sounds exactly like the plot of a Hollywood thriller, and now Affleck has made it into just that; art imitating life imitating art, as it were.  The real-life "Argo" never got made, but Affleck's "Argo" is an out-and-out triumph.  It seems to be the new favorite to win Best Picture, and truthfully I'm having a hard time coming up with arguments against that.

Generally, there are three themes that tend to be favored by award community and film critics, the winning themes are about humanity ("Schindler's List" {1993}, "The Shawshank Redemption {1994}, "Slumdog Millionaire" {2008}, etc.), patriotism ("Saving Private Ryan" {1998}, "Black Hawk Down" {2001}, "Lincoln" {2012}, etc.) and the world of cinema itself ("Cinema Paradiso" {1998}, "Hugo" {2011}, "The Artist" {2011}, etc.). Well, thiz movie has all three of them. Producer, Director and Actor Ben Affleck is smart enough to realize it and takes advantage of that. Ben Affleck is Tony Mendez, a CIA agent who is responsible for covert operation to extract six American embassy employees out of the rage of Iran revolutionary by pretending to be Canadian film crew.  It seems that Ben Affleck has done a tremendous job as the Director. He starts with an effective prologue to provide sufficient information and every time the scene heats up, particularly when the scene of American embassy is invaded, he cleverly adds relaxing piano instrumental music to cool things down and doesn't try to provoke audience into infuriated reactions. Thiz is his third feature films behind the camera after "Gone Baby Gone" (2007) and "The Town" (2010). For the acting, Ben Afflecks looks cool, calm and confident. John Goodman, Bryan Cranston and Victor Garber give brief but consistent performances and the last but definitely not least, Alan Arkin creates a powerful and believable emotion as fearless Hollywood Producer. Thiz is a good example of what you can get when great script and great editing are perfectly combined. My heart nearly stopped while watching thiz final scene which takes place in Iran airport. They use almost all aspects to create tensions from ticket, telephone, soldier, bus, you name it and they have done it. When it's over, there will be some satisfying and gratifying feelings. After a great directorial debut with "Gone Baby Gone" in 2007 and a brilliant sophomore effort with "The Town" in 2010, all eyes were on Ben Affleck in his third outing as director. Questions were asked as to whether he could do it again. And the answer? The answer is a resounding, 'Yes'. Argo completes Affleck's hat-trick behind the camera and confirms that he's definitely a director that has an abundance of talent and awareness.
 Based on true events in a post-revolution Iran in 1979. A mob of Ayatollah supporters storm the US Embassy and take 56 American hostages. 6 officers managed to escape, however, and take refuge in the home of a Canadian Ambassador. After two months in hiding and their sanctuary becoming increasingly risky, the CIA hatch a plan to get them home and extraction officer Tony Mendez (Ben Affleck) is given that responsibility. His plan is to create a fake movie called "Argo" and pretend that the six officers in hiding are his crew, scouting for shooting locations within the country.
 Before going into Argo, I admittedly expected a heavy-handed political thriller but that's not exactly what it delivers. Apart from the first five minutes of a brief overview of the, questionable, political relations between the U.S. and Iran, it sidesteps any political agenda and gets down to capturing the thrilling, human drama at it's core. I'm not adverse to political film's at all. In fact, I thoroughly enjoy them but Affleck is wise not to get too bogged down in boardroom banter and bureaucracy when there's an brilliantly exciting story to tell. It does share similarities with the great political tinged thrillers of the 1970's like Alan J. Pakula's "All The Presidents Men" or "The Parallax View". The late 70's and early 80's style is captured to perfection by cinematographer Rodrigo Prieto and Affleck's orchestration can sit comfortably beside any from that great decade of cinema.
 Chris Terrio's solid screenplay delivers many dialogue driven scenes but Affleck keeps things moving at a frantic pace and not for a second, does the film ever get dull or drawn out. The tension is almost unbearable at times. Why Affleck didn't, at the very least, nab an Oscar nomination for his substantial and well-constructed direction here is beyond me. There's no doubt that he's in complete command of his material as he leaps from Tehran to Washington to Tinseltown and delivers completely satisfying environments and effortless shifts in tone for the whole film to gel and come to life. He has the ability to capture a politically ravaged country; the backroom jargon of the CIA and the dark humour of Hollywood (that shares a strong resemblance to Barry Levinson's "Wag The Dog"). In order to capture this ludicrous, stranger-than-fiction story in it's entirety, it demands a maestro at work and Affleck can certainly consider himself one.
 This is the edge-of-your-seat tension that "Zero Dark Thirty" wishes it had. With only three film's under his hat, you'd be forgiven for thinking that Affleck has been at this directing malarky for a very long time. The comparisons with actor, turned quality director, Clint Eastwood will rage on and if anyone thinks otherwise, then Affleck can tell them to "Argo fuck yourself".

This film wouldn't be doing its job as a rescue thriller too well if it disregarded the people who our protagonists were going to rescue, especially when their subplot merges with the core story half-way through the film, so of course, before Ben Affleck's Tony Mendez character confronts the hostages about an hour into this film, storytelling switches focus onto the hostages in Iran, whose story's presentation is inspired enough to compel and all, but would have been even more engaging if the hostage point-of-view switches didn't feel rather obligatory, to where the film jars into its crucial, but repetitious subplot with little grace, thus sparking a bit awkward focal unevenness. If nothing else's consistency is thrown off by sudden focal shifts, then it's tone's consistency, as this film's core story will often keep up a lively atmosphere, only to swiftly shift into darker notes with the presentation of people who are pretty much just sitting around, waiting to die, which isn't to say that tonal inconsistency occurs only when we switch focus onto the hostages' subplot, because even though this film is generally organic in its tonal layers, there come times in which the film finds itself too eager to abandon all of the fun and games and get into more tense moments that are indeed effective, but would have been more potent if their incorporation wasn't so sudden. Needless to say, the lack of full assurance in tonal dynamicity dilutes this film's kick, though it's not like the film at least keeps consistent in having a firm grip on the intrigue within whichever tone its focusing upon in the first place, because as entertaining and compelling as this film is, slow spells never drift too far away from pacing momentum, not quite looming over this film as much as they did in Affleck's previous effort, "The Town", but being pronounced enough to bland things up a smidge, and help in making shifts in pacing every bit as inorganic as shifts in tone and focus. Pacing is generally tight and gripping in this film, but grip goes loosened time and again by a kind of awkward unevenness in pacing that has this film dancing between smooth and gritty in progression so often that, after a while, repetition hits rears its ugly head into things, leaving you to slowly, but surely predict the next beat in this film's formula, which is so engaging, but not enough to obscure Affleck's further proving that he's just not entirely ready to be the directorial heavyweight that many people are calling him. Each one of his three films, including this one, acclaimed, Affleck, as director, is recieving a lot of praise as a revelatory filmmaker, and I'm happy to pay Affleck some pretty high compliments, as I have found every one of his films, including this one, rewarding, yet I couldn't ever shake some sense of awkwardness within Affleck's previous efforts, as surely as I can't fully shake some sense of awkwardness within this effort, which is inspired enough to compel thoroughly, same as "Gone Baby Gone" and "The Town", but not as assured as it should be. Tonally, Affleck feels a bit distanced as storyteller, and that gives you enough time to meditate upon all of the unevenness and repetition that can't battle back this film's reward value, but holds the final product back when it comes to achieving full potential. Nevertheless, this film accles more than it trips up, being neither as smoothly structured or confidently told as it should be, but still charged enough to sustain your investment through and through, while the film's musicality helps in sustaining entertainment value.

Set in the final days of the 1970s, as well as so soon in the early days of the '80s that some cheesy '80s tunes don't have enough time to kick in, this film boasts the potential to deliver on an awesome soundtrack, and sure enough, while this film's mainstream soundtrack isn't too heavily played up, you can expect plenty of lively '70s tunes - from Booker T. and the MG's' "Hip Hug-Her" and Van Halen's "Dance the Night Away", to Dire Strait's "Sultans of Swing" and Led Zeppelin's "When the Levee Breaks" - to liven things up, while Alexandre Desplat delivers on a score that isn't too upstanding or refreshing, but still quite strong in its diverse and atmospherically pronounced kick and rhythm to both entertain and add a bit of color to this film's substance. What further adds to the kick of this thriller is, of course, William Goldenberg's editing, which occasionally gets to be kind of overbearing its being so actively tight, but is generally just comfortable enough in its tightness to really grip, slickly snapping footage together with a nifty storytelling style that both augments liveliness and helps you in getting a grip on the freneticism that drives much of this film's intrigue. Musically and technically, at the very least, the film accels with just enough assurance to spark a sense of style that breathes quite a bit of life into this film's substance, though it's not like substance needs such reinforcements a style to earn your investment, being gripping in concept, alone. There are times when real life offers a better story than any Hollywood writer could possibly come up with. This is the case with Argo. Argo tells the real life story of how a CIA operative named Tony Mendez (Ben Affleck), rescued 6 American embassy workers from Iran under the facade of a fake movie. 

After movies like Gone Baby Gone, The Town, and now Argo Ben Affleck has quietly become one of the better directors out there. The fact that he is not nominated for a best director Oscar this year is a serious snub. Argo is by far his best work and I will not be surprised when it is this year's best picture. 

Across the board the acting in this movie is top notch. They did a fantastic job in casting for this movie.  Ben Affleck is great as the lead and you can tell he poured himself into this picture. Jon Goodman and Alan Arkin are both very entertaining as his Hollywood support team. Lastly, Bryan Kranston is fantastic as Affleck's CIA boss. Kranston is a seriously underrated actor and needs to start getting some lead roles.

The key of putting together a good thriller is the right mix of suspense and enough character development that you are invested in the characters. Argo nails this on the head. You are rooting for these characters to succeed from the get go. There are a few parts of the movie that I did find slow and the family issues that Mendez deals with seem to be just tacked on for the sake of showing his life outside his job. These however, are very minor complaints on what is otherwise a fantastic movie. 
This year is going to be very interesting when it comes to best picture.  Argo, Zero Dark Thirty, or Lincoln could come away winning best picture and I would be okay with any of them. Argo is one of the shining moments in the history of the CIA and is a story worth knowing. If you haven't seen this movie yet, go out and see it!!!

Overall 9 out of 10:  adding to what is already one of the best years ever for spy movies.

I don't usually go out of my way to see political thrillers. If I catch them on a lazy Sunday afternoon, I'll end up liking most of the ones I watch. "Argo" is one of those movies I would have passed up watching had it not been for one catch. The idea of the government using the making of a fake space / fantasy film to free hostages from Iran intrigued me. Once again, I'm very glad I listened to my instincts and took it in.

In 1979, six Americans are put in hiding by the Canadian Embassy when the U.S. Embassy is raided in Iran by militants. Everyone else in the building is taken hostage. The U.S. government decides to take the unconventional advice of CIA operative Tony Mendez (Ben Affleck) to get the six diplomats out of the country. He will enter Iran and smuggle them out as a group of filmmakers scouting for shooting locations for a fake science fiction / fantasy film entitled "Argo."

Ben Affleck continues to surprise me. He's always done his own thing in Hollywood. He'll do smaller films playing less conventional characters like "Dazed and Confused," "Mallrats," and "Chasing Amy." The next thing you know he's taking the lead in blockbusters and popcorn flicks such as "Armageddon," "Daredevil," "Pearl Harbor," and "The Sum of All Fears." Affleck's had his share of stinkers and received some unwanted attention in the tabloids as well. What actor hasn't?

One thing Affleck has done is prove he's a versatile talent in Tinseltown and isn't going away any time soon. He won an Oscar for his "Good Will Hunting" script and continues to collect awards for "Argo." The movie is nominated for an Oscar for "Best Picture" and it deserves the honor.

"Argo" appealed to me in so many ways. I was born in 1972 and was completely caught up in "Star Wars," "Star Trek," and "Planet of the Apes" fevers. A movie based in that time period about people making a fake sci-fi movie as a front to save hostages is captivating.

Add to that the fact that award-winning "Planet of the Apes" makeup artist John Chambers helped the government get the hostages out of Iran. I remember seeing the news broadcasts about the hostage situation as a boy, but I didn't understand what was going on at the time. The whole event is interesting to learn about.

"Argo" is an exciting political thriller which will have you white-knuckled and gripping the edge of your seat. Director Ben Affleck did a great job keeping up the suspense and pacing in the film. Even though you know how it's going to end, you are still nervous for the characters as you watch. That's just good filmmaking in my book.

Well, what can I say?  I had been wanting to catch this for a while but I was out of the country when it was playing near me, so I missed it.  But after it won the Oscar for Best Picture this year I made an effort to download it and watch it.  
First of all, out of all the other films nominated in the same catagory, I think Argo definitely deserved to win the award.  It's extremely tense in the exact places it needs to be, and since I made a point of not researching the real events the film is based on, I genuinely didn't know how things were going to "go down" (Although, of course, I assumed they'd succeed)  But Affleck has done such a good job that even though I subconsciously "knew" what was going to happen, I didn't know at the same time, if that makes any sense?  
It also uses humour very well.  I'm not saying it's a funny film by any means, but when comic relief is employed it does so extremely effectively.  
If I have any criticism (There isn't much I didn't like) I would have liked the film to delve a little deeper into Ben Affleck's strained relationship with his wife, and how he copes being so far away from his son.  It's briefly touched upon early in the film, but I feel if it was done a little more extensively, we as an audience would have felt even more tense and nervous during the Iran hostage extraction because there would have been a whole lot more for Ben Affleck to lose.  
So yes, a very tight and well done film that hits all it's marks very well.  It's still not my favourite film of 2012, but that doesn't take away from how good I think it is.

"Argo" is based on the real events surrounding the 1979 Iran hostage crisis when nearly 70 US embassy employees were taken hostage by protesting Iranian students.  Six employees escaped and eventually were able to hide at the Canadian embassy. But the real adventure is their harrowing escape from manufactured by the CIA and the Canadian government,

November 4th 1979, Iranians violently stormed the American Embassy and siezed hostages for 444 days. It was an intense and frightening era in modern history; this film chronicles the daring operation to rescue six of the hostages after they fled the besieged embassy.

I'm not at all familiar with the Iranian Hostage Crisis, so I have no idea how much of Argo is fiction and how much of it is fact (reading up on it, I see that the film is criticized for over-emphasizing the role of the CIA, and for presenting more peril than what really happened). Regardless, the film made the events feel very real. The film does it best to replicate the era, the settings, and the danger to immerse the viewers into the situation and make them feel the suspense. I certainly felt the suspense, as the characters ran up against all manner of political, diplomatic, and cultural barriers in a frantic race to escape a treacherous and unstable country. The film definitely kept my attention and had me at the edge of my seat.

The story is well-told, presenting its ideas and sequence of events on a manner that's both logical and sensical. Even though there is a lot of political intruige involved, the film never looses its audience with jargon or politics. It also looks and feels very realistic; despite some thrilling scenes, the events appear plausible and the various interactions between people and governments appear authentic. Characters have just enough depth and emotion to make audiences care for them, and once again, come off as seeming authentic.

Even the film itself feels authentic, featuring some rough and gritty-looking camera work and editing. The camera is steady and solid, as is the editing, but it looks like a film that could have been made in the 70s, due to the way it's composed and put together. Same goes for its production design, which goes to great lengths to replicate genuine-looking sets, props, and costumes. Acting is decent: Ben Affleck is surprisingly strong in his role, Bryan Cranston is a fun to watch as ever, and everybody else fulfills their parts admirably. Writing is great. Music isn't bad either.

Argo might just stand as a new favorite among political thriller movies; it's certainly one of the most real-looking and historically interesting films I've seen in the genre. Above all, it's intense enough to maintain interest.  Recommended!

"Argo fuck yourself." After watching Argo post Oscar ceremony, I remain unconvinced that the film warranted the top prize at the award ceremony, as well as the best writing award. While the film itself was well made, it was never stellar or mind blowing. The story follows CIA agent Tony Mendez as he tries to get six Americans out of Iran by posing as a Hollywood filmmaker to get them out safely. Admittedly the finale was tense and thrilling but there was nothing bold or riveting about the film that gave it the privilege to be called the best picture of the year. Fun, simple and safe, Argo is not a bad piece of entertainment, but when the ever deviant line "based on a true story" comes up on screen, in this case it looses merits as Affleck took some creative liberties with the story, specifically the role of the Canadians in the film. While Affleck's Mendez's story is the focal point and was the part that was hushed by the government, the portrayal of the Canadian involvement in the "Canadian Caper" as it was called was cut very short, making the involvement almost none existent. Of course I was not around during this event and I did not know about the caper before Argo, but that's not to say what Hollywood says is true. Also, the film never reveals the fate of the other hostages left in the American Embassy, where the film opens up, leaving that piece of information  very open and unfinished. So if you want a fun, quick, easy spy thriller that doesn't get political, Argo is a fun distraction. If you wanted a deep political thriller with answers, well you may want to finance your own movie.

All'inizio della crisi degli ostaggi in Iran, un piccolo gruppo fuoriuscito dall'ambasciata degli Stati Uniti durante l'assalto alla stessa finisce per ritrovarsi in una posizione più pericolosa rispetto ai diplomatici rimasti prigionieri: riparati in casa dell'ambasciatore canadese, non hanno addosso gli occhi del mondo e ogni giorno che passa il rischio di venir scoperti e processati aumenta. Per portarli a casa, la Cia si inventa un falso film di fantascienza, 'Argo', da girarsi in esotiche locations persiane: sul filo del rasoio, l'operazione riesce, ma l'agente Mendez - che il tutto ha apparecchiato e portato a termine - non può ricevere i pubblici elogi fino a quando Clinton, vent'anni dopo, non toglie il segreto sulla missione. Per raccontarne la storia, l'esordiente Affleck gira un film d'azione senza pecche, basato su di una sceneggiatura di Chris Terrio che segue la traccia dei fatti drammatizzandone alcune parti (una questione che appare secondaria, non trattandosi di un documentario). Nella prima ora, la tensione si stempera grazie ai tocchi di commedia che si possono trovare nei dialoghi serrati all'interno dell'Agenzia e durante la parentesi holliwoodiana (alcune battute sono un po' telefonate ma pazienza...), poi il ritmo si fa sempre più serrato, fra montaggio incrociato - con qualche discrepanza sui fusi orari - e possibili pericoli evitati per un soffio che lasciano con il fiato sospeso. L'occhio del regista restituisce in modo efficace un mondo del tutto analogico, fatto di telescriventi e grossi nodi alla cravatta, raggiungendo i risultati migliori negli interni ambientati a Langley e inquadrati come negli anni Settanta. Alla riuscita collabora un cast esperto e ben assortito, in cui - oltre all'Affleck attore, con barba e capello lungo molto Seventies - spiccano Cranston (il capo duro ma sensibile) e, soprattutto, la coppia Arkin/Goodman che, a Los Angeles, fornisce la base logistica al falso film strappando anche qualche sorriso: in confronto, risultano meno definiti i sei in fuga, con il solo Scoot McNairy che ha la possibilità di rendere un po' meno bidimensionale il suo personaggio, il più dubbioso nei confronti del piano di Mendez. Detto tutto questo, e confermato che le due ore scorrono veloci e coinvolgenti, lascia perplessi che 'Argo' sia stato preferito a 'Lincoln' nella corsa agli Oscar e l'unico motivo che pare plausibile è l'eccesso patriottico. Non che il film di Spielberg manchi di retorica a stelle e strisce, ma vuoi mettere un film ambientato un secolo e mezzo fa che parla di una spaccatura interna non del tutto superata neppure oggi con uno costruito attorno a un momento storico che tantissimi di noi hanno vissuto e ha il pregio di poter nettamente separare i buoni dai cattivi? Se non fosse per il prologo - in cui si accenna alla responsabilità anglo-americana nella caduta di Mossadeq che spianò la strada al feroce regime di Reza Pahlavi - la Cia ne esce candida come un giglio (e alla fine rinuncia anche ad appuntarsi la medaglia al merito) mentre gli iraniani sono rappresentati, a parte la barba, alla stregua degli indiani dei film di una volta - violenti, urlanti e pure un po' tonti: se è un dato di fatto che la Rivoluzione Islamica non sia stata un pranzo di gala, la banalizzazione risulta comunque fastidiosa.

Introduction

This film is about a secret CIA operation in 1979 that saved 6 hostages that escaped from Iranian control and were in hiding.

Plot Summary

In this movie, a riot starts in Iran at a US embassy and they capture about 40 people. Six US ambassadors escaped and went into hiding at the Canadian embassy. The CIA found out they escaped and started to try and come up with ideas on how to get them out. They agreed on an idea to make a fake movie and say they were scouting locations to film in Iran. They came up with a fake script and storyboard and everything to make it as believable as possible. To get them out, they would say that the six of them were part of the production crew. The man that came up with the idea went to Iran and ended up getting them all out just barely. He later was presented with the highest award a civilian can receive for his brave actions.

Awards Won

This movie won the award for best picture in 2013. I think this is justified because when I was watching this, it seemed to have very good camera angles and picture.

Themes

I think the theme of this movie is stick together. I think this because the six of them that escaped stuck together and never left each other. Also, the US didn't forget about them and went and saved them.

Technical Elements

This film had very creative camera angles and very good picture. Which is probably why it won best picture. Also on very suspenseful moments, they would add very suspenseful music to it. This made the movie very engaging. Overall this film had very good technical elements.

Conclusion

This film was very good. I would highly recommend for people to watch this. One because it is a very engaging movie, and it also it is a true story so you can learn a lot from it. Overall this was a very great film and I can see why it won an award.

Marvelous true story of the political thriller film. Congratulations to Ben Affleck for his Oscar (R) winner in this film's Best Picture at the first time, believe me it's his second Oscar (R) since he was awarded for his 1998's Best Original Screenplay in Good Will Hunting with Matt Damon. And it was disappointed Affleck wasn't entitled to be nominated for the Best Director Oscar (R). 
In the past five years, Affleck has mad the kind of comeback usually reserved for Rocky films. having been written off as "the least talented one" in the Affleck-Damon combo, the lantern-jawed actor has found a second life as a director with two acclaimed films. here he adds "producer" to the mix and sets about proving his "Bennifer" days are long behind him.
Based on the true story of a covert operation that was declassified in 1997, Argo sets about weaving together multiple elements with great efficiency: a handy history lesson on the conflict within Iran segues into armrest-gripping tension as 52 Americans are taken hostage from the US Embassy in 1979. Soon we're deep within the bowels of the CIA as troubled exfiltration specialist Tony Mendez (Affleck) relays "the best bad idea we've got" to the Powers That Be on how to save the six diplomats: enter Iran under the pretense of location scouting for a film, then smuggle out the quarry as crew members.
The film then successfully shifts tone as Mendez hits LA and Argo briefly becomes a biting (and hilarious) Hollywood satire. Alan Arkin steals every scene he's in as a wily producer who helps Mendez; John Goodman a delight as the make-up artist assisting in the charade. It's a short breather before the movie kicks back into "political thriller" mode as the director skillfully ratchets up the tension to unbearable levels.
Affleck again proves himself a talent behind the camera: Argo is well paced and several story strands are juggled skillfully. He's ably assisted by an A-grade cast: Bryan Cranston as a CIA higher-up, six relative unknowns as the diplomats and Goodman and Arkin in fine form. And proving he's better off directing himself, Affleck is solid as a CIA man-on-the-edge who everyone thinks is on a suicide mission. The sharp screenplay from Chris Terro is terrific, and despite a tying-up-the-loose-ends finale that reminds you you're still watching a Hollywood film, this is a triumph for all involved.

Ben Affleck's Argo, his third feature is a consummate piece of work. From the direction including the incorporation of archival footage in a delicate yet effective fashion really lent itself to the time period and the mayhem that was sweeping the nation and the world at the time. Several standout stars - Alan Arkin and John Goodman in particular really brought the work to new heights. However, there were several glaring issues with the script including an unnecessary and very cartoonish opening sequence that didn't let things off with a bang. Also, being that this film was supposed to be so focused on the hostages and their mission the hostages themselves barely got any lines of dialogue which seemed counterproductive to the action at stake. The most obvious and unfortunate issue with the whole film is the immense screen time that Ben Affleck took up himself. Many of those scenes were wasted with close ups of his eyes, smirking or brooding. All in all though, an impressively mounted and faithful production but nothing to really write home about.

It did not take long for to know that Argo would be a great film. Directed and starring by Ben Affleck (Reindeer Games, Phantoms), Argo tells the true accounts of a declassified operation launched by CIA during the hostage crisis in Iran. The film opens up with a prelude into Iranian history, setting up the events of the film. It is 1979 and Shah or Iran flees the turbulent country. The people still unhappy and looking to even the score, seize the United States Embassy in Tehran taking a number of hostages. However, six workers have managed to escape and hide in house of a Canadian ambassador. Back in the US, the country is in cahoots with half of the Americans hoping and praying for the release of the hostages while the other half take vengeance on the mosques, Iranian flags, and people. The politicians are running around in circles while Jimmy Carter makes it clear they do not negotiate with terrorist. The CIA is pretty much bewildered, but find out six employees have escaped. They try and figure out a plan. This is when Tony Mendez comes in played by a shaggy Ben Affleck. He notices and objects to all the terrible plans proposed from bike riding out of Iran to farmers to Tehran while there is snow. Okay, you figure it out then Mr. Smart Pants. While on the phone with his son, Tony suddenly gets an idea while watching Battle for the Planet of the Apes. Why don't we make a fake movie and set it in Iran and have the hostages pose as our crew to get them out! His supervisor Jack O'Donnell and him then contact John Chambers (John Goodman). Chambers then gets producer Lester Siegel (Alan Arkin) to produce the fake film only on one condition: if I am gonna make a fake movie, it is going to be a fake hit!The film then transpires into a story of hope and determination. Tony tries to keep the mission going despite doubt and skepticism from superiors. Scripts are looked for possible production until a scripted titled Argo is chosen.  When asked what does Argo stands for, Siegel replies "Argo f**k yourself!" This fake film is will be in the spirit or more correctly, Star Wars rip off. The plans is "hi, we are Canadians looking to make a movie, so I came here to Iran for that exotic location." Get to Canadian ambassador and pick up the six Americans and have them play Canadians and then get to the airport and get out! Director Ben Affleck then takes us inside Iran. There is not a whole lot of personalities and identities just shots here and there along with turmoil going around the country. He meets up with the six which feel rather mixed at the idea. Tony does not have a lot of time because sooner or later the Iranian government is going to find out six embassy employees have escaped and will hunt them down. Director Affleck delivers a strong and effective film. It was intense watching this film as days go and every minute is crucial for the mission. Despite the turmoil, there are some delightful, feel good, and entertaining moments with Arkin stealing most of the laughs. Affleck also manages to deliver a darn good performance even though he also was in the director's chair. Goodman and the supporting cast are excellent in their parts. Now, like all films based on a true story, there are controversies. First, I am not sure about the history in the film; however, I do believe there are significant inaccuracies since this is history according to Hollywood. I also believe some scenes were added to jerk us around especially in one climatic scene. Argo does generalize some crucial points prior to the Iranian revolution, but was there any depth to it? I would imagine, but that is another film for another time. Anyways, it did not take too long for the film to click inside my head. I immediately sat back and watched the film. It is also no wonder it won Best Picture at the Academy Awards.

Argo, directed and starring Ben Affleck (The Town), is centred around the 1979 Iran hostage crisis and the efforts of one CIA agent, Tony Mendez (Ben Affleck). When the embassy in Iran gets raided, and seized by Islamic militants, six American diplomats managed to escape and find secret sanctuary with the Canadian ambassador. Months later, Mendez devises an audacious plan to get the six diplomats back to America, posing as a film crew looking for locations to shoot, along with the help of John Goodman (The Big Lebowski, Flight) and Alan Arkin (Little Miss Sunshine).

I feel as a whole Argo is the weakest Best Picture winner in many, many years. Although a technically very sound film, it suggests that the film business can solve the world's problems, including terrorism. For this reason I can see why those in Hollywood love this picture.

The film is well directed, I am under the opinion that Ben Affleck can direct anything that he is given, yet, for me, Affleck is better suited to Boston thrillers, he should stick to what he knows.  Furthermore, it's interesting that his portrayal of Tony Mendez is one that focuses on his trusting nature and smarts in terms of his mission, yet it fails to question Mendez' separation from his wife. It seems to me that that sub-story is just included so that it will form a nice ending when his wife takes him back.

One thing that surprised me about Argo is that the story expands in an oddly uncomplicated and non-shocking way. This creates a much more believable environment. If this film was a fiction, and not 'based on truth', there would be many more plot twists, or tense encounters that would dramatise and, in a sense, take the film too far into the realms of a Hollywood, fiction, action/thriller.

An extremely enjoyable film, although not Affleck's best.
